fig.cap: The four answer choices with the α-carbon shaded and its four groups listed. Only glycine's α-carbon carries two identical groups (two H atoms).
fig.alt: Structures of alanine, proline, glycine and cysteine. Alanine is chiral S, proline chiral S, glycine achiral with groups H, H, NH₃⁺ and COO⁻, cysteine chiral R.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.1 Structures of Amino Acids

ox: Not quite. Alanine's α-carbon holds four different groups: H, a CH₃ side chain, the amino group and the carboxyl group. Four different groups make a stereocenter, so alanine comes in two mirror-image forms (L and D). A methyl group is small, but small isn't the same as identical to H.

Not quite. Proline's side chain loops back and bonds to its own amino nitrogen, making a five-membered ring. Even so, the α-carbon still has four different neighbors: H, a ring CH₂, the ring nitrogen and the carboxyl carbon. The ring makes proline stiff, not symmetric, so its α-carbon is still a stereocenter.

Correct. A stereocenter is a carbon bonded to four different groups. Glycine's side chain is just a hydrogen, so its α-carbon holds two identical H atoms plus the amino and carboxyl groups. With two matching groups, glycine is identical to its mirror image, so it has no L or D form and no R or S label. It's the only standard amino acid that isn't chiral.

Not quite. Cysteine is chiral: its α-carbon holds H, CH₂SH, the amino group and the carboxyl group, all different. People remember it because natural L-cysteine is labeled R instead of S, but that's just a naming quirk caused by sulfur's high priority in the ranking rules. An unusual label doesn't mean there's no stereocenter.

p: A carbon is a stereocenter (chiral center) when its four attached groups are all different. Then the molecule and its mirror image can't be stacked on top of each other, like your left and right hands. Those two mirror-image forms are called enantiomers.

Every standard amino acid has an α-carbon bonded to H, an amino group, a carboxyl group and a side chain (the R group). Glycine is the one exception to chirality: its R group is H, so two of the four groups match. The other 19 are chiral, and threonine and isoleucine even have a second stereocenter in their side chains.

Keep two questions separate. First: is the carbon chiral (four different groups)? Second: what's its label (L/D or R/S)? Cysteine is chiral but labeled R, and proline's ring doesn't remove its chirality.

x1A_001.trap: Look for two identical groups on the carbon. Only glycine (H and H) lacks a stereocenter. An odd R/S label doesn't mean a molecule isn't chiral.

fig.cap: Fischer projections of L- and D-alanine. With COO⁻ on top and the side chain at the bottom, the amino group is on the left in the L form used by ribosomes.
fig.alt: Two Fischer projections. L-alanine has NH₃⁺ on the left and H on the right and is labeled S and used by ribosomes. D-alanine has H on the left and NH₃⁺ on the right and is labeled R and found in bacterial cell walls.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram drawn from coordinates.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.1 Structures of Amino Acids

ox: Correct. Human ribosomes build proteins only from L-amino acids. The enzymes that load amino acids onto tRNAs (aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases) and the ribosome itself are 'handed' molecules, so they only accept the L form. If you draw an L-amino acid as a Fischer projection, with the COO⁻ at the top and the side chain at the bottom, the amino group sits on the left.

Not quite. D-amino acids are the mirror images of the L forms. They do exist in nature, like D-alanine and D-glutamate in bacterial cell walls and in some antibiotics, but enzymes outside the ribosome make those. The ribosome doesn't put D-amino acids into human proteins.

Not quite. A racemic mix is 50:50 of both mirror images, which is what you get from a simple lab reaction that doesn't care about handedness. Living things do care: the loading enzymes and the ribosome pick one form only. A protein made from a random mix couldn't fold into one reliable shape.

Not quite, and it's wrong in two ways. First, R/S is a different labeling system from L/D, so you can't swap one for the other. Second, most L-amino acids are actually S. Only L-cysteine (and selenocysteine) is R, because its sulfur (or selenium) changes the priority ranking.

p: Most amino acids are 'chiral': they come in two mirror-image forms that can't be stacked on top of each other, like your left and right hands. L and D are the names for those two forms. To tell them apart, draw a Fischer projection with COO⁻ at the top and the side chain at the bottom. If the NH₃⁺ is on the left, it's L. If it's on the right, it's D.

Ribosomes only use L-amino acids to build proteins. D-amino acids still show up in biology, in bacterial cell walls, some antibiotics, and as signals like D-serine in the brain, but they aren't built into proteins by ribosomes.

R and S are a separate system based on ranking the four groups around the carbon. The two systems don't line up neatly: most L-amino acids are S, but L-cysteine is R. Glycine is neither L nor D, because its side chain is just H, so it has no mirror-image form.

x1A_002.trap: Treating L/D and R/S as the same thing. They're separate systems, and most L-amino acids are S, not R.
x1A_002.plain: Your proteins are built from 'right-handed gloves' only. The cell's machinery is shaped to fit one hand, so the mirror-image version just doesn't get used.

fig.cap: L-serine, L-methionine and L-cysteine have the same 3D arrangement, but only in cysteine does the side chain outrank the carboxyl, so only cysteine is R.
fig.alt: Structures of L-serine (S), L-methionine (S) and L-cysteine (R) with side chains shaded and the CIP priority list for each: for cysteine, NH₃⁺, CH₂SH, COO⁻, H.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 5.5 Sequence Rules for Specifying Configuration

ox: Not quite. In L-serine the groups rank NH₃⁺ first, then COO⁻, then CH₂OH, then H. The carboxyl carbon counts as (O, O, O) (the C=O double bond counts its O twice), while the CH₂OH carbon has only (O, H, H). The carboxyl wins at the first difference, so serine keeps the usual order and is S like most amino acids.

Not quite. Methionine does contain sulfur, but it's two carbons away from the α-carbon. The first side-chain carbon carries (C, H, H), which ranks below the carboxyl carbon's (O, O, O). The usual order holds, so L-methionine is S. Sulfur only flips the label when it sits on the very first side-chain carbon.
Not quite. Glycine has two H atoms on its α-carbon, so it isn't a stereocenter and gets no R or S label (and no L or D either). A molecule with no stereocenter can't be the exception to an R/S rule.

Correct. In L-cysteine, the atoms touching the α-carbon are N, C, C and H, so N ranks first. To break the tie between the two carbons, look at what's on each: CH₂SH has (S, H, H) and COO⁻ has (O, O, O). Compare the biggest atoms first: S (16) beats O (8), so CH₂SH ranks second and COO⁻ third. The 3D shape matches other L-amino acids, but swapping ranks 2 and 3 turns the label from S to R.

concept.t: Ranking groups for R and S (CIP rules)
p: To label a stereocenter R or S, you rank its four groups. The rule is simple: the atom with the higher atomic number wins. If two groups start with the same atom, like two carbons, you list what's attached to each one and compare those lists, biggest atom first. The first difference decides it.

In most L-amino acids, the ranking goes NH₃⁺ first, COO⁻ second, the side chain third and H last. That gives the label S. A double bond counts as two of that atom, so the carboxyl carbon counts as (O, O, O), which beats almost any side-chain carbon.

Cysteine breaks the pattern because sulfur sits right on the first side-chain carbon. (S, H, H) beats (O, O, O) because the comparison stops at the first difference, S versus O. The molecule's actual shape doesn't change; only the ranking does, so the label becomes R.

x1A_003.trap: Compare atoms at the first point of difference: one S on CH₂SH beats three O's on COO⁻. The sulfur has to be on the first side-chain carbon, which is why methionine stays S.

fig.cap: Each answer pair drawn as it exists at pH 7.4, side chains shaded. Only aspartate and glutamate carry a negative side chain.
fig.alt: Structures of aspartate, glutamate, asparagine, glutamine, lysine, arginine, serine and threonine at pH 7.4 with side-chain charges −1, −1, 0, 0, +1, +1, 0, 0.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Not quite. Asparagine and glutamine are the amide versions of aspartate and glutamate: the side-chain COOH is swapped for CONH₂. Amides don't act as acids or bases in water (the N–H pKₐ is about 15 to 17), so these side chains stay neutral at pH 7.4. They're polar and form hydrogen bonds well, which makes them tempting, but polar doesn't mean charged.

Correct. Aspartate and glutamate both have a side-chain carboxylic acid with pKₐ ≈ 3.9 to 4.2. At pH 7.4, the pH is more than 3 units above the pKₐ, so for every COOH there are about 10³ (1000) COO⁻. Essentially every side chain has a −1 charge. That's why they're called the acidic amino acids, and why they often bind positive ions like Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺.

Not quite. Lysine (side-chain amine, pKₐ ≈ 10.5) and arginine (guanidinium group, pKₐ ≈ 12.5) are the basic amino acids. At pH 7.4, well below their pKₐ values, they keep their extra proton and carry +1. So the idea of a charged side chain is right, but the sign is wrong.

Not quite. Serine and threonine have side-chain OH groups with pKₐ around 13 or higher. At pH 7.4 they keep their protons and stay neutral. They're polar, and they're the residues kinases add phosphate to, but they have no charge unless they're phosphorylated.

concept.t: Which side chains are charged at body pH
p: pKₐ is the pH at which a group is half protonated and half not. A simple rule: if the pH is above the pKₐ, the group has mostly lost its proton; if the pH is below the pKₐ, it mostly still has it.

Acid groups like COOH go from neutral (COOH) to negative (COO⁻) when they lose a proton. Aspartate and glutamate have COOH side chains with pKₐ ≈ 4, so at pH 7.4 they're negative. Basic groups like NH₃⁺ go from positive to neutral when they lose a proton. Lysine, arginine and (partly) histidine stay positive at pH 7.4.
Watch the look-alikes. Asparagine and glutamine have an amide (CONH₂) instead of COOH. Amides don't gain or lose protons in water, so these two are polar but never charged.

x1A_004.trap: Asn and Gln look like Asp and Glu, but they're amides: polar, never charged.

fig.cap: Percent protonated against pH for each answer choice. At pH 7 only histidine has substantial amounts of both forms; Lys and Arg are stuck protonated and Asp is stuck deprotonated.
fig.alt: Four sigmoid curves of percent protonated versus pH with midpoints at pH 3.9 (Asp), 6.0 (His), 10.5 (Lys) and 12.5 (Arg). A dashed line at pH 7 crosses His at about 9 percent, Lys and Arg at about 100 percent and Asp near 0 percent.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation with the pKₐ values in the question.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Not quite. Lysine's side-chain amine has pKₐ ≈ 10.5. pH 7 is 3.5 units below that, so protonated lysine outnumbers the neutral form about 10³·⁵ to 1, roughly 3000 to 1. It can donate a proton, but there's almost no NH₂ form around to accept one back. Lysine only works as a catalytic base when its surroundings shift its pKₐ.

Correct. A group that both donates and accepts protons near pH 7 needs a pKₐ near 7, so good amounts of both forms are present. Histidine's imidazole side chain has pKₐ ≈ 6, the closest of any standard side chain. At pH 7 about 9% is protonated and 91% neutral, and inside an active site its pKₐ is often nudged even closer to 7. That's why histidine is the classic acid-base catalyst, for example in the catalytic triad of serine proteases.

Not quite. Arginine's guanidinium group has pKₐ ≈ 12.5, so at pH 7 the protonated form wins by about 10⁵·⁵ to 1. Its positive charge is spread over three nitrogens, which makes it very stable. Arginine is great at holding onto negative groups like phosphate, but it basically never gives up its proton at pH 7, so it can't shuttle protons.

Not quite. Aspartate's side-chain carboxyl has pKₐ ≈ 3.9, so at pH 7 about 99.9% of it is COO⁻. It could accept a proton in theory, but the protonated form is so rare that it can't donate one too. Aspartate often helps catalysis in another way, like holding histidine in the right position in the catalytic triad.

concept.t: Why histidine is the go-to proton shuttle
p: Many enzymes speed up reactions by handing a proton to the substrate and then taking one back (general acid-base catalysis). To do both, the catalytic group has to exist in both forms, protonated and not, at the pH where the enzyme works.

The pKₐ tells you where that balance sits. When pH equals pKₐ, the group is 50:50. Each pH unit away from the pKₐ shifts the ratio 10-fold. So a group with pKₐ 10.5 at pH 7 is about 3000:1 protonated, which is useless for shuttling.
Histidine's imidazole has pKₐ ≈ 6, so near pH 7 it's a working mix of both forms. That's why histidine shows up in so many active sites, like the Ser-His-Asp catalytic triad of chymotrypsin.

x1A_005.trap: A charged residue isn't automatically a good catalyst. What matters is having both protonation states present, which needs pKₐ close to pH.

fig.cap: Lysine's average net charge across the pH scale. At pH 7 the curve sits on the +1 plateau; +2, 0 and −1 occur only well below pH 2.2, near pH 9.75 and well above pH 10.5.
fig.alt: Net charge of lysine versus pH, falling from +2 at low pH to +1 between pH 3 and 8, to 0 near 9.75, and to −1 above 12. At pH 7 the value is about +0.99.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation with the pKₐ values in the question.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Not quite. A net charge of −1 needs both amino groups to be neutral (NH₂) while the carboxyl is COO⁻. That only happens at very high pH, about 12 and up, where both amines have lost their protons. At pH 7 the pH is 2 units below the α-amino pKₐ (9.0) and 3.5 units below the side-chain pKₐ (10.5), so both amines still have their protons.

Not quite. A net charge of 0 counts the carboxyl (−1) and the α-amino group (+1) but forgets the side-chain amine. That would be right for a plain amino acid like alanine, but lysine has a third group that can carry charge. Lysine is only neutral near its pI, (9.0 + 10.5) ÷ 2 = 19.5 ÷ 2 = 9.75.

Correct. Compare pH 7 with each pKₐ. The α-COOH (pKₐ 2.2) is below the pH, so it has lost its proton: −1. The α-NH₃⁺ (pKₐ 9.0) and the side-chain NH₃⁺ (pKₐ 10.5) are above the pH, so both keep their protons: +1 each. Total: −1 + 1 + 1 = +1. That's why lysine counts as a basic, positively charged amino acid in the body.

Not quite. +2 would mean the carboxyl is still COOH (charge 0) while both amines are NH₃⁺. That fully protonated form only dominates below about pH 2.2. At pH 7, nearly 5 units above the carboxyl's pKₐ, COO⁻ outnumbers COOH by about 10⁴·⁸ to 1, so the carboxyl is basically always charged.

concept.t: Counting an amino acid's net charge
p: Each group that can gain or lose a proton contributes its own charge. To find the net charge at a given pH, check each group one at a time and add them up.

The rule is the same for every group: if the pH is below the group's pKₐ, the group has its proton; if the pH is above it, the group has lost it. What changes is what 'has its proton' means. For an acid like COOH, protonated is 0 and unprotonated is −1. For a base like NH₃⁺, protonated is +1 and unprotonated is 0.

Lysine has three such groups: the α-carboxyl, the α-amino group and a side-chain amine. At pH 7 that's −1, +1 and +1, so lysine is +1. That's what makes it one of the basic amino acids, along with arginine and histidine.

x1A_006.trap: Acids are 0 or −1, bases are +1 or 0. 'Below pKₐ means protonated' is true for both, but protonated means a different charge for each kind of group.
mem: Group keeps its proton if pH < pKₐ
At pH 7: COOH (2.2) → COO⁻ = −1; NH₃⁺ (9.0) = +1; side-chain NH₃⁺ (10.5) = +1
Lysine is basic: net +1 at pH 7

fm.f: Net charge = sum of each group's charge, where a group keeps its proton when pH < pKₐ
fm.v: pH = 7.0; α-COOH pKₐ = 2.2; α-NH₃⁺ pKₐ = 9.0; side-chain NH₃⁺ pKₐ = 10.5; net charge = ?
fm.why: Comparing pH with each pKₐ tells you whether each group is holding its proton.
fm.nc: Acid groups are 0 when protonated; base groups are +1 when protonated.

steps: Write the formula: net charge = sum of the charges on each group.
Write down the values: pH = 7.0; α-COOH pKₐ = 2.2; α-NH₃⁺ pKₐ = 9.0; side-chain NH₃⁺ pKₐ = 10.5.
α-COOH: 7.0 is above 2.2, so it has lost its proton. COO⁻ = −1.
α-NH₃⁺: 7.0 is below 9.0, so it keeps its proton. NH₃⁺ = +1.
Side-chain NH₃⁺: 7.0 is below 10.5, so it keeps its proton. NH₃⁺ = +1.
x1A_006.sc: pKₐ below 7: that group has lost its proton (acid → −1). pKₐ above 7: it still has its proton (amine → +1). −1 + 1 + 1 = +1.
x1A_006.mn: HKR are the basic ones: Histidine, Lysine, Arginine can all carry a plus.
x1A_006.plain: Think of each group as a light switch. A group is 'on' (holding its proton) when the pH is below its pKₐ. Count what each switch adds and total it up.

fig.alt: Titration curve of glycine, pH versus equivalents of hydroxide from 0 to 2, with buffering plateaus at pH 2.3 and 9.7 and a steep rise at 1 equivalent where pH 6.0 is marked as the isoelectric point. Wrong values 7.0, 9.7 and 12.0 are marked.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the two pKₐ values in the question.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Correct. The pI is the pH where the average net charge is zero. Fully protonated glycine (⁺H₃N–CH₂–COOH) is +1. Losing the carboxyl proton (pKₐ 2.3) gives the zwitterion ⁺H₃N–CH₂–COO⁻, net 0. Losing the amino proton (pKₐ 9.7) gives the −1 form. The neutral form sits between the two pKₐ values, so pI = (2.3 + 9.7) ÷ 2 = 12.0 ÷ 2 = 6.0.

Not quite. pH 7.0 is neutral for water, meaning equal H⁺ and OH⁻, but that says nothing about an amino acid's charge. The pI depends only on the molecule's own pKₐ values. For glycine it's 6.0, for aspartate it's near 2.8, and for arginine it's near 10.8, all far from 7.

Not quite. 9.7 is the pKₐ of the amino group, where half the amino groups are NH₃⁺ and half are NH₂. At that pH, half the molecules are neutral (0) and half are −1, so the average charge is −0.5, not zero. The pI sits between the two pKₐ values, not on one of them.

Not quite. 12.0 is just the sum, 2.3 + 9.7, without dividing by 2. At pH 12 more than 99% of glycine is in the −1 form, H₂N–CH₂–COO⁻. Quick check: the pI always lies between the two pKₐ values, and 12.0 is outside that range.

p: An amino acid's charge changes with pH because its groups gain or lose protons. The isoelectric point (pI) is the pH where the average net charge is exactly zero. At the pI, the molecule won't move in an electric field.

Glycine has two such groups. Fully protonated, it's +1. Past pKₐ₁ (2.3) the carboxyl loses its proton and the molecule becomes a zwitterion: one + and one −, net 0. A zwitterion is a molecule carrying both a positive and a negative charge that cancel. Past pKₐ₂ (9.7) the amine loses its proton too, and the molecule is −1.

The neutral zwitterion lives between the two pKₐ values, so the pI is their average. For amino acids with a side chain that also carries charge, you average the two pKₐ values on either side of the neutral form instead.

fm.f: pI = (pKₐ₁ + pKₐ₂) ÷ 2, where pKₐ₁ = pKₐ of the α-carboxyl, pKₐ₂ = pKₐ of the α-amino group
fm.v: pKₐ₁ = 2.3; pKₐ₂ = 9.7; pI = ?
fm.why: The neutral form exists between the two pKₐ values, so the point of zero charge is halfway between them.
fm.nc: This simple form is for amino acids with no charged side chain. Otherwise, average the two pKₐ values around the neutral form.

steps: Write the formula: pI = (pKₐ₁ + pKₐ₂) ÷ 2.
Write down the values: pKₐ₁ = 2.3 (carboxyl), pKₐ₂ = 9.7 (amino group).
Check that these two bracket the neutral form. Below 2.3 glycine is +1. Between 2.3 and 9.7 it's the zwitterion, net 0. Above 9.7 it's −1.
Add first: 2.3 + 9.7 = 12.0. Then divide: 12.0 ÷ 2 = 6.0.
x1A_007.trap: The pI always lies between two pKₐ values. Average them, don't just add them, and don't assume it's 7.

fig.cap: Glutamate's titration curve. The pI (3.2) sits between the first two pKₐ plateaus. The three wrong values all fall where glutamate is already net −1.
fig.alt: Titration curve of glutamate, pH against equivalents of hydroxide, with plateaus at pH 2.2, 4.2 and 9.7; the isoelectric point 3.2 is marked at one equivalent; wrong values 5.4, 6.0 and 7.0 are marked on the steep jump near two equivalents.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the three pKₐ values in the question.

ox: Correct. Start fully protonated (net +1: α-COOH 0, side-chain COOH 0, α-NH₃⁺ +1) and remove protons in pKₐ order. After the α-COOH (2.2) loses its proton, the net charge is 0. After the side-chain COOH (4.2) loses its proton, it's −1. The neutral form sits between pKₐ 2.2 and 4.2, so pI = (2.2 + 4.2) ÷ 2 = 6.4 ÷ 2 = 3.2.

Not quite. 5.4 is the average of all three pKₐ values: (2.2 + 4.2 + 9.7) ÷ 3 = 16.1 ÷ 3 ≈ 5.4. The pI is never the average of every pKₐ. It's the average of the two that sit on either side of the neutral form. At pH 5.4 both carboxyls have lost their protons and the amine still has one, so glutamate is −1, not neutral.

Not quite. 6.0 comes from averaging only the α-carboxyl and α-amino pKₐ values: (2.2 + 9.7) ÷ 2 = 11.9 ÷ 2 ≈ 6.0. That works for amino acids whose side chain doesn't carry charge, like glycine or alanine. Glutamate has an extra acid group you have to count, and ignoring it puts the pI almost 3 units too high.

Not quite. 7.0 averages the side-chain and α-amino pKₐ values: (4.2 + 9.7) ÷ 2 = 13.9 ÷ 2 ≈ 7.0. That's the pattern for a basic amino acid like lysine, where the neutral form lies between the two highest pKₐ values. For an acidic amino acid like glutamate, the neutral form lies between the two lowest.

concept.t: pI of an acidic amino acid
p: The pI is the pH where an amino acid's net charge is zero. When the side chain can also gain or lose a proton, there are three pKₐ values, and you need to pick the right two.

The method: start fully protonated, then remove protons in order from lowest pKₐ to highest, tracking the net charge each time. Find the form with net charge 0, and average the pKₐ just below it and the pKₐ just above it.

For acidic amino acids (aspartate, glutamate) the neutral form is between the two lowest pKₐ values, so the pI is low, around 3. For basic amino acids (lysine, arginine) it's between the two highest, so the pI is high, around 10.

fm.f: pI = (pKₐ below + pKₐ above) ÷ 2, where pKₐ below and pKₐ above = the two pKₐ values on either side of the neutral (net 0) form
fm.v: pKₐ below = 2.2 (α-COOH); pKₐ above = 4.2 (side-chain COOH); pI = ?
fm.why: The pI is halfway between the two pKₐ values that bracket the neutral form.
fm.nc: Acidic amino acid: average the two lowest pKₐ values. Never average all three.

steps: Write the formula: pI = (pKₐ below + pKₐ above) ÷ 2, using the two pKₐ values around the neutral form.
Write down the values: pKₐ = 2.2 (α-COOH), 4.2 (side-chain COOH), 9.7 (α-NH₃⁺).
Fully protonated glutamate: 0 + 0 + (+1) = +1.
Remove the proton at 2.2: (−1) + 0 + (+1) = 0. This is the neutral form.
Remove the proton at 4.2: (−1) + (−1) + (+1) = −1.
The neutral form sits between 2.2 and 4.2. Plug in: pI = (2.2 + 4.2) ÷ 2 = 6.4 ÷ 2 = 3.2.
x1A_008.trap: Find the neutral form first, then average the two pKₐ values on either side of it. Never average all three.

fig.cap: Arginine's titration curve computed from pKₐ 2.2, 9.0 and 12.5. The pI (10.75) is at two equivalents of base, between the two highest pKₐ plateaus; 5.6 and 7.9 fall where arginine is still +1.
fig.alt: Titration curve of arginine, pH versus equivalents of hydroxide from 0 to 3, with plateaus at 2.2, 9.0 and 12.5. The isoelectric point 10.75 is marked at 2 equivalents; wrong values 5.6 and 7.9 are marked on the steep rise at 1 equivalent and 12.5 at the last plateau.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the three pKₐ values in the question (water autoionization ignored).

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Not quite. 5.6 averages the α-carboxyl and α-amino pKₐ values: (2.2 + 9.0) ÷ 2 = 11.2 ÷ 2 = 5.6. That shortcut works when the side chain can't carry charge, but arginine's side chain stays +1 until pH 12.5. At pH 5.6 arginine is −1 + 1 + 1 = +1, not neutral.

Not quite. 7.9 is the average of all three: (2.2 + 9.0 + 12.5) ÷ 3 = 23.7 ÷ 3 = 7.9. Averaging every pKₐ doesn't mean anything chemically. Only the two pKₐ values on either side of the neutral form matter. At pH 7.9 both amino groups still have their protons, so arginine is +1.

Correct. Start fully protonated: COOH (0), α-NH₃⁺ (+1) and the side-chain guanidinium (+1), net +2. Losing the carboxyl proton (pKₐ 2.2) gives +1. Losing the α-amino proton (pKₐ 9.0) gives 0. Losing the side-chain proton (pKₐ 12.5) gives −1. The neutral form sits between 9.0 and 12.5, so pI = (9.0 + 12.5) ÷ 2 = 21.5 ÷ 2 = 10.75. That's the 'average the two highest' rule for basic amino acids.

Not quite. 12.5 is the side chain's pKₐ. At that pH half the side chains have their proton and half don't, so the average charge is −0.5 (halfway between the neutral form and the −1 form). A pI never equals a single pKₐ; it's the midpoint between two of them.

concept.t: pI of a basic amino acid
p: The pI is the pH where the net charge is zero. When the side chain can gain or lose a proton too, you need to figure out which two pKₐ values surround the neutral form.

Start fully protonated and remove protons in order from lowest pKₐ to highest, tracking the charge. For arginine that goes +2 → +1 → 0 → −1. The neutral form appears after the second proton leaves and disappears after the third, so it's bracketed by the two highest pKₐ values.
That's the pattern for every basic amino acid (lysine, arginine, histidine): average the two highest pKₐ values. Acidic amino acids are the mirror image: average the two lowest.

fm.f: pI = (pKₐ below + pKₐ above) ÷ 2, where pKₐ below and pKₐ above = the two pKₐ values on either side of the neutral (net 0) form
fm.v: pKₐ below = 9.0 (α-NH₃⁺); pKₐ above = 12.5 (side chain); pI = ?
fm.why: The pI is halfway between the two pKₐ values that bracket the neutral form.
fm.nc: Basic amino acid: average the two highest pKₐ values.

steps: Write the formula: pI = (pKₐ below + pKₐ above) ÷ 2, using the two pKₐ values around the neutral form.
Write down the values: pKₐ = 2.2 (α-COOH), 9.0 (α-NH₃⁺), 12.5 (side chain).
Fully protonated: 0 + (+1) + (+1) = +2.
After pKₐ 9.0: (−1) + 0 + (+1) = 0. This is the neutral form.
The neutral form sits between 9.0 and 12.5. Plug in: pI = (9.0 + 12.5) ÷ 2 = 21.5 ÷ 2 = 10.75.
x1A_009.trap: For a basic amino acid the neutral form sits between the two highest pKₐ values. Averaging the α-groups or all three gives a pH where arginine is still +1.

fig.cap: Percent of histidine side chains protonated against pH for pKₐ 6.0. At pH 7 the curve gives 9%; the wrong answers correspond to pH 8 (1%), pH 6 (50%) and pH 5 (91%).
fig.alt: Falling sigmoid curve of percent protonated versus pH from 2 to 10, midpoint at pH 6. Points mark 91 percent at pH 5, 50 percent at pH 6, 9 percent at pH 7 (correct) and 1 percent at pH 8.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation with the pKₐ in the question.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Not quite. 1% protonated means about 100 unprotonated for every 1 protonated. Since log(100) = 2, that needs pH − pKₐ = 2, so pH 8.0. At pH 7.0 the pH is only 1 unit above the pKₐ, so the ratio is 10 : 1, and about 10 times more side chains are protonated than this choice says.

Correct. Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKₐ + log([base] ÷ [acid]). Here 7.0 = 6.0 + log(ratio), so log(ratio) = 1 and the ratio is 10¹ = 10. For every 10 neutral side chains there's 1 protonated one, so the protonated share is 1 ÷ (10 + 1) = 1 ÷ 11 ≈ 0.09, about 9%. Note the bottom is 11, not 10, because the total includes both forms.

Not quite. 50% protonated means equal amounts of both forms, and that only happens when pH = pKₐ, here pH 6.0. At pH 7.0 the solution is 1 unit more basic, which shifts the balance 10-fold toward the unprotonated form.

Not quite. 91% is 10 ÷ 11, the unprotonated share at pH 7.0, not the protonated one. This is the classic flipped ratio. When pH is above pKₐ, the unprotonated (base) form wins. 91% protonated would be right at pH 5.0, 1 unit below the pKₐ.

concept.t: Using Henderson-Hasselbalch to find percent protonated
p: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation connects pH, pKₐ and the ratio of the two forms of a group: pH = pKₐ + log([base] ÷ [acid]). Here 'acid' is the form holding the proton and 'base' is the form without it. For histidine's side chain, the acid form is positively charged and the base form is neutral.

You rarely need a calculator. Every 1 unit the pH sits away from the pKₐ multiplies the ratio by 10. pH = pKₐ means 1 : 1. One unit above means 10 : 1 in favor of the base form. Two units above means 100 : 1.
To turn a ratio into a percentage, divide by the total. A 10 : 1 ratio means 11 molecules total, so the smaller group is 1 ÷ 11 ≈ 9% and the bigger group is 10 ÷ 11 ≈ 91%.

x1A_010.trap: Turn the ratio into a fraction using the total on the bottom (1 ÷ 11, not 1 ÷ 10), and remember pH above pKₐ favors the unprotonated form.
mem: pH = pKₐ + log([base] ÷ [acid])
Each 1 pH unit away from pKₐ = a 10 : 1 ratio
Histidine side chain pKₐ ≈ 6, the only one near body pH

fm.f: pH = pKₐ + log([A⁻] ÷ [HA]), where pH = acidity of the solution, pKₐ = pH at which the group is half protonated, [A⁻] = unprotonated (base) form, [HA] = protonated (acid) form
fm.why: Henderson-Hasselbalch turns a pH and a pKₐ into a ratio of the two forms.
fm.nc: Log just reads off the exponent of 10: log(10) = 1.

fm.f: fraction protonated = [HA] ÷ ([HA] + [A⁻]), where [HA] = protonated form, [A⁻] = unprotonated form
fm.v: [HA] = 1 part; [A⁻] = 10 parts; fraction protonated = ?
fm.why: A percentage is one part divided by the whole, and the whole includes both forms.
fm.nc: Don't divide by 10. The total is 11.

steps: Write the formula: pH = pKₐ + log([base] ÷ [acid]).
Write down the values: pH = 7.0, pKₐ = 6.0.
Plug in: 7.0 = 6.0 + log(ratio). Subtract 6.0 from both sides: log(ratio) = 1.
Log reads off the exponent of 10, so ratio = 10¹ = 10. That's 10 unprotonated for every 1 protonated.
Total = 10 + 1 = 11. Protonated share = 1 ÷ 11 ≈ 0.091.
Turn it into a percent by multiplying by 100: 0.091 × 100 ≈ 9%.
x1A_010.sc: pH − pKₐ = 1 means a 10 : 1 ratio. No calculator needed. The smaller form is 1 ÷ 11 ≈ 9%.
x1A_010.mn: pH over pKₐ, the proton goes away.
x1A_010.plain: Think of histidine as a dimmer switch whose halfway point is pH 6.0. At pH 7.0 the dial is one notch toward 'off' (no proton), so only 1 in 11 is still holding its proton.

fig.cap: Titration curve computed for pKₐ 2.2, 9.0 and 10.5. The third buffering region at 10.5 is lysine's ε-amino group; glutamate or histidine would buffer at 4.2 or 6.0, and alanine would stop after two equivalents.
fig.alt: Titration curve with a plateau at pH 2.2, a steep jump at 1 equivalent, and a long gently sloping region containing pKₐ 9.0 and 10.5, ending at 3 equivalents. Dotted lines at pH 4.2 and 6.0 show where glutamate and histidine would buffer instead.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the three pKₐ values in the question (water autoionization ignored).

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Not quite. Glutamate does have three groups that can lose a proton, so its curve also has three flat parts. But they sit near 2.2 (α-COOH), 4.2 (side-chain COOH) and 9.7 (α-NH₃⁺). Its extra plateau is in the acidic range because the side chain is a carboxylic acid, and this curve has nothing near pH 4.

Not quite. Histidine's three flat parts sit near 1.8, 6.0 and 9.2. Its imidazole side chain is the one that buffers near neutral pH, at about 6.0. This curve has no plateau between pH 3 and 8, so the side chain can't be histidine's.

Not quite. Alanine's side chain is a CH₃ group, which can't gain or lose a proton. Its curve has only two flat parts (about 2.3 and 9.7) and needs only two equivalents of base. A third plateau rules out any amino acid whose side chain doesn't ionize.

Correct. Each flat region is centered on one pKₐ, so this amino acid has three groups with pKₐ 2.2, 9.0 and 10.5. Every amino acid has the α-COOH (about 2) and the α-NH₃⁺ (about 9 to 10), so 10.5 belongs to the side chain. That's lysine's ε-amino group, a basic side chain that stays protonated until well above body pH.

p: In a titration you add base (like NaOH) bit by bit and track the pH. The curve has flat parts and steep parts. A flat part is a buffering region: a group is about half protonated, so it soaks up added base without the pH moving much. The center of each flat part is that group's pKₐ.

So you can count the groups that lose protons by counting the flat parts. Every amino acid has two: the α-COOH near pH 2 and the α-NH₃⁺ near pH 9 to 10. A third flat part means the side chain can lose a proton too.

The position of that third plateau tells you which amino acid it is: about 3.9 for aspartate, 4.2 for glutamate, 6.0 for histidine, 8.3 for cysteine, 10.5 for lysine, 10.1 for tyrosine and 12.5 for arginine.

x1A_011.trap: Count flat parts to count groups that lose protons, then name the amino acid from the pKₐ that isn't the α-COOH or α-NH₃⁺.

fig.cap: Glycine titration with each answer choice located on the curve. The pI at one equivalent is the steepest point; the flat buffer zones are at the two pKₐ values.
fig.alt: Glycine titration curve, pH versus equivalents of hydroxide. Shaded buffer zones around 0.5 and 1.5 equivalents mark pH 2.3 and 9.7. The pI at 1.0 equivalent, pH 6.0, is on the steep jump and labeled net charge 0; the starting point is labeled net +1 and the end point net −1.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from glycine's pKₐ values (2.3 and 9.7).

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Correct. Glycine reaches its pI (about 6.0) after exactly one equivalent of base. By then every carboxyl has lost its proton and almost no amino group has. That's an equivalence point: neither group is present as a half-and-half buffering pair. So each small bit of OH⁻ changes the tiny amount of NH₂ by a big factor, and the pH jumps. On the curve, the pI is the steepest spot between the two flat parts.

Not quite. The pH resists change most (the best buffering) at a pKₐ, where a group is half protonated and half not, so it can soak up added acid or base. For glycine that's pH 2.3 and 9.7. The pI sits halfway between them, where buffering is weakest.

Not quite. The pH equals the amino group's pKₐ (about 9.7) after 1.5 equivalents of base, when half the NH₃⁺ groups have lost their proton. The average charge there is −0.5, not 0. The pI is the average of the two pKₐ values: (2.3 + 9.7) ÷ 2 = 12.0 ÷ 2 = 6.0.

Not quite. A net charge of +1 (⁺H₃N–CH₂–COOH) is glycine at the very start of the titration, below pH 2.3. At the pI the main form is the zwitterion ⁺H₃N–CH₂–COO⁻, whose +1 and −1 cancel to net 0. That's exactly what isoelectric point means.

concept.t: Flat parts and steep parts of a titration curve
p: A buffer is a mix of a weak acid and its unprotonated partner, and it resists pH change. On a titration curve, buffering shows up as a flat part. It's flattest at the pKₐ, where the two forms are 50:50.

Between flat parts are steep parts called equivalence points. There, one group has just finished losing its protons and the next hasn't started. Nothing is around to buffer, so a small amount of base causes a big jump in pH.
For glycine, the first equivalence point is the pI. Almost every molecule is the zwitterion, a molecule with one + and one − charge that cancel. Neutral, but no buffering at all.

x1A_012.trap: Flat parts of a titration curve are the pKₐ values (best buffering). The pI is a steep equivalence point (worst buffering).

fig.cap: Each answer choice located on glycine's titration curve. Only 1.0 equivalent gives the zwitterion with net charge 0; 0.5 and 1.5 equivalents are the pKₐ points and 2.0 is fully −1.
fig.alt: Glycine titration curve, pH versus equivalents of hydroxide. Points at 0.5 equivalents (pH 2.3, net +0.5), 1.0 equivalent (pH 6.0, pI, net 0, correct), 1.5 equivalents (pH 9.7, net −0.5) and 2.0 equivalents (fully −1).
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from glycine's pKₐ values (2.3 and 9.7).

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Not quite. After 0.5 equivalents, only half the carboxyl groups have lost their proton. The pH equals pKₐ₁ (about 2.3), and the solution is a 1 : 1 mix of the +1 form and the zwitterion (0), so the average charge is +0.5. That's the middle of the first buffering region, not the pI.

Correct. Fully protonated glycine, ⁺H₃N–CH₂–COOH, is +1 and has two protons it can lose. The carboxyl proton (pKₐ ≈ 2.3) comes off first. One equivalent of OH⁻ removes exactly one proton from every molecule, turning them all into the zwitterion ⁺H₃N–CH₂–COO⁻, net 0. That's the isoelectric point, at pH (2.3 + 9.7) ÷ 2 = 12.0 ÷ 2 = 6.0.

Not quite. At 1.5 equivalents, the carboxyl is fully deprotonated and half the amino groups have lost their proton too. The pH equals pKₐ₂ (about 9.7), and the mix is 1 : 1 zwitterion (0) and −1 form, so the average charge is −0.5. That's the second buffering region.
Not quite. Two equivalents remove both protons, giving H₂N–CH₂–COO⁻ with net charge −1. That's the end of the titration. The molecule has gone past neutral, not stopped at it.

concept.t: Equivalents of base on a titration curve
p: An 'equivalent' of base is one OH⁻ for every molecule of amino acid. Each equivalent removes one proton per molecule, and the most acidic proton (lowest pKₐ) goes first.

Half-equivalents (0.5, 1.5) land in the middle of a buffering region, where one group is half done. There the pH equals that group's pKₐ. Whole equivalents (1.0, 2.0) land on the steep parts, where a group has just finished.
Glycine starts at +1. After 1.0 equivalent it's the neutral zwitterion, the pI. After 2.0 it's −1, fully deprotonated.

fm.f: net charge = starting charge − equivalents of OH⁻ added, where each equivalent removes one proton per molecule
fm.v: starting charge = +1; target net charge = 0; equivalents = ?
fm.why: Each OH⁻ takes one proton, and each lost proton lowers the charge by 1.
fm.nc: Works for whole equivalents when protons come off one group at a time.

steps: Write the formula: net charge = starting charge − equivalents of OH⁻ added.
Write down the values: fully protonated glycine is COOH (0) + NH₃⁺ (+1) = +1; target net charge = 0.
Plug in: 0 = +1 − equivalents, so equivalents = 1.0.
Check which proton leaves: the carboxyl (pKₐ 2.3) goes first, giving the zwitterion.
Check the other choices: 0.5 gives +0.5, 1.5 gives −0.5, 2.0 gives −1.
x1A_013.trap: Half-equivalents put the pH at a pKₐ (half-charged mixes). Glycine's pI needs a whole equivalent.

fig.cap: Glycine and alanine condense into the dipeptide Gly-Ala. The atoms that leave as water and the new peptide bond are shaded.
fig.alt: Glycine plus alanine gives glycylalanine and water; the carboxyl OH of glycine and the amino group of alanine are highlighted, and the new amide bond is highlighted in the product.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Not quite. Hydrolysis is the reverse reaction: water is added across the C–N bond to split a peptide into a free carboxyl and a free amine. That's how proteases and stomach acid break proteins down, not how they're built. 'Hydro-lysis' literally means splitting with water.

Not quite. Oxidizing two cysteine thiols (SH groups) joins them into a disulfide bond (S–S). That's a covalent cross-link that helps hold a folded protein's shape, especially in proteins the cell sends outside. It links side chains, not the backbone, and it's not how amino acids are joined in a chain.

Correct. A peptide bond is an amide. The carboxyl carbon of one amino acid bonds to the amino nitrogen of the next, and the OH from the carboxyl plus an H from the amine leave as H₂O. That's a condensation (dehydration) reaction. In cells the ribosome drives it using an amino acid that's been 'charged' onto a tRNA, because the reaction doesn't happen easily on its own in water.

Not quite. An ester forms from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, giving a C–O–C=O link, like in fats and phospholipids. Peptide bonds link carbon to nitrogen, not oxygen. And two OH groups joining would make an ether or anhydride, not an ester.

p: Proteins are chains of amino acids linked by peptide bonds. Each amino acid has an amino group on one end and a carboxyl group on the other. A peptide bond joins the carboxyl carbon of one amino acid to the amino nitrogen of the next.

Building the bond releases a water molecule, so it's called a condensation or dehydration reaction. Breaking it takes a water molecule back, which is hydrolysis. This same pattern holds for most biological polymers: sugars into starch, nucleotides into DNA.
Don't mix up the other links. Disulfide bonds (S–S) connect cysteine side chains. Esters (C–O–C=O) show up in fats. Neither one forms the protein backbone.

x1A_014.trap: Building polymers releases water (condensation). Breaking them uses water (hydrolysis).

fig.cap: The two resonance contributors of a peptide group (modeled by N-methylacetamide). The real bond is a hybrid with partial double-bond character, which locks the group flat.
fig.alt: Two structures linked by a double-headed resonance arrow: on the left C=O and C–N single; on the right C–O minus and C=N plus double. A box states the real C–N bond is about 1.33 angstroms, between single and double, so rotation is restricted.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app. Bond lengths are standard textbook values.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.4 Peptides and Proteins

ox: Not quite. Side chains hang off the α-carbons, not the peptide C–N bond, and the bond is stiff even between two glycines, which have no real side chains at all. Bulky side chains do limit how the backbone can twist at other bonds, but that's a separate, space-crowding effect.

Not quite. A full C=N double bond would be about 1.27 Å long, and the C=O would become a single bond. Real peptide C–N bonds are about 1.33 Å, between a single C–N (about 1.47 Å) and a double C=N. The true structure is a resonance blend with partial double-bond character, not a full double bond.

Not quite. Water does hydrogen-bond to the C=O and N–H, but those bonds are weak and keep breaking and re-forming. Peptide groups buried deep in a protein, away from water, are still flat. The stiffness comes from the amide's own electrons, not from the water around it.

Correct. The nitrogen's lone pair spreads into the C=O, so the amide is a blend of two drawings: C(=O)–N and C(–O⁻)=N⁺. That gives the C–N bond partial double-bond character, roughly 40%. Twisting it would break the overlap that makes that partial double bond, which costs a lot of energy. So the six atoms (Cα, C, O, N, H and the next Cα) stay in one plane.

concept.t: Why the peptide bond is flat
p: Resonance means the electrons in a molecule are spread out over more than one bond, so no single drawing shows the real structure. The true molecule is a blend of the drawings.

In a peptide bond, the nitrogen's lone pair spreads into the neighboring C=O. One drawing has a C–N single bond; the other has a C=N double bond with a negative charge on oxygen. The real bond is in between, with about 40% double-bond character.

A double bond can't rotate without breaking, and a partial double bond is hard to rotate too. That's why the peptide group is flat and rigid, while the bonds on either side of the α-carbon can still twist. Those twists are what let a protein fold.

x1A_015.trap: Partial double bond, not full. The peptide bond is a resonance blend: shorter than a single bond, longer than a double.

fig.cap: Planar peptide units in the trans and cis forms. In trans the two α-carbons are on opposite sides; in cis they are on the same side and clash.
fig.alt: Two planar peptide units drawn with 120 degree angles inside dashed rectangles. Trans: O and the second C-α point up, the first C-α and H point down. Cis: both C-α atoms point down with a red dashed line showing their clash.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram drawn from coordinates.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.4 Peptides and Proteins

ox: Not quite. The bond is planar, but cis is the rare one. In cis, both α-carbons sit on the same side of the C–N bond and crowd each other. Cis makes up well under 1% of ordinary peptide bonds. It shows up mostly before proline (about 5% of those bonds), because proline's ring crowds both arrangements about equally.

Not quite. Trans is right, but 'freely rotating' isn't. Resonance gives the C–N bond partial double-bond character, so twisting it takes about 80 kJ/mol, far more than the body's heat provides. The bond is locked. Flipping between cis and trans, mostly at prolines, is so slow that cells have special enzymes (prolyl isomerases) to speed it up.

Correct. Two facts combine. Resonance makes the C–N bond partly double, so the peptide group is flat. Of the two flat arrangements, trans puts the α-carbons on opposite sides of the C–N bond, keeping their side chains apart. Cis puts them on the same side and they clash, so more than 99.9% of non-proline peptide bonds are trans.

Not quite. A tetrahedral nitrogen (sp³, like in ammonia) would keep its lone pair to itself, unable to share it with the C=O. In amides the nitrogen is flat (sp²) so its lone pair can spread into the C=O. That flatness is exactly what resonance needs.

p: Because of resonance, the peptide group (Cα, C, O, N, H, next Cα) is flat. A flat group can still be arranged two ways: cis, with the two α-carbons on the same side of the C–N bond, or trans, with them on opposite sides.
Trans wins almost every time because it keeps the bulky parts of neighboring amino acids apart. Cis crowds them together.

Proline is the exception worth knowing. Its side chain loops back onto its own nitrogen, so the ring crowds the previous residue whether the bond is cis or trans. That makes cis possible, and about 5% of bonds right before proline are cis.

x1A_016.trap: Planar and trans. Free rotation and a tetrahedral nitrogen both contradict the resonance that makes the peptide bond what it is.

fig.cap: A stretch of backbone with each bond labeled. φ (N–Cα) and ψ (Cα–C) rotate; ω (the peptide bond) is fixed; χ angles belong to side chains.
fig.alt: Zigzag backbone N, C-α, C, N, C-α, C with carbonyl oxygens and side chains R. N to C-α bonds labeled phi and C-α to C bonds labeled psi in green; the C to N peptide bond labeled ω in red; side-chain bonds labeled chi in purple.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram drawn from coordinates.

ox: Not quite. The peptide C–N bond is partly double and stays flat; its twist angle is called ω and stays near 180° (trans). The C=O is a full double bond and doesn't rotate at all. These are exactly the bonds that don't give the backbone any flexibility, so they can't be what φ and ψ describe.

Correct. Each residue's backbone runs N–Cα–C. The bonds on either side of the α-carbon are ordinary single bonds that can twist: φ is the angle around N–Cα, and ψ is the angle around Cα–C(=O). Since the peptide bond is stiff, the backbone's 3D path is set by the string of φ and ψ pairs. Ramachandran plots show which pairs are allowed.

Not quite. Twists around side-chain bonds are called χ (chi) angles: χ₁ around Cα–Cβ, χ₂ around Cβ–Cγ, and so on. They decide where a side chain points, not where the backbone goes. φ and ψ are saved for the two backbone bonds next to the α-carbon.

Not quite. Disulfide bonds link the side chains of two cysteines and can tie together distant parts of a chain, or two different chains. They help hold a fold together, but they aren't part of the backbone, so they aren't what φ and ψ describe.

concept.t: φ and ψ: where the backbone bends
p: A protein backbone repeats N–Cα–C over and over. The C–N peptide bond between residues is flat and stiff because of resonance, so it can't twist.

That leaves two bonds per residue that can twist: N–Cα (the φ angle) and Cα–C (the ψ angle). Think of each flat peptide group as a stiff card, and each α-carbon as a hinge between two cards. The φ and ψ angles at each hinge decide the whole backbone shape.
Not every combination works, because some make atoms crash into each other. A Ramachandran plot maps the allowed φ/ψ pairs. α-helices and β-sheets each sit in their own allowed region.

x1A_017.trap: φ and ψ are the two single bonds touching the α-carbon. The peptide bond itself (called ω) doesn't rotate.

fig.cap: Met-Gly-Ser drawn left to right: Met carries the free amino group (N-terminus) and Ser carries the free carboxyl (C-terminus).
fig.alt: Structure of the tripeptide Met-Gly-Ser with a free NH₂ on methionine at the left, glycine in the middle, and serine with a free COOH at the right; an arrow beneath shows the N to C direction.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.4 Peptides and Proteins

ox: Correct. By convention, sequences run from the N-terminus (the residue with a free amino group) on the left to the C-terminus (the residue with a free carboxyl group) on the right. In Met-Gly-Ser, Met's amino group is free, Gly sits in the middle with both its groups in peptide bonds, and Ser's carboxyl group is free. This matches translation, which starts with Met and adds each new residue to the C-terminal end.

Not quite. This is the reverse of the convention. Ser-Gly-Met would be a different peptide with Ser at the N-terminus, because peptide bonds have a direction: each one links the carboxyl of the residue on the left to the amino group of the residue on the right. Reading it backward changes which ends are free.

Not quite. Peptide bonds join the α-carboxyl of one residue to the α-amino group of the next. They're backbone bonds, not side-chain bonds. Glycine's side chain is just a hydrogen and can't form any bond. The Gly in the middle uses its amino group for one peptide bond and its carboxyl for the other.

Not quite. Order matters. The sequence of residues is the protein's primary structure, set by the gene and held by peptide bonds. Met-Gly-Ser, Ser-Gly-Met and Gly-Met-Ser are three different molecules, just like rearranging letters changes a word.

p: Every peptide has two ends. The N-terminus has a free amino group (NH₃⁺) and the C-terminus has a free carboxyl group (COO⁻). Each peptide bond inside the chain joins one residue's carboxyl to the next residue's amino group, so the chain has a direction.
The rule is always N-terminus on the left, C-terminus on the right. Ribosomes build proteins in that same direction, starting with methionine at the N-terminus.
The order of amino acids is called the primary structure. Because the chain has a direction, reversing the order gives a different molecule with different properties.

x1A_018.trap: Always N-terminus on the left, C-terminus on the right. Reversing the order gives a different peptide.

fig.cap: Ala-Gly-Ser has two peptide bonds (shaded); breaking both with two water molecules releases alanine, glycine and serine.
fig.alt: Structure of the tripeptide Ala-Gly-Ser with its two amide groups shaded, plus 2 H₂O, and an arrow to free alanine, glycine and serine.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Not quite. One water breaks one peptide bond. A tripeptide has two, so one water gives you one free amino acid plus a dipeptide (two amino acids still joined), not three free amino acids. Complete hydrolysis means every bond is broken.

Correct. Three amino acids are joined by n − 1 = 3 − 1 = 2 peptide bonds (first to second, and second to third). Making each bond released one H₂O, so breaking each one takes one H₂O back: an OH goes onto the carbonyl carbon and an H onto the nitrogen. Two bonds, two waters, three free amino acids.

Not quite. Three is the number of amino acids, not the number of bonds between them. A chain of three beads has only two links. This slip assumes each amino acid needs a water, but the two end residues already have one free end each.
Not quite. Four waters would break a pentapeptide, five amino acids with 5 − 1 = 4 bonds. Each peptide bond uses exactly one water. There's no extra water for the ends or the side chains.

p: When two amino acids join, a water molecule is released (condensation). When a peptide bond is broken, a water molecule is used up (hydrolysis). So it's one water per bond, in either direction.
In a straight chain of n amino acids, the number of bonds is n − 1, the same way a row of 3 fence posts has 2 gaps between them. A dipeptide has 1 bond, a tripeptide has 2, a decapeptide has 9.
If the chain is a closed ring (a cyclic peptide), the two ends are joined too, so there are n bonds instead of n − 1.

fm.f: bonds = n − 1, where n = number of amino acids in a straight (not cyclic) chain
fm.v: n = 3; waters per bond = 1; bonds = ?
fm.why: Each peptide bond needs exactly one water to break.
fm.nc: For a cyclic peptide, bonds = n.

steps: Write the formula: number of peptide bonds = n − 1.
Write down the values: n = 3 amino acids; 1 water per bond.
Plug in: bonds = 3 − 1 = 2.
Multiply by one water per bond: 2 × 1 = 2 water molecules.
x1A_019.trap: Count the bonds between amino acids (n − 1), not the amino acids themselves.

fig.cap: Schematic free-energy profile for peptide hydrolysis. Products lie below reactants (ΔG < 0), but the uncatalyzed barrier is high; a protease lowers the barrier without changing ΔG.
fig.alt: Reaction coordinate diagram: reactants peptide plus water on the left, products two amino acids lower on the right. A tall red barrier is labeled very high activation energy, half-life of years; a lower green dashed barrier is labeled with a protease. ΔG less than 0 is marked.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest schematic; curve drawn from a smooth function with illustrative relative heights, not measured values.

ox: Not quite. 'Endergonic' means ΔG > 0, but the question says hydrolysis has ΔG < 0, which makes it exergonic (favorable) at neutral pH. It's making peptide bonds that's endergonic, which is why ribosomes use tRNAs loaded with energy from ATP.

Not quite. Most backbone peptide bonds on a protein's surface, and every one in an unfolded protein or a short peptide, are fully exposed to water. Short peptides in water also last for years without enzymes, so lack of water can't be the reason.

Correct. ΔG only says whether a reaction can happen. The speed depends on the activation energy, the energy hill the molecules must get over. For peptide hydrolysis that hill is high, partly because the resonance-stabilized amide resists attack by water. So a peptide bond in neutral water lasts on the order of years. Proteases lower the hill and make the same reaction happen in milliseconds.

Not quite. Re-forming a peptide bond in water is the unfavorable direction (ΔG > 0), so it doesn't happen on its own fast enough to balance breakdown. The balance lies far toward hydrolysis. Proteins last only because the reaction takes so long to get there.

concept.t: Favorable vs fast: thermodynamics and kinetics
p: Two separate questions apply to any reaction. Thermodynamics asks: can it happen? That's ΔG. If ΔG < 0, the products are lower in energy and the reaction is favorable (spontaneous). Kinetics asks: how fast? That depends on the activation energy, the energy hill between reactants and products.

A reaction can be very favorable and still very slow. Diamonds turning into graphite is the classic example. Peptide hydrolysis is another: downhill overall, but with a big hill to climb first, so it barely happens in plain water.
Enzymes are catalysts. They lower the activation energy, which speeds a reaction up enormously, but they don't change ΔG or where the equilibrium lies.

x1A_020.trap: Spontaneous (ΔG < 0) doesn't mean fast. The speed depends on the activation energy.

fig.cap: The four choices at pH 7.4 with side chains shaded. Only proline's shaded ring includes the backbone α-nitrogen; the other rings and amines hang free.
fig.alt: Structures of proline, lysine, histidine and tryptophan. Proline's pyrrolidine ring including the NH₂+ is shaded and marked correct; lysine's free terminal NH₃⁺ and the imidazole and indole rings attached at the β carbon are marked wrong.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.1 Structures of Amino Acids

ox: Correct. Proline's three-carbon side chain curls back and bonds to its own α-amino nitrogen, closing a five-membered ring (a pyrrolidine). Its nitrogen is now bonded to two carbons, making it a secondary amine. The ring locks the φ angle near −60°, and once proline is in a chain, its nitrogen has no H to donate. So proline breaks α-helices and often shows up in turns.

Not quite. Lysine's side chain is a straight chain of four CH₂ groups ending in a free amino group (NH₃⁺ at body pH). That amine is far from the backbone and isn't bonded to the α-nitrogen. It stays free to form salt bridges or to pick up tags like acetyl groups or ubiquitin.

Not quite. Histidine's side chain is an imidazole ring attached to the backbone through one CH₂ group. The ring has two nitrogens, but neither is the backbone nitrogen. Having a ring in the side chain isn't the same as having the side chain bonded back to the backbone.

Not quite. Tryptophan's side chain is an indole (two fused rings) attached through a CH₂ group. Its ring nitrogen belongs to the indole, not the amino group. Tryptophan is big and aromatic, but its backbone nitrogen is ordinary, like most amino acids'.

concept.t: Proline, the ring that includes the backbone
p: In most amino acids the side chain hangs off the α-carbon and leaves the backbone alone. Proline is different: its side chain bonds back onto its own amino nitrogen, making a closed ring that includes part of the backbone.

That ring has two big effects. It locks the φ angle, so the backbone can't twist freely at proline. And once proline is linked into a chain, its nitrogen has no H, so it can't donate the hydrogen bond that α-helices rely on.
So proline acts as a helix breaker and is common in turns and loops. It's also plentiful in collagen, where its stiffness helps form the tight triple helix.

x1A_021.trap: Having a ring in the side chain isn't the same as being bonded onto the backbone. Only proline's ring includes the α-nitrogen.

fig.cap: The four choices at pH 7.4 with side chains shaded. Only leucine's side chain is pure hydrocarbon.
fig.alt: Structures of serine with a hydroxyl, glutamine with an amide, aspartate with a carboxylate and leucine with an isobutyl group; leucine is marked nonpolar and correct.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Not quite. Serine's side chain is CH₂OH. The OH group can hydrogen-bond with water, both giving and taking an H, so serine is polar but uncharged. It usually sits on a protein's surface or in active sites, not in the water-free core.

Not quite. Glutamine's side chain ends in an amide (CONH₂), with a polar C=O and N–H bonds. It hydrogen-bonds well with water, so glutamine is polar, though uncharged at body pH. It's the amide version of glutamate, not a hydrophobic residue.

Not quite. Aspartate's side-chain carboxyl (pKₐ ≈ 3.9) has lost its proton at body pH, so it carries a negative charge. Charged groups attract water strongly, making aspartate one of the most water-loving residues, the opposite of hydrophobic.

Correct. Leucine's side chain is CH₂CH(CH₃)₂, all carbon and hydrogen. C–H bonds are almost nonpolar, so the side chain can't hydrogen-bond or form ionic bonds with water. Water molecules around it get forced into a more ordered arrangement, which is unfavorable, so leucine side chains cluster together in the protein's core.

p: Water molecules are polar: they have slightly positive and slightly negative ends. They get along well with other polar or charged groups, like OH, C=O, NH₃⁺ or COO⁻. 'Hydrophilic' means water-loving.

Groups made only of carbon and hydrogen have no such charged ends, so water can't grab them. Those are hydrophobic (water-avoiding). When a protein folds, its hydrophobic side chains bunch together in the middle, away from water, like oil drops merging in a salad dressing.

The nonpolar amino acids are glycine, alanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, methionine, proline, phenylalanine and tryptophan. Leucine, isoleucine, valine and phenylalanine are the classic core residues.

x1A_022.trap: Glutamine isn't glutamate. It's uncharged, but its amide still makes it polar.
mem: Nonpolar: G, A, V, L, I, M, P, F, W
Polar uncharged: S, T, C, N, Q, Y
Acidic: D, E. Basic: H, K, R
x1A_022.sc: Look for the side chain that's only carbon and hydrogen. That's the hydrophobic one.
x1A_022.mn: GAV LIMP FW for the nonpolar ones: Grandma Always Visits London; Irene Makes Perfect Fresh Waffles.
x1A_022.plain: Leucine's side chain is greasy, like oil. Oil and water don't mix, so leucine hides in the protein's core, away from water.

fig.cap: Top: the four choices; only threonine has a side-chain hydroxyl. Bottom: a kinase transfers a phosphate from ATP to that hydroxyl, making phosphothreonine.
fig.alt: Structures of alanine, threonine, phenylalanine and valine with side chains shaded; threonine's OH is marked correct. Below, threonine reacts with ATP via a kinase to give phosphothreonine with a doubly negative phosphate ester and ADP.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Not quite. Alanine's side chain is a single CH₃ group. It has no oxygen and no OH, so there's nothing to attack ATP's phosphate. Alanine is a small nonpolar residue that can't be phosphorylated.

Correct. Kinases move the last phosphate of ATP onto a side-chain OH, forming a phosphate ester. The three standard residues with OH side chains are serine, threonine and tyrosine; threonine's is CH(OH)CH₃. The added phosphate brings about two negative charges at body pH, which can switch a protein's shape, activity or partners. Enzymes called phosphatases take it back off.

Not quite. Phenylalanine is tyrosine without the OH on the ring: its side chain is pure carbon and hydrogen. Tyrosine kinases need that OH, so phenylalanine can't be phosphorylated. Researchers actually swap tyrosine for phenylalanine on purpose to block phosphorylation at a site.
Not quite. Valine's side chain is CH(CH₃)₂, all carbon and hydrogen. With no OH it can't take a phosphate. Valine is a branched, water-avoiding residue.

p: Phosphorylation means adding a phosphate group to a protein. Kinases do it, using ATP as the phosphate source. Phosphatases do the reverse and remove it.

The phosphate attaches to an oxygen, so the side chain needs an OH group. In human proteins those are serine, threonine and tyrosine. Kinases are often grouped by which they target: serine/threonine kinases or tyrosine kinases.

A phosphate carries about two negative charges at body pH. Adding it to a protein can change its shape, turn it on or off, or create a docking spot for other proteins. It's one of the main on/off switches in cell signaling.

x1A_023.trap: Phosphorylation needs a side-chain OH: serine, threonine or tyrosine. Phenylalanine is tyrosine minus the OH, so it can't be phosphorylated.

fig.cap: N-acetylglucosamine bonded to the side-chain amide nitrogen of asparagine, the first link of every N-linked glycan. Tags show why the other residues do not fit.
fig.alt: Structure of β-N-acetylglucosamine attached through its anomeric carbon to the side-chain amide nitrogen of asparagine, with the N-glycosidic linkage shaded. Tags: asparagine amide N correct; serine OH is O-linked; glutamate carboxylate has no N; lysine is not the N-glycan acceptor.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 4.4 The Endomembrane System and Proteins

ox: Not quite. Serine's side chain is an OH, so a sugar attached to it is bonded through oxygen. That's O-linked glycosylation, which happens mostly in the Golgi and also targets threonine. It's real and common, but it isn't the N-linked kind the question asks about.

Correct. 'N-linked' means the sugar is bonded to a nitrogen, and the acceptor is the side-chain amide nitrogen of asparagine. Inside the rough ER, an enzyme (oligosaccharyltransferase) moves a ready-made 14-sugar chain from a lipid carrier called dolichol onto Asn. It only does this when Asn sits in the pattern Asn-X-Ser/Thr, where X is anything except proline. The sugar chain is then trimmed in the ER and Golgi.

Not quite. Glutamate's side chain ends in a carboxylate (COO⁻), which has no nitrogen, so it can't form an N-linked bond. Glutamine, the amide version of glutamate, does have a side-chain nitrogen, but it isn't used for N-linked glycosylation either.

Not quite. Lysine's side-chain amino group is a nitrogen, which makes this tempting, but it isn't the acceptor for enzyme-driven N-linked glycosylation. Lysine amines get other tags instead, like acetyl, methyl or ubiquitin groups. In collagen, sugars attach to the oxygen of hydroxylysine, which makes that O-linked.

p: Glycosylation means attaching sugar chains to a protein. It's common on proteins that are secreted or sit on the cell surface, and it helps with folding, stability and cell recognition.

N-linked glycosylation attaches sugars to the side-chain nitrogen of asparagine. It starts in the rough ER while the protein is still being made, by transferring a pre-built sugar chain all at once. The asparagine has to be in the pattern Asn-X-Ser/Thr.

O-linked glycosylation attaches sugars to the oxygen of a serine or threonine OH. It happens mostly in the Golgi, and the sugars are added one at a time. The letter in the name tells you the atom: N for nitrogen, O for oxygen.

x1A_024.trap: N-linked = asparagine's amide nitrogen (ER). O-linked = serine or threonine OH (Golgi).

fig.cap: Molar absorption coefficients at 280 nm: tryptophan dominates, tyrosine is second, and histidine, leucine and serine contribute essentially nothing.
fig.alt: Bar chart of molar absorption coefficient at 280 nanometers: tryptophan 5500, tyrosine 1490, cystine 125, histidine, leucine and serine about zero.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph; values from Pace et al., Protein Science 1995.

ox: Not quite. Histidine's ring is aromatic, but it's small and absorbs mostly below about 220 nm. At 280 nm its absorbance is close to zero. Being aromatic isn't enough; the ring system has to be big enough to absorb near 280 nm.

Not quite. Leucine's side chain has only single C–C and C–H bonds. Those electrons need much higher-energy light (below 200 nm) to absorb, so leucine is see-through at 280 nm. Side chains with no rings never add to a protein's 280 nm signal.
Not quite. Serine's CH₂OH has only single bonds, and those absorb far into the UV, well below 280 nm. With no ring of alternating double bonds, it doesn't absorb at 280 nm.

Correct. Absorbance at 280 nm comes from rings with alternating double bonds. Tryptophan's indole (a benzene ring fused to a five-membered ring) is the biggest such system among the side chains. Each tryptophan absorbs about 5500 M⁻¹cm⁻¹ at 280 nm, almost four times tyrosine's (about 1490). Using Beer's law, A = εlc, you can turn A280 into a protein concentration.

p: Molecules absorb light when the light has just the right energy to bump an electron to a higher level. Single bonds need very high-energy UV light. Rings with alternating double bonds (conjugated π systems) can absorb lower-energy UV light, and the bigger the ring system, the longer the wavelength it absorbs.
Among the amino acids, only tryptophan and tyrosine have ring systems big enough to absorb strongly at 280 nm. Tryptophan absorbs the most. Phenylalanine absorbs weakly, nearer 257 nm.

Labs use this to measure protein concentration. Beer's law, A = εlc, says absorbance is proportional to concentration, so a higher A280 means more protein (as long as the protein has some Trp or Tyr).

fx.w: Beer's law. A = absorbance (no units), ε = how strongly 1 mol absorbs (M⁻¹cm⁻¹), l = path length of light through the sample (cm), c = concentration (M). Double the concentration and the absorbance doubles.

x1A_025.trap: A280 comes from tryptophan and tyrosine (big aromatic rings). Histidine is aromatic but absorbs far below 280 nm.

fig.cap: Lysine's NH₃⁺ and glutamate's COO⁻ attract each other across a short distance: a salt bridge. The table shows what each other interaction would require.
fig.alt: Lysine side chain ending in NH₃⁺ and glutamate side chain ending in COO⁻ connected by a dashed line labeled ionic attraction. Below, salt bridge is marked correct; disulfide needs two cysteine thiols; hydrophobic interaction needs nonpolar side chains; peptide bond joins backbone groups.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Correct. At pH 7, lysine's side-chain amine (pKₐ ≈ 10.5) still has its proton, NH₃⁺, and glutamate's side-chain carboxyl (pKₐ ≈ 4.2) has lost its proton, COO⁻. Opposite charges a short distance apart attract, and the N–H groups can also hydrogen-bond to the carboxylate oxygens. This combined attraction is a salt bridge, one of the weak bonds that help hold a folded protein's shape.

Not quite. A disulfide bond is a covalent S–S bond made by oxidizing the SH groups of two cysteines. Neither lysine nor glutamate has sulfur, so they can't form one. Disulfides are also mostly found in proteins outside the cell, because the inside of the cell tends to break them.

Not quite. Hydrophobic interactions happen between water-avoiding side chains like leucine, valine and phenylalanine. Lysine and glutamate end in charged groups that water loves. Their attraction comes from their charges, not from avoiding water.

Not quite. A peptide bond is a covalent amide between one amino acid's α-carboxyl and the next one's α-amino group, made by the ribosome during translation. It joins backbone groups, not side chains, and it doesn't just form between side chains in a folded protein.

concept.t: Salt bridges between charged side chains
p: Some side chains carry a charge at body pH. Aspartate and glutamate are negative (they've lost a proton from their COOH). Lysine and arginine are positive (they hold an extra proton), and histidine is partly positive.

When a positive and a negative side chain end up close together in a folded protein, they attract like opposite ends of two magnets. That's a salt bridge. It's a noncovalent bond, weaker than a covalent one, but many of them together help hold the protein's shape.

Each kind of interaction has its own requirements. Salt bridges need opposite charges. Disulfides need two cysteines. Hydrophobic interactions need water-avoiding side chains. Hydrogen bonds need an H on N or O near another N or O.

x1A_026.trap: Match the interaction to the chemistry. Oppositely charged side chains form salt bridges; only cysteines form disulfides.
mem: Negative at pH 7: D (aspartate), E (glutamate)
Positive at pH 7: K (lysine), R (arginine), H (histidine, partly)
Salt bridge = + next to −
x1A_026.sc: Opposites attract: one positive (K, R, H) plus one negative (D, E) means a salt bridge.
x1A_026.mn: D and E are the two negatives; H, K, R are the three positives.
x1A_026.plain: Lysine (positive) and glutamate (negative) act like the opposite poles of two magnets: they snap together into a salt bridge.

fig.cap: Each answer as a before-and-after pair with side chains shaded. Only leucine to isoleucine keeps size, shape and polarity nearly unchanged.
fig.alt: Four panels of amino acid pairs: leucine to aspartate (nonpolar to charged), glycine to tryptophan (smallest to bulkiest), leucine to isoleucine (isomers, both nonpolar, correct), and lysine to glutamate (plus one to minus one charge).
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Not quite. Leucine is water-avoiding and usually buried in the protein's core. Aspartate is negatively charged at body pH. Swapping one for the other would push a charge into the core, where there's no water around it, or break up how the core packs together. That's a drastic swap, not a conservative one.

Not quite. Glycine's side chain is just an H, which lets the backbone bend in unusual ways. Tryptophan has the biggest side chain of all, a double ring. Replacing glycine with tryptophan takes away that flexibility, say in a tight turn, and jams in a bulky group that may not fit. That's a huge change in size and shape.

Correct. A conservative mutation uses an amino acid that's similar in size, shape and chemistry, so the structure is least likely to change. Leucine and isoleucine are isomers: both side chains are C₄H₉, branched, and water-avoiding. They only differ in where the branch sits (one carbon further out in leucine), so isoleucine can usually fill leucine's spot in the core.

Not quite. Lysine is positive (+1) and glutamate is negative (−1) at pH 7.4. Both are charged and water-loving, but flipping the charge breaks any salt bridge the lysine made and can cause repulsion with nearby negative groups. A conservative swap for lysine would be arginine, which has the same charge.

p: A point mutation can swap one amino acid for another. How much that matters depends on how different the two are.

A conservative swap keeps the same general properties: size, shape, polarity and charge. Leucine to isoleucine, aspartate to glutamate, and lysine to arginine are classic examples. The protein usually folds and works about the same.

A drastic (nonconservative) swap changes one of those properties a lot: putting a charge in the core, flipping a charge, or swapping a tiny side chain for a huge one. These are much more likely to change the protein's shape or function.

x1A_027.trap: Both residues being charged isn't conservative if the charges are opposite. Check size, polarity and the sign of the charge together.

fig.cap: Schematic: in HbA the charged Glu at β6 stays hydrated; in HbS the nonpolar Val at β6 docks into a hydrophobic pocket on a neighboring deoxy tetramer, building fibers.
fig.alt: Cartoon of two pairs of hemoglobin circles. HbA has a red E on its surface that does not bind the neighbor's pocket. HbS has an orange V that fits a hydrophobic pocket on the neighbor, leading to long fibers and sickled cells. Tags mark the hydrophobic patch correct and disulfides, iron oxidation and blocked assembly wrong.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest schematic; content from standard biochemistry texts (Lehninger, Principles of Biochemistry).

ox: Not quite. Disulfide bonds only form between the SH groups of cysteines. Valine's side chain has no sulfur, so the mutation can't make one. The HbS fibers are held together by noncovalent contacts, which is why they can come apart again when the hemoglobin picks oxygen back up.

Not quite. Oxidizing heme iron from Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ makes methemoglobin, which can't carry O₂. That's caused by oxidizing chemicals or by mutations right near the heme, not by this surface change. In HbS the iron stays Fe²⁺ and still binds oxygen.

Not quite. HbS still assembles into normal α₂β₂ tetramers (four chains: two α, two β) and still picks up and drops off oxygen. The problem is between tetramers, not inside one: deoxy HbS molecules stick to each other. If they couldn't assemble, there'd be nothing to stick together.

Correct. In sickle-cell disease, one DNA change swaps glutamate for valine at position 6 of β-globin, on the protein's surface. The charged glutamate was surrounded by water; the water-avoiding valine makes a sticky patch. In the deoxy form, a matching water-avoiding pocket is exposed on other HbS molecules, so the valine of one fits into the pocket of the next. These contacts chain the molecules into long fibers that warp red cells into a sickle shape.

concept.t: Sickle-cell disease: one amino acid, big effect
p: Hemoglobin is made of four chains, two α and two β. In sickle-cell disease, a single DNA change swaps glutamate for valine at position 6 of the β chain. That spot is on the outside of the protein.
Glutamate is charged and comfortable in water. Valine is water-avoiding. Putting valine on the surface creates a sticky patch that wants to hide from water.

When hemoglobin drops off its oxygen, its shape shifts and exposes a matching water-avoiding pocket. The valine on one molecule plugs into the pocket on the next, over and over, building long fibers. These fibers bend red blood cells into a stiff sickle shape that can block small blood vessels.

x1A_028.trap: HbS isn't misfolded, and it can still bind O₂. Its deoxy form clumps together through a new water-avoiding contact between molecules.

fig.cap: Electrophoresis at pH 6.0: aspartate (pI 2.8) is negative and runs to the anode, glycine (pI 6.0) stays at the origin, and lysine (pI 9.7) is positive and runs to the cathode.
fig.alt: Gel strip with the cathode (minus) on the left and anode (plus) on the right. Aspartate band moves right toward the anode, glycine stays at the origin, lysine moves left toward the cathode.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram using the pI values in the question.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Not quite. Glycine's pI is 6.0, the same as the buffer pH. At its pI a molecule has zero net charge (mostly the zwitterion ⁺H₃N–CH₂–COO⁻, with one + and one − that cancel), so the electric field doesn't push it either way. Glycine stays near where it was loaded.

Not quite. Lysine's pI is 9.7, above the buffer pH of 6.0. When pH is below the pI, a molecule holds extra protons and is positive (lysine is about +1 here). Positive molecules move toward the negative electrode, the cathode, which is the opposite direction from the anode.

Correct. The anode is the positive electrode, so only negative molecules move toward it. Aspartate's pI is 2.8, and the buffer pH (6.0) is well above it.
