When pH is above the pI, a molecule has lost extra protons and is negative: at pH 6 both carboxyls are COO⁻ (−2) and the amino group is NH₃⁺ (+1), so the net charge is −2 + 1 = −1. Aspartate moves toward the anode.

Not quite. All three have a zwitterion backbone, with one + and one −, but that doesn't make every one of them neutral overall. Aspartate has an extra negative side chain and lysine an extra positive one. Only glycine, whose pI equals the buffer pH, has zero net charge. The other two move.

p: Electrophoresis separates molecules by pulling them through a gel with an electric field. Negative molecules move toward the positive electrode (the anode). Positive molecules move toward the negative electrode (the cathode).

To know which way an amino acid or protein moves, compare the buffer pH to its pI. pH above pI: it has given up extra protons, so it's negative. pH below pI: it's holding extra protons, so it's positive. pH equal to pI: net charge zero, so it doesn't move.
Memory hook: in electrophoresis, the anode is positive. 'An ion' that's negative (an anion) goes to the anode.

x1A_029.trap: pH above pI means negative, which means it moves to the anode (+). Don't flip the sign, and don't assume a zwitterion is always neutral overall.

fig.cap: A pH 3 to 10 gradient with the anode at the acidic end. The protein loaded at pH 8 is negative, moves toward the anode, and stops at pH 5.5, its pI.
fig.alt: Horizontal gel with a pH gradient from 3 at the anode (plus, left) to 10 at the cathode (minus, right). A negatively charged protein loaded at pH 8 moves left and stops as a green band at pH 5.5.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; band position computed on a linear pH 3 to 10 gradient.

ox: Not quite. The stopping point (pH 5.5) is right, but the direction is wrong. At pH 8, above the pI of 5.5, the protein is negative. Negative molecules are pushed away from the negative cathode and toward the positive anode. It would move toward the cathode only if it started at a pH below its pI.

Correct. The IEF gel has a fixed pH gradient: low pH at the anode (+) and high pH at the cathode (−). Starting at pH 8, above its pI, the protein is negative and moves toward the anode, which is also toward lower pH. As the gel gets more acidic, the protein picks up protons and becomes less negative. At pH 5.5 its net charge is zero, so it stops in a sharp band. If it drifts past, it turns positive and gets pushed back.

Not quite. Running to the end of the gel is what happens in regular electrophoresis at one pH, where the charge never changes. In IEF the pH changes along the gel, so the protein's charge drops as it travels. It stops when its charge hits zero at pH 5.5, long before the end.
Not quite. A protein only stays still where the local pH equals its pI. At pH 8, the pI of 5.5 is 8 − 5.5 = 2.5 units lower, so the protein has a sizeable negative charge and moves in the field.

p: Isoelectric focusing (IEF) separates proteins by their pI, the pH where their net charge is zero. The gel contains a pH gradient that runs from acidic at the anode (+) to basic at the cathode (−).

A protein placed where the pH is above its pI is negative, so it moves toward the anode and into more acidic gel. A protein placed where the pH is below its pI is positive, so it moves toward the cathode and into more basic gel. Either way, it's moving toward the spot where pH equals its pI.
Once it gets there, its charge is zero and it stops. That's why IEF gives sharp bands: each protein 'focuses' at its own pI and stays there.

x1A_030.trap: In IEF a protein doesn't run off the gel. Its charge drops to zero where pH = pI, and it stops there.

fig.cap: Charge of each ionizable group of Lys-Glu-His at pH 7.0, computed from its pKₐ. The positive and negative contributions cancel to about zero.
fig.alt: Bar chart of charges at pH 7: N-terminal amino +0.91, Lys side chain +1.00, Glu side chain −1.00, His side chain +0.09, C-terminal carboxyl −1.00; the sum is about 0.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation with the side-chain pKₐ values in the question and typical terminal pKₐ values (8.0 and 3.5).

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Not quite. −1 is what you get if you count Lys (+1), Glu (−1) and the C-terminus (−1) but leave out the N-terminal amino group. In a peptide, the first residue's amino group is free (pKₐ about 8), so at pH 7 it mostly keeps its proton and adds about +1. Forgetting the ends is the most common slip in peptide charge problems.

Correct. Compare pH 7.0 with each group's pKₐ. N-terminal NH₃⁺ (≈ 8): pH below pKₐ, keeps its proton, +1. Lys side chain (10.5): +1. Glu side chain (4.2): pH above pKₐ, lost its proton, −1. His side chain (6.0): pH above pKₐ, mostly neutral, about +0.09. C-terminal COO⁻ (≈ 3.5): −1. Sum: +1 + 1 − 1 + 0 − 1 = 0. The α-groups in the middle of the chain are tied up in peptide bonds and don't carry charge.

Not quite. +1 comes from counting histidine's side chain as fully protonated. Its pKₐ is 6.0, so at pH 7.0 the unprotonated form wins 10 to 1, and only 1 in 11 (about 9%) carries a proton. Histidine adds about +0.09, not +1, so the total stays near 0.

Not quite. +2 counts the two positive amines (N-terminus and Lys) but skips both negative groups: the Glu side chain and the C-terminal carboxyl. At pH 7 both are far above their pKₐ values (4.2 and about 3.5), so each has lost its proton and adds −1.

p: Inside a peptide, most amino and carboxyl groups are used up in peptide bonds and can't carry charge. What's left are the two ends (a free amino group at the N-terminus and a free carboxyl at the C-terminus) plus any side chains that can gain or lose a proton.

For each one, compare the pH to its pKₐ. Below the pKₐ, the group keeps its proton; above it, the group loses it. Then remember what that means for charge: amines are +1 with the proton and 0 without; carboxyls are 0 with it and −1 without.
Histidine is the tricky one at pH 7, because its pKₐ (6.0) is close by. It's only about 9% protonated, so it counts as roughly neutral.

steps: Write the formula: net charge = sum of the charges on every group that can gain or lose a proton.
Write down the values: pH = 7.0; N-terminus pKₐ ≈ 8 (a typical peptide value, not given in the question); Lys 10.5; Glu 4.2; His 6.0; C-terminus pKₐ ≈ 3.5 (also a typical value).
N-terminus: 7.0 is below 8, so it keeps its proton: +1 (about +0.91).
Lys: 7.0 is below 10.5, so +1. Glu: 7.0 is above 4.2, so −1. C-terminus: 7.0 is above 3.5, so −1.
His: 7.0 is 1 unit above 6.0, so only 1 in 11 (about 9%) is protonated: about +0.09.
x1A_031.trap: Count the free ends of the peptide, and treat histidine as mostly neutral at pH 7.

fig.cap: Gly-Lys-Asp as it exists at pH 1, with the two NH₃⁺ groups shaded blue and the two neutral COOH groups shaded gray. The tally gives +2.
fig.alt: Structure of the tripeptide Gly-Lys-Asp fully protonated: NH₃⁺ at the N-terminus and on the lysine side chain, COOH on the aspartate side chain and C-terminus. A table sums the charges to +2.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Not quite. 0 would need negative charges to cancel the positive ones, but at pH 1 there aren't any. Both carboxyls (the Asp side chain, pKₐ 3.9, and the C-terminus, pKₐ about 3) have pKₐ values above pH 1, so they keep their protons as neutral COOH. A net charge near 0 is what this peptide has closer to neutral pH.
Not quite. +1 counts only one positive group, usually the N-terminus. Lysine's side-chain amine (pKₐ 10.5) is also protonated at pH 1, nearly 10 units below its pKₐ, so it adds a second +1.

Correct. At pH 1 the solution is more acidic than every pKₐ in the peptide, so every group holds its proton. The N-terminal NH₃⁺ is +1 and the Lys side-chain NH₃⁺ is +1. The Asp side chain and the C-terminus are COOH, which is neutral (0). Net charge = +1 + 1 + 0 + 0 = +2. The α-groups in the middle of the chain are in peptide bonds and don't carry charge.

Not quite. +3 treats the protonated Asp side chain as positive. A carboxyl goes from COO⁻ (−1) to COOH (0) when it picks up a proton, and that's as far as it goes. Only basic groups like amines turn positive when protonated. With two amines here (N-terminus and Lys), the most this peptide can be is +2.

concept.t: Peptide charge at very low pH
p: At very low pH there are lots of protons around, so every group grabs one. That's true whenever the pH is below all of the groups' pKₐ values.

What 'grabbing a proton' does to the charge depends on the group. An amine goes from NH₂ (0) to NH₃⁺ (+1). A carboxyl goes from COO⁻ (−1) to COOH (0). So at low pH, amines are positive and carboxyls are neutral.
That means the maximum positive charge of a peptide equals its number of basic groups: the N-terminus plus any Lys, Arg or His side chains. Carboxyls never add positive charge.

steps: Write the formula: net charge = sum of the charges on every group that can gain or lose a proton.
Write down the values: pH = 1; N-terminal NH₃⁺ pKₐ ≈ 8; Lys side chain 10.5; Asp side chain 3.9; C-terminal COOH pKₐ ≈ 3.
pH 1 is below every pKₐ, so every group keeps its proton.
Amines with a proton are +1: N-terminus +1, Lys +1.
Carboxyls with a proton are neutral: Asp COOH 0, C-terminal COOH 0.
x1A_032.trap: A protonated carboxyl is neutral, not positive. Only basic groups add positive charge.

fig.cap: The four choices with side chains shaded. Methionine's sulfur sits between two carbons (thioether); cysteine's carries an H (thiol); serine and threonine have –OH and no sulfur.
fig.alt: Structures of methionine with CH₂CH₂-S-CH₃ shaded, cysteine with CH₂-SH shaded, serine with CH₂-OH shaded and threonine with CH(OH)CH₃ shaded; methionine is marked as the thioether.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.1 Structures of Amino Acids

ox: Correct. A thioether is a sulfur bonded to two carbons, C–S–C. Methionine's side chain is CH₂CH₂–S–CH₃, so its sulfur sits between a CH₂ and a CH₃. With no H on the sulfur, methionine can't form disulfide bonds and is fairly water-avoiding. In the form S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), it donates the methyl group used in many methylation reactions.

Not quite. Cysteine has sulfur too, but its side chain is CH₂–SH, a thiol: sulfur bonded to one carbon and one hydrogen. That S–H is what lets two cysteines link up into a disulfide (S–S) bond. A thiol isn't a thioether.
Not quite. Serine's side chain is CH₂OH, an alcohol. It has oxygen, not sulfur, so it can't be a thioether. Serine is the oxygen version of cysteine (OH instead of SH).
Not quite. Threonine's side chain is CH(OH)CH₃, an alcohol with no sulfur. It's polar and can be phosphorylated or get O-linked sugars, but it has no thiol and no thioether.

p: Only two standard amino acids contain sulfur: cysteine and methionine. The difference is what the sulfur is bonded to.

Cysteine's sulfur is bonded to one carbon and one hydrogen (SH, a thiol). That hydrogen can be removed, so two cysteines can be oxidized to form a disulfide bond (S–S), which can cross-link parts of a protein.

Methionine's sulfur is bonded to two carbons (C–S–C, a thioether). With no H, it can't form disulfides. Methionine is also the first amino acid in nearly every newly made protein, since the start codon AUG codes for it.

x1A_033.trap: Cysteine and methionine both have sulfur, but only methionine has S between two carbons (a thioether). Cysteine has SH (a thiol).

fig.cap: The four choices as they exist at pH 7.4, side chains shaded. Glutamine's amide is polar but carries no charge.
fig.alt: Structures of glutamate (charged −1), isoleucine (nonpolar), glutamine (polar uncharged, correct) and lysine (charged +1) with side chains shaded.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Not quite. Glutamate is polar, but it's charged. Its side-chain carboxyl (pKₐ ≈ 4.2) is more than three units below pH 7.4, so it has lost its proton and carries −1. It belongs with the acidic (negative) amino acids, not the polar uncharged ones.
Not quite. Isoleucine's side chain, CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, is only carbon and hydrogen. It's water-avoiding and uncharged. It matches the 'uncharged' part but not the 'polar' part.

Correct. Glutamine's side chain ends in an amide, CH₂CH₂C(=O)NH₂. Its C=O and N–H bonds are very polar, so glutamine hydrogen-bonds with water. But amides aren't acids or bases in water: the N–H pKₐ is about 15 to 17, and the nitrogen's lone pair is shared with the C=O, so it doesn't pick up a proton. Glutamine stays uncharged at body pH.
Not quite. Lysine is polar, but its side-chain amine (pKₐ ≈ 10.5) holds its proton at pH 7.4, giving it +1. It belongs with the basic (positive) amino acids.

p: Polar and charged aren't the same thing. A polar group has electrons shared unevenly, like O–H or C=O, so it has slightly positive and slightly negative ends that attract water. A charged group has a full + or − because it gained or lost a proton.
Every charged side chain is also polar, but not every polar side chain is charged. The polar uncharged amino acids are serine, threonine, cysteine, asparagine, glutamine and tyrosine.
Asparagine and glutamine are easy to confuse with aspartate and glutamate. The '-ate' ones have COO⁻ and are negative. The '-ine' ones have CONH₂, an amide, and stay neutral.

x1A_034.trap: Polar doesn't mean charged. Glutamine and asparagine are polar amides with no charge, unlike glutamate and aspartate.

fig.cap: The ratio [COO⁻] : [COOH] for aspartate's side chain on a log scale against pH. At pH 4.9 (one unit above pKₐ 3.9) the ratio is 10 : 1; the other choices belong to pH 3.9, 2.9 and 5.9.
fig.alt: Straight line of log ratio versus pH passing through 1 to 1 at pH 3.9. Points mark 10 to 1 at pH 4.9 (correct), 1 to 10 at pH 2.9, and 100 to 1 at pH 5.9.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation with the pKₐ in the question.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Correct. Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKₐ + log([A⁻] ÷ [HA]). Rearranged, log([A⁻] ÷ [HA]) = pH − pKₐ = 4.9 − 3.9 = 1, so the ratio is 10¹ = 10. There are 10 COO⁻ side chains for every COOH. Since the pH is above the pKₐ, the deprotonated form is the majority, as it should be.

Not quite. 1 : 10 is the ratio flipped. It would be right at pH 2.9, one unit below the pKₐ, where the protonated form wins. When pH is above pKₐ, the group is mostly deprotonated, so the deprotonated number has to be the bigger one.

Not quite. A 1 : 1 ratio means log(ratio) = 0, which only happens when pH = pKₐ, here pH 3.9. At pH 4.9 the solution is one unit more basic, so the balance shifts 10-fold toward the deprotonated form.
Not quite. 100 : 1 means log(ratio) = 2, which needs pH − pKₐ = 2, so pH 5.9. Each pH unit changes the ratio by 10 times, not 100, so one unit above the pKₐ gives only 10 : 1.

p: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation links pH, pKₐ, and the ratio of a group's two forms: pH = pKₐ + log([A⁻] ÷ [HA]). [A⁻] is the form without the proton and [HA] is the form with it.

The shortcut: look at pH − pKₐ. If it's 0, the ratio is 1 : 1. If it's +1, the deprotonated form wins 10 : 1. If it's +2, it wins 100 : 1. If it's negative, the protonated form wins by the same factors.
Sanity check every time: when pH is above pKₐ, the deprotonated form should be the bigger number.

fm.f: pH = pKₐ + log([A⁻] ÷ [HA]), where [A⁻] = deprotonated form (COO⁻), [HA] = protonated form (COOH)
fm.why: Henderson-Hasselbalch turns a pH and a pKₐ into the ratio of the two forms.
fm.nc: Log just reads off the exponent of 10: if log(ratio) = 1, ratio = 10¹ = 10.

steps: Write the formula: pH = pKₐ + log([A⁻] ÷ [HA]).
Write down the values: pH = 4.9, pKₐ = 3.9.
Plug in: 4.9 = 3.9 + log(ratio).
Subtract 3.9 from both sides: log(ratio) = 4.9 − 3.9 = 1.
Log reads off the exponent of 10, so ratio = 10¹ = 10.
Deprotonated : protonated = 10 : 1. Check: pH is above pKₐ, so the deprotonated form should win, and it does.
x1A_035.trap: pH above pKₐ means the deprotonated form is the bigger number. One unit is a 10-fold change, not 100-fold.

fig.cap: Percentage of alanine present as cation, zwitterion and anion across the pH scale, computed from pKₐ 2.3 and 9.7. At pH 7 the zwitterion is about 99.8%.
fig.alt: Three species curves: the cation falls from 100 percent below pH 2.3, the zwitterion is near 100 percent from pH 4 to 8, and the anion rises above pH 9.7. A dashed line at pH 7 marks the zwitterion at 99.8 percent.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from alanine's pKₐ values (2.3 and 9.7).

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.1 Structures of Amino Acids

ox: Not quite. The fully uncharged form, with NH₂ and COOH, is how amino acids are often drawn, but in water it's a tiny minority at every pH. The carboxyl (pKₐ ≈ 2.3) is a much stronger acid than the NH₃⁺ group (pKₐ ≈ 9.7), so the proton moves from the carboxyl to the amine. The zwitterion outnumbers the uncharged form by roughly 10⁵ (100,000) to 1.
Not quite. ⁺H₃N–CH(CH₃)–COOH has both groups protonated, net +1. It only wins below pH 2.3, the carboxyl's pKₐ. At pH 7, almost five units above that, the carboxyl has lost its proton.
Not quite. H₂N–CH(CH₃)–COO⁻ has both groups deprotonated, net −1. It only wins above pH 9.7, the amino group's pKₐ. At pH 7 the amino group is still more than 99% protonated.

Correct. Compare pH 7 with each pKₐ. The carboxyl (pKₐ ≈ 2.3) is below pH 7, so it has lost its proton: COO⁻. The amino group (pKₐ ≈ 9.7) is above pH 7, so it keeps its proton: NH₃⁺. That gives the zwitterion ⁺H₃N–CH(CH₃)–COO⁻, net charge 0. Worked out from the pKₐ values, about 99.8% of alanine is in this form at pH 7.

p: A zwitterion is a molecule with both a positive and a negative charge that cancel out, so its net charge is zero. Amino acids in water near neutral pH are zwitterions.

It happens because the carboxyl group is a fairly strong acid (pKₐ around 2) and the amino group is a base that holds its proton until about pH 9 to 10. Anywhere between those, the carboxyl is COO⁻ and the amine is NH₃⁺.
Textbooks often draw amino acids as H₂N–CHR–COOH, fully uncharged. That's just a drawing habit. In water, that form is basically never the main one.

x1A_036.trap: The uncharged H₂N–CHR–COOH drawing is just a convention. In water at neutral pH, the real form is the zwitterion.

fig.cap: Acetic acid (pKₐ ≈ 4.8) and glycine's α-COOH (pKₐ ≈ 2.3). The shaded –NH₃⁺ next to the carboxyl stabilizes the carboxylate and makes the acid more than 100 times stronger.
fig.alt: Acetic acid structure with the COOH shaded and pKₐ about 4.8 beside glycine in its cationic form with NH₃⁺ shaded and pKₐ about 2.3. Tags mark NH₃⁺ stabilization correct and resonance, hydration and size wrong.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app. pKₐ values are standard textbook values.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 20.4 Substituent Effects on Acidity

ox: Not quite. Resonance would need an unbroken chain of double bonds linking the side chain to the COO⁻. The α-carbon has only single bonds and breaks any such chain. And glycine, with no real side chain, has the same low pKₐ (about 2.3). So resonance with the side chain can't be the reason.

Correct. An acid's strength depends on how stable its conjugate base is. In an amino acid, a positive NH₃⁺ sits right next to the carboxyl. It pulls electrons through the bonds (inductive effect), and its + charge directly steadies the − charge on COO⁻. A more stable conjugate base means a stronger acid, so the carboxyl's pKₐ drops from about 4.8 to about 2.3, more than 100 times more acidic.

Not quite. Water does affect pKₐ values, but differences in how water hydrogen-bonds to two small carboxylic acids wouldn't shift the pKₐ by more than two units on their own. The big difference between acetic acid and an amino acid is the charged NH₃⁺ right next to the carboxyl.

Not quite. Spreading a charge over a bigger area can steady an anion, but just adding atoms doesn't do that unless they're linked by double bonds or pull electrons. Glycine is barely bigger than acetic acid, yet it's over 100 times more acidic. The nearby positive NH₃⁺ does the work, not size.

p: An acid's strength is measured by its pKₐ: lower pKₐ means stronger acid. The key question is how stable the leftover piece (the conjugate base) is after the proton leaves. The more stable it is, the more willing the acid is to give up its proton.

Nearby groups that pull electrons toward themselves help steady a negative charge. This is the inductive effect, and it gets weaker with distance. A nearby positive charge helps even more, because it directly attracts the negative charge.
In amino acids, the NH₃⁺ sits on the very next carbon from the COOH. That's why an amino acid's carboxyl (pKₐ about 2) is much more acidic than acetic acid's (about 4.8).

x1A_037.trap: Ask what stabilizes the conjugate base. Here it's the neighboring NH₃⁺ (inductive and electrostatic), not resonance or size.

fig.cap: Percent of cysteine present as thiolate against pH for pKₐ 8.3 (normal) and 6.5 (next to His). At pH 7.4 the shifted cysteine is 89% thiolate versus 11% normally.
fig.alt: Two rising sigmoid curves of percent thiolate versus pH, centered at pH 6.5 (green) and 8.3 (red). At the dashed line pH 7.4, green is at 89 percent and red at 11 percent.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation with the pKₐ values in the question.

ox: Not quite. That would be true for a normal cysteine (pKₐ 8.3), which is about 89% protonated at pH 7.4. But the histidine drops the pKₐ to 6.5. With pH 7.4 now above the pKₐ, the protonated SH becomes the minority (about 11%). Lowering a pKₐ favors losing the proton.

Correct. With pKₐ 6.5 and pH 7.4, pH − pKₐ = 7.4 − 6.5 = 0.9, so [S⁻] ÷ [SH] = 10⁰·⁹ ≈ 7.9. That means about 7.9 ÷ 8.9 ≈ 89% of the cysteine is the thiolate anion. Thiolate has a full negative charge and a lone pair ready to attack, so it's a much stronger nucleophile than SH. The nearby positive histidine steadies the thiolate, which is how cysteine proteases like caspases and papain work.

Not quite. A disulfide bond needs two SH groups, one from each of two cysteines. Histidine's ring has nitrogen, not sulfur, so it can't form an S–S bond. The histidine-cysteine pairing is an ion pair plus a hydrogen bond, not a covalent link.

Not quite. A thiol is an acid: losing its proton turns neutral SH into negative S⁻. Cysteine's side chain is never positive in the body. The positive charge in this pair is on the histidine, and that's what steadies the thiolate.

concept.t: Tuning a pKₐ to make a better nucleophile
p: A nucleophile is a group with an electron pair it can donate to attack another atom. A negatively charged group is usually a much better nucleophile than its neutral form. For cysteine, the thiolate (S⁻) is far more reactive than the thiol (SH).

Normally cysteine's SH has pKₐ ≈ 8.3, so at body pH (7.4) only about 11% is thiolate. Enzymes can change that. A nearby positive group, like a protonated histidine, steadies the negative S⁻, which lowers the pKₐ.
With the pKₐ dropped to 6.5, the same cysteine is about 89% thiolate at pH 7.4. That's how cysteine proteases get a reactive cysteine ready to attack peptide bonds.

fm.f: pH = pKₐ + log([S⁻] ÷ [SH]), where [S⁻] = thiolate (deprotonated), [SH] = thiol (protonated)
fm.why: Henderson-Hasselbalch turns pH and pKₐ into the ratio of the two forms.
fm.nc: 10⁰·⁹ is a bit under 10¹ = 10; it's about 7.9.

fm.f: fraction thiolate = [S⁻] ÷ ([S⁻] + [SH]), where [S⁻] and [SH] are the amounts of each form
fm.v: [S⁻] = 7.9 parts; [SH] = 1 part; fraction = ?
fm.why: A percentage is one part divided by the total of both forms.
fm.nc: With the normal pKₐ of 8.3, the same math gives only about 11% thiolate.

steps: Write the formula: pH = pKₐ + log([S⁻] ÷ [SH]).
Write down the values: pH = 7.4; new pKₐ = 6.5.
Plug in: log(ratio) = pH − pKₐ = 7.4 − 6.5 = 0.9.
Undo the log: ratio = 10⁰·⁹ ≈ 7.9, so about 7.9 S⁻ for every 1 SH.
Find the share that's thiolate: 7.9 ÷ (7.9 + 1) = 7.9 ÷ 8.9 ≈ 0.89, about 89%.
Compare with the normal pKₐ of 8.3: pH − pKₐ = 7.4 − 8.3 = −0.9, ratio = 10⁻⁰·⁹ ≈ 0.126, share = 0.126 ÷ 1.126 ≈ 0.11, about 11%.
x1A_038.trap: A lower pKₐ means more deprotonated at a given pH. For a thiol, deprotonated means the negative thiolate.

fig.cap: SDS-PAGE sample preparation: β-mercaptoethanol reduces the disulfide between chains, while SDS (with heat) unfolds them and supplies the negative charge.
fig.alt: Schematic of a two-chain protein linked by an S-S bond turning into two separate unfolded chains coated with negative charges and ending in SH groups. A table lists β-mercaptoethanol reduces disulfides, SDS denatures and adds negative charge, heat speeds unfolding.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest schematic diagram.

ox: Not quite. Breaking peptide bonds takes hydrolysis, done by proteases or by strong acid with heat. β-mercaptoethanol (HS–CH₂CH₂–OH) is a small reducing agent that only reacts with disulfide bonds and leaves the backbone alone. Cutting peptide bonds would ruin the size measurement SDS-PAGE is meant to make.

Not quite. Giving every protein the same kind of negative coating is the job of SDS (sodium dodecyl sulfate), a negatively charged detergent that sticks along the unfolded chain. That drowns out the protein's own charge, so movement depends on size. β-mercaptoethanol doesn't carry a charge that could do this.

Not quite. SDS-PAGE samples are unfolded on purpose, with SDS and heat. β-mercaptoethanol helps by removing disulfide cross-links that would hold parts of the fold together. Native PAGE, which keeps proteins folded, leaves out both SDS and the reducing agent.

Correct. Disulfide bonds (S–S) are covalent, so they survive SDS, which only breaks noncovalent interactions. β-mercaptoethanol reduces each disulfide into two free SH groups (it gets oxidized itself in the process). That separates subunits linked by disulfides between chains and fully opens chains with disulfides inside them, so each chain runs at the spot set by its own mass.

p: SDS-PAGE separates proteins by size. The protein is boiled with SDS, a detergent that unfolds it and coats it with negative charge in proportion to its length. In the gel, smaller chains move faster through the mesh.
SDS breaks hydrophobic contacts, ionic bonds and hydrogen bonds, but not covalent bonds. Disulfide bonds between cysteines are covalent, so they stay intact unless you add a reducing agent.
A reducing agent like β-mercaptoethanol or DTT breaks S–S bonds into SH groups. Running a sample with and without it tells you whether chains are linked by disulfides.

x1A_039.trap: SDS breaks noncovalent bonds and gives the charge. β-mercaptoethanol only breaks disulfides.

fig.cap: Gel lanes for the observed result (green) and what the two other models would show (red): a noncovalent dimer runs at 50 kDa in both lanes, and a 60 + 40 kDa disulfide dimer gives two bands when reduced.
fig.alt: Schematic SDS-PAGE gel with a molecular weight ladder from 150 to 20 kDa. Observed lanes: 100 kDa without β-mercaptoethanol and 50 kDa with it. Noncovalent dimer lanes: 50 kDa in both. 60 plus 40 lanes: 100 kDa without and two bands at 60 and 40 kDa with reducing agent.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; band positions computed as linear in log(molecular weight).

ox: Correct. SDS alone breaks all noncovalent contacts, so the 100 kDa form that survives without reducing agent must be held together covalently. Adding reducing agent turns it into 50 kDa, so those covalent links are disulfide bonds. A single 50 kDa band after reduction means every released chain is the same size. So the best answer is two equal 50 kDa chains joined by disulfides: 2 × 50 = 100 kDa.

Not quite. SDS alone separates a noncovalent dimer, because it breaks water-avoiding, ionic and hydrogen-bond contacts. That dimer would run at 50 kDa even without reducing agent. The 100 kDa band seen without reducing agent rules this out.

Not quite. β-mercaptoethanol and similar reducing agents only act on disulfide bonds. They don't break peptide bonds. A single 100 kDa chain with only internal disulfides would still run near 100 kDa after reduction, not at 50 kDa.

Not quite. Two different chains of 60 and 40 kDa linked by a disulfide would also run at 60 + 40 = 100 kDa without reducing agent. But after reduction they'd separate into two bands, at 60 and 40 kDa. The single 50 kDa band shows both chains are the same size.

p: Running the same protein with and without a reducing agent tells you how its chains are held together. SDS is always there, so noncovalent contacts are always broken.
If the size is the same in both lanes, the chains aren't linked by disulfides (or it's a single chain). If the size drops only when reducing agent is added, the chains were linked by disulfide bonds.

Count the bands after reduction. One band means all the chains are the same size. Two or more bands mean different chains. Dividing the unreduced size by the reduced size tells you how many equal chains there are.

steps: Write the formula: number of chains = unreduced size ÷ reduced size (when all chains are the same size).
Write down the values: without reducing agent (SDS only) = 100 kDa; with reducing agent = 50 kDa, one band.
SDS alone didn't split it, so the chains are linked covalently.
The reducing agent did split it, so those covalent links are disulfide bonds.
Only one band after reduction, so all chains are the same size.
Plug in: 100 kDa ÷ 50 kDa = 2 chains of 50 kDa each.
x1A_040.trap: SDS alone already separates noncovalent subunits. Only disulfide-linked subunits need the reducing agent to come apart.

fig.cap: Schematic cross-section of a soluble globular protein: nonpolar side chains such as Phe pack in the core, while charged Lys, Arg, Glu and Asp line the water-facing surface.
fig.alt: A circle representing a protein surrounded by water. The inner core contains Phe, Leu, Ile and Val; the rim carries charged Lys+, Arg+, Glu- and Asp-. Tags mark phenylalanine in the core as correct and lysine, glutamate and arginine on the surface.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest schematic diagram.

ox: Not quite. Lysine's side chain ends in NH₃⁺ at body pH. Burying a charge in the oily core would strip away the water around it, which costs a lot of energy, with nothing to replace it. So lysine almost always sits on the surface, where its long, floppy side chain lets the charged end reach the water.

Not quite. Glutamate's side chain is negatively charged at pH 7.4 and surrounded by water. Like other charged residues, it prefers the surface, where it can also form salt bridges or bind metal ions. A buried glutamate usually means it has a special job, like in an active site.

Correct. Phenylalanine's side chain is a ring of carbon and hydrogen that can't hydrogen-bond with water. When the protein folds, burying these side chains in the core frees the water molecules that were forced into neat cages around them. Water gains freedom (entropy goes up), and that's the main push behind folding. So phenylalanine, leucine, isoleucine, valine and methionine pile up in the core.

Not quite. Arginine's side chain is positively charged at body pH (pKₐ ≈ 12.5) and forms many hydrogen bonds with water. Like lysine and glutamate, it usually sits on the surface, often grabbing phosphate groups or other negative molecules.

concept.t: The hydrophobic effect and protein folding
p: Water molecules like to hydrogen-bond with each other. When a water-avoiding side chain sits in water, the water around it has to arrange itself into a tidy cage, which lowers water's freedom (its entropy). That's unfavorable.

When a protein folds, it tucks those water-avoiding side chains into the middle, away from water. The water cages break up, the water gains freedom, and the overall energy drops. This hydrophobic effect is the main driving force of folding.
The result is a typical pattern: water-avoiding residues (Phe, Leu, Ile, Val, Met) in the core, and charged or polar residues (Lys, Arg, Glu, Asp, Ser) on the surface.

x1A_041.trap: The hydrophobic effect is driven mainly by water gaining freedom (entropy), not by nonpolar groups attracting each other. Charged residues go to the surface.

fig.cap: A 20-residue α-helix of hydrophobic residues spanning the 30 Å hydrocarbon core of a phospholipid bilayer, drawn to scale.
fig.alt: Schematic phospholipid bilayer with head groups as circles and tails as lines. An orange helix containing letters L, I, V and F spans the core, with a bracket labeled about 30 angstroms, 20 residues times 1.5 angstroms. Tags mark leucine, isoleucine and valine correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram drawn to scale from a 1.5 Å rise per residue and a 30 Å hydrophobic core.

ox: Not quite. Aspartate, glutamate and lysine are charged at body pH. Moving a charge from water into the oily middle of a membrane costs a huge amount of energy, so charged residues are kept out of the middle of membrane-crossing helices. They usually show up at the ends, near the lipid heads and water.

Not quite. Serine, asparagine and glutamine are polar and hydrogen-bond with water. Inside the membrane there's no water for those hydrogen bonds, so a helix full of these would rather be in water. They're common in loops and on the surfaces of water-soluble proteins.

Not quite. Proline's nitrogen has no H to make the helix's internal hydrogen bonds, and its ring bumps into the turn before it, so it breaks or kinks α-helices. Glycine is so floppy that it weakens them. A segment full of these wouldn't form one steady helix across the membrane.

Correct. The middle of a membrane is made of fatty acid tails, about 30 Å thick and completely nonpolar. An α-helix rises 1.5 Å per residue, so 20 residues × 1.5 Å = 30 Å, enough to span it. The side chains point out toward the lipid tails, so they need to be water-avoiding. Leucine, isoleucine and valine fit that and are good helix formers. The helix's own backbone C=O and N–H groups hydrogen-bond to each other, so the whole segment is happy in the oily interior.

p: A cell membrane is a lipid bilayer: two layers of phospholipids with their water-loving heads facing out and their fatty acid tails pointing in. The middle is an oily layer about 30 Å thick with no water.

Proteins that cross the membrane often do it with an α-helix about 20 residues long. In a helix, the backbone C=O and N–H groups bond to each other, so the backbone doesn't need water. The side chains stick out and touch the lipid tails, so they have to be water-avoiding.

That's why prediction programs look for stretches of about 20 water-avoiding residues (Leu, Ile, Val, Phe, Ala) to spot membrane-crossing segments. Charged residues tend to cluster at the ends, where the helix meets the lipid heads and water.

fm.f: helix length = rise per residue × number of residues, where rise per residue = how far the helix climbs per amino acid
fm.v: rise per residue = 1.5 Å; number of residues = 20; helix length = ?
fm.why: This checks that a 20-residue helix is long enough to cross the membrane's oily core.

steps: Write the formula: helix length = rise per residue × number of residues.
Write down the values: rise per residue = 1.5 Å; number of residues = 20.
Plug in: 1.5 Å × 20 = 30 Å.
Compare: the membrane's oily core is about 30 Å thick, so 20 residues are just enough to cross it.
The side chains face the lipid tails, so pick the water-avoiding, helix-friendly residues: leucine, isoleucine and valine.
x1A_042.trap: The middle of the membrane is oil. Membrane-crossing helices need water-avoiding, helix-friendly residues, not charged ones or helix breakers.

fig.cap: The four choices with the side-chain carbon in question shaded and its four groups listed. Only threonine's Cβ carries four different groups.
fig.alt: Structures of serine, valine, threonine and leucine with CIP labels. Serine's β carbon has two H, valine's β carbon two CH₃, leucine's γ carbon two CH₃; threonine's β carbon has H, CH₃, OH and C-α and is labeled R, giving two stereocenters.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 5.5 Sequence Rules for Specifying Configuration

ox: Not quite. Serine's α-carbon is a stereocenter, but its β-carbon (CH₂OH) holds two identical H atoms plus OH and the α-carbon. With two matching groups, that carbon isn't a stereocenter, so serine has only one.

Not quite. Valine's β-carbon holds H, the α-carbon and two CH₃ groups. The two matching CH₃ groups mean it isn't a stereocenter, so valine has only its α-carbon. Branching alone doesn't create a second stereocenter.

Correct. Threonine's α-carbon has four different groups (H, NH₃⁺, COO⁻ and the side chain). Its β-carbon, CH(OH)CH₃, also has four different groups: H, OH, CH₃ and the α-carbon. So threonine has two stereocenters. With two of them, there are 2² = 2 × 2 = 4 possible stereoisomers, which is why a form called allothreonine exists.

Not quite. Leucine branches at its γ-carbon (two carbons out), which holds H, the β-carbon and two matching CH₃ groups, so it isn't a stereocenter. Only leucine's α-carbon is chiral. Its isomer isoleucine branches one carbon closer, where the four groups are all different (H, CH₃, CH₂CH₃ and the α-carbon), so isoleucine does have two.

p: A stereocenter (chiral center) is a carbon with four different groups attached. Every standard amino acid except glycine has one at the α-carbon.

Two amino acids, threonine and isoleucine, have a second stereocenter at the β-carbon, the first carbon of the side chain. Threonine's β-carbon holds H, OH, CH₃ and the α-carbon. Isoleucine's holds H, CH₃, CH₂CH₃ and the α-carbon.

Branching isn't the same as chirality. Valine and leucine branch into two identical CH₃ groups, so their branch carbons aren't stereocenters. A molecule with n stereocenters can have up to 2ⁿ stereoisomers, so threonine has 2² = 4.

x1A_043.trap: Branching isn't chirality. Valine and leucine branch into two identical CH₃ groups. Only threonine and isoleucine have a second stereocenter.

fig.cap: Phenylalanine and tyrosine side by side: adding one para-OH to the ring converts Phe into Tyr. The other choices have different ring systems or no ring.
fig.alt: Structure of phenylalanine with its ring shaded and tyrosine with the hydroxylated ring shaded, labeled para-OH added. Below, tryptophan (indole, two rings), histidine (imidazole) and serine (OH, no ring) are marked wrong.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.1 Structures of Amino Acids

ox: Not quite. Tryptophan's side chain is an indole: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered ring containing N–H. It's aromatic but has no OH, and it looks quite different from phenylalanine's single ring. It's the biggest standard side chain.

Correct. Tyrosine is phenylalanine with an OH on the ring carbon straight across from (para to) where the ring attaches. That's exactly how the body makes it: phenylalanine hydroxylase adds the OH. The OH makes tyrosine more polar than phenylalanine, gives it a weakly acidic side chain (pKₐ ≈ 10), and makes it a target for tyrosine kinases.

Not quite. Histidine's side chain is an imidazole, a five-membered ring with two nitrogens, attached by a CH₂. It's basic (pKₐ ≈ 6), not a benzene ring with an OH, so it doesn't match phenylalanine plus one OH.
Not quite. Serine does have an OH, but its side chain is just CH₂OH, with no ring. It matches the OH but not the ring.

p: Phenylalanine's side chain is a CH₂ attached to a benzene ring (six carbons in a flat ring). It's water-avoiding.

Tyrosine is the same thing with an OH added to the ring carbon directly opposite the CH₂ (the para position). The body makes tyrosine from phenylalanine using phenylalanine hydroxylase. If that enzyme is missing, phenylalanine builds up, which is the disease phenylketonuria (PKU).

That one OH changes a lot. Tyrosine is more polar, can hydrogen-bond, and can be phosphorylated by tyrosine kinases. Tyrosine is also the starting material for dopamine, adrenaline and thyroid hormone.

x1A_044.trap: Tyrosine = phenylalanine + an OH at the para position. Serine also has an OH but no ring; tryptophan and histidine have different rings.

fig.cap: Free glycine (α-NH₃⁺ pKₐ ≈ 9.6) next to the N-terminus of Gly-Ala (pKₐ ≈ 8). In the peptide the stabilizing COO⁻ neighbor has been replaced by a neutral amide.
fig.alt: Glycine zwitterion with its carboxylate shaded and pKₐ about 9.6 beside the dipeptide Gly-Ala with the amide next to the N-terminus shaded and pKₐ about 8. Tags mark the loss of the adjacent carboxylate as correct.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app. pKₐ values are typical textbook values.

ox: Correct. In a free amino acid, the COO⁻ on the same carbon is a nearby negative charge. It attracts the positive NH₃⁺, making its proton harder to remove and raising the pKₐ to about 9.6. In a peptide, the N-terminal residue's carboxyl has become a neutral amide, which also pulls electrons away a little. Without its negative neighbor, the NH₃⁺ gives up its proton more easily, so its pKₐ drops to about 8.

Not quite. A lower pKₐ for NH₃⁺ means it's a stronger acid, so the NH₂ left behind is a weaker base. This choice gets it backward. If the N-terminal amine were a stronger base, it would hold its proton tighter and its pKₐ would be higher, not lower.

Not quite. The N-terminal amino group is, by definition, the one amine not used in a peptide bond. It stays free as NH₃⁺ or NH₂. It's that residue's carboxyl that forms the peptide bond to the next residue. If the nitrogen were in an amide, it wouldn't be basic at all and wouldn't have a pKₐ near 8.

Not quite. Groups that push electrons onto a nitrogen make the protonated form more stable, which raises an amine's pKₐ. That would push the value above 9.6, not lower it. The real drop comes from losing the nearby COO⁻.

concept.t: Why terminal pKₐ values shift in peptides
p: A group's pKₐ depends on its neighbors. Anything that makes the protonated form more comfortable raises the pKₐ (it holds its proton longer). Anything that makes the deprotonated form more comfortable lowers it.

In a free amino acid, the α-NH₃⁺ and α-COO⁻ sit on the same carbon and steady each other with their opposite charges. That's why the free amine's pKₐ is high (about 9.6) and the free carboxyl's is low (about 2.3).
In a peptide, each end has lost its partner charge. The N-terminal amine's pKₐ drops to about 8, and the C-terminal carboxyl's pKₐ rises to about 3 to 3.5.

x1A_045.trap: A lower pKₐ for an NH₃⁺ group means a weaker base, not a stronger one. Look for what steadies or unsettles the protonated form.

fig.cap: Glycine's zwitterion can accept a proton (acting as a base) to become the cation, or donate one (acting as an acid) to become the anion.
fig.alt: Three glycine structures: cation with COOH on the left, zwitterion in the middle, anion with NH₂ on the right. Arrows show plus H⁺ toward the cation (acts as base) and minus H⁺ toward the anion (acts as acid). Tags mark amphoteric correct and hydrophobic, chiral and aromatic wrong.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.1 Structures of Amino Acids

ox: Not quite. Hydrophobic means water-avoiding: a nonpolar group that water pushes away. It says nothing about giving or taking protons. Many amino acids aren't hydrophobic at all, yet every one of them can act as an acid and a base.

Not quite. Chiral means a molecule can't be stacked on its mirror image, usually because a carbon has four different groups. That's about shape, not acids and bases. Glycine isn't chiral, but it can still give and take protons.

Correct. Amphoteric means a substance can act as either an acid or a base. Amino acids have a carboxyl group, which can give away a proton (COOH → COO⁻), and an amino group, which can take one (NH₂ → NH₃⁺). In acid they pick up protons and turn positive; in base they lose them and turn negative. Water and bicarbonate are other amphoteric examples.

Not quite. Aromatic describes flat rings with a special, extra-stable arrangement of electrons, like those in phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan. It's about ring electrons, not protons, and most amino acids aren't aromatic.

p: An acid gives away a proton (H⁺). A base takes one. Some substances can do both, depending on what's around them. Those are called amphoteric.

Every amino acid is amphoteric because it has two groups: a carboxyl (an acid) and an amino group (a base). In water near neutral pH, the carboxyl has already given its proton to the amine, making a zwitterion with one + and one − charge.

Add acid and the COO⁻ grabs a proton back, so the molecule turns positive. Add base and the NH₃⁺ gives its proton away, so the molecule turns negative. Water (H₂O ↔ H₃O⁺ or OH⁻) is the most familiar amphoteric substance.

x1A_046.trap: Amphoteric is about passing protons both ways. Hydrophobic, chiral and aromatic describe water behavior, shape and ring electrons.

fig.cap: Buffer capacity of free histidine computed from its three pKₐ values. Capacity peaks at each pKₐ; pH 6.0 is a peak, while 3.9, 7.6 (the pI) and 11.0 sit in troughs or on the tail.
fig.alt: Curve of relative buffer capacity versus pH with three equal peaks at pH 1.8, 6.0 and 9.2. The peak at 6.0 is marked correct; points at 3.9, 7.6 and 11.0 lie at low values and are marked wrong.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the three pKₐ values in the question (buffer capacity = ln10 × Σ f(1 − f)).

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Not quite. pH 3.9 sits between histidine's first two pKₐ values (1.8 and 6.0), about 2 units from each. There the carboxyl has almost entirely lost its proton and the side chain has almost entirely kept its, so neither group is a useful half-and-half pair. That's close to a steep spot on the curve, where buffering is weak.

Correct. A buffer works best when both forms of a group are present in equal amounts, which happens when pH = pKₐ. Histidine's pKₐ values are 1.8 (α-COOH), 6.0 (side chain) and 9.2 (α-NH₃⁺). Of the choices, only 6.0 sits right on a pKₐ, where the side chain is 1 : 1 protonated to unprotonated. This side-chain buffering near neutral pH is part of why histidines in hemoglobin help buffer blood.

Not quite. 7.6 is histidine's pI: (6.0 + 9.2) ÷ 2 = 15.2 ÷ 2 = 7.6. The pI is a steep spot between two buffering regions. The side chain has mostly lost its proton and the α-amino group has mostly kept its, so buffering is close to its lowest. Mixing up the pI with the best buffering pH is a classic trap.

Not quite. pH 11.0 is 11.0 − 9.2 = 1.8 units above the highest pKₐ, so the α-amino group has mostly (about 98%) lost its proton. Very little of the protonated form is left to soak up added base, so buffering is poor. Good buffering needs the pH within about 1 unit of a pKₐ.

concept.t: Where an amino acid buffers best
p: A buffer is a mix of a weak acid and its unprotonated partner. Add acid, and the partner soaks it up. Add base, and the acid neutralizes it. It works best when you have equal amounts of both, which is exactly when pH = pKₐ.
On a titration curve, buffering regions are the flat parts, each centered on a pKₐ. The useful range is about 1 pH unit on either side.
Between flat parts are steep parts, where one group is done and the next hasn't started. The pI is one of these steep spots, so it's where buffering is weakest, not strongest.

x1A_047.trap: Best buffering is at a pKₐ (a flat part of the curve). The pI is a steep spot where buffering is weakest.

fig.cap: The peptide Ala-Lys-Gly-Arg-Phe-Lys with trypsin's two cut sites (after Lys2 and Arg4). The C-terminal Lys6 has no bond after it, so three fragments result.
fig.alt: Six residue boxes Ala, Lys, Gly, Arg, Phe, Lys with Lys and Arg highlighted and dashed red cut lines after positions 2 and 4. Below, three fragments Ala-Lys, Gly-Arg and Phe-Lys and the label 2 cuts give 3 fragments.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. Two fragments means only one cut. This peptide has two cut sites inside the chain: after the Lys in position 2 (followed by Gly) and after the Arg in position 4 (followed by Phe). Missing one usually comes from forgetting that trypsin cuts after arginine as well as lysine.

Correct. Trypsin cuts the peptide bond right after (on the C-terminal side of) a Lys or Arg, unless the next residue is Pro. In Ala-Lys-Gly-Arg-Phe-Lys: the 2nd-position Lys is followed by Gly, so cut; the Arg is followed by Phe, so cut; the final Lys has no bond after it, so no cut. Two cuts in a straight chain give 2 + 1 = 3 pieces: Ala-Lys, Gly-Arg and Phe-Lys. Each piece ends in Lys or Arg, just as expected for trypsin.

Not quite. Four fragments would need three cuts, which counts the final Lys. But an enzyme cuts a bond, and there's no bond after the last residue. Only Lys and Arg residues inside the chain make new pieces.

Not quite. Six fragments would mean all five peptide bonds were cut, freeing all six amino acids. Trypsin is picky: its binding pocket has a negative aspartate that grabs the positive side chain of Lys or Arg. It doesn't cut after Ala, Gly or Phe.

p: Proteases are enzymes that cut peptide bonds, and many only cut at specific spots. Trypsin cuts right after lysine or arginine, the two positively charged residues. The one exception: it won't cut if the next residue is proline.
To predict the pieces, walk down the sequence and mark every Lys or Arg that has a non-Pro residue after it. A Lys or Arg at the very end doesn't count, because there's no bond after it.
In a straight chain, each cut adds one piece, so pieces = cuts + 1. Other enzymes have their own rules. Chymotrypsin, for example, cuts after big aromatic residues like Phe, Tyr and Trp.

fm.f: fragments = cuts + 1, where cuts = number of Lys or Arg inside the chain not followed by Pro
fm.v: cut after 2nd-position Lys (next is Gly) = yes; cut after Arg (next is Phe) = yes; cut after final Lys = no (nothing after it); cuts = 2; fragments = ?
fm.why: Each cut in a straight chain splits one piece into two, adding one piece.
fm.nc: A Lys or Arg at the C-terminus has no bond after it, so it's never a cut site.

steps: Write the formula: fragments = cuts + 1.
Write down the values: the sequence is Ala-Lys-Gly-Arg-Phe-Lys. Trypsin cuts after Lys or Arg unless Pro is next.
Lys in position 2 is followed by Gly: cut.
Arg in position 4 is followed by Phe: cut.
Lys in position 6 is the last residue, with no bond after it: no cut. So cuts = 2.
Plug in: fragments = 2 + 1 = 3. The pieces are Ala-Lys, Gly-Arg and Phe-Lys.
x1A_048.trap: A Lys or Arg at the C-terminus has no bond after it to cut. Count only sites inside the chain that aren't followed by Pro.

fig.cap: A glycine residue (side chain H) next to an alanine residue (side chain CH₃) in a short peptide. With no Cβ, glycine avoids steric clashes and can take backbone angles other residues cannot.
fig.alt: Two tripeptides: Ala-Gly-Ala with the glycine residue shaded and labeled side chain H, few clashes, wide phi/psi range; Ala-Ala-Ala with the middle alanine and its methyl shaded, labeled C-β clashes limit phi/psi. Tags mark tiny side chain flexible backbone correct.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Correct. Glycine's side chain is a single H, so its α-carbon has no extra carbon sticking out. For other residues, many backbone angle combinations are off-limits because that carbon would crash into backbone atoms. Glycine avoids those crashes and can take on many more angles. That lets the chain reverse direction sharply, so glycine is common in tight turns and floppy loops (and in collagen, at every third position where the chains pack closely).

Not quite. Glycine's 'side chain' is just a hydrogen bonded to carbon, which can't form hydrogen bonds. Glycine's love of turns comes from having no real side chain, not from any bond it makes. Residues like asparagine and serine also show up in turns, but for a different reason.

Not quite. Glycine forms normal peptide bonds through its amino and carboxyl groups on both sides, just like every other amino acid. Something that couldn't form a peptide bond on one side could only sit at the end of a chain, not in the middle of a turn.
Not quite. Glycine's side chain is H, which has no acid or base group, so it has no charge at body pH. Charge isn't why glycine likes turns.

p: A protein's backbone can twist at two bonds around each α-carbon. How far it can twist depends on what's attached. In most amino acids, the first side-chain carbon gets in the way of certain twists.
Glycine has only a hydrogen as its side chain, so almost nothing gets in the way. It can take on backbone angles that are blocked for every other residue, including ones needed for tight turns.

That's a double-edged sword. Glycine is great in turns and loops, and it's essential in collagen, where chains pack tightly. But it's a poor helix former, because a helix forces it into one shape and it loses all that freedom. Proline is the opposite: too stiff.

x1A_049.trap: Glycine's special behavior comes from what it lacks (any real side chain), not from any interaction it makes.

fig.cap: Alanine's average net charge against pH, computed from pKₐ 2.3 and 9.7. At pH 9.7 the curve passes through −0.5; +0.5, 0 and −1 belong to pH 2.3, 6.0 and well above 9.7.
fig.alt: Net charge of alanine falling from +1 at low pH through +0.5 at pH 2.3, 0 from pH 4 to 8, −0.5 at pH 9.7 (correct, green point), and approaching −1 above pH 12.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the two pKₐ values in the question.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Not quite. A charge of −1 means every molecule is H₂N–CH(CH₃)–COO⁻, with every amino group deprotonated. That needs a pH well above 9.7 (about 11.7 or higher to reach 99%). At pH 9.7 exactly half the amino groups are still NH₃⁺.

Correct. pH 9.7 equals the amino group's pKₐ, so by Henderson-Hasselbalch the ratio of NH₂ to NH₃⁺ is 10⁰ = 1: half and half. Half the molecules are zwitterions (net 0) and half are the −1 form. The carboxyl (pKₐ 2.3) has fully lost its proton at this pH. Average charge = (0 + (−1)) ÷ 2 = −1 ÷ 2 = −0.5. Any time pH equals a pKₐ, that group adds half its full charge.

Not quite. An average charge of 0 happens at the pI: (2.3 + 9.7) ÷ 2 = 12.0 ÷ 2 = 6.0, where nearly all alanine is the zwitterion. At pH 9.7, which is 9.7 − 6.0 = 3.7 units higher, half the amino groups have already lost their proton.

Not quite. +0.5 is the average charge at the other pKₐ, 2.3, where half the molecules are +1 and half are 0. The sign is wrong for pH 9.7: above the pI, an amino acid is negative on average, not positive.

p: In a solution, each molecule has a whole-number charge, but the average across all the molecules can be a fraction. That's what 'average net charge' means.

At pH = pKₐ, a group is exactly 50% protonated and 50% not. So it adds half of its full charge to the average. An amino group (+1 when protonated) adds +0.5. A carboxyl (−1 when deprotonated) adds −0.5.
For alanine: at pKₐ₁ (2.3) the average is +0.5, at the pI (6.0) it's 0, and at pKₐ₂ (9.7) it's −0.5. The charge drops steadily as the pH rises.

fm.f: average charge of a group = (charge with proton × fraction with proton) + (charge without proton × fraction without proton), where fraction with proton = 0.5 when pH = pKₐ
fm.v: amino group: charge with proton = +1, without = 0, each fraction = 0.5; carboxyl: fully deprotonated = −1; net average charge = ?
fm.why: At pH = pKₐ the group is half protonated, so it adds half its full charge.
fm.nc: The carboxyl is fully −1 here because pH 9.7 is far above its pKₐ of 2.3.

steps: Write the formula: net average charge = average charge of the carboxyl + average charge of the amino group.
Write down the values: pH = 9.7; carboxyl pKₐ = 2.3; amino pKₐ = 9.7.
Carboxyl: pH 9.7 is far above 2.3, so it has fully lost its proton: −1.
Amino group: pH = pKₐ, so it's half NH₃⁺ (+1) and half NH₂ (0): (+1 × 0.5) + (0 × 0.5) = +0.5.
x1A_050.trap: At a pKₐ the group is half charged. The pI (zero charge) sits between the two pKₐ values, not on one of them.

fig.cap: The four levels of structure with the bonds that hold each one. Only the primary level (the covalent sequence) survives boiling or urea.
fig.alt: Four panels: primary shown as a chain of lettered beads held by peptide bonds; secondary as a helix and two sheet arrows held by backbone hydrogen bonds; tertiary as a folded chain with a nonpolar core; quaternary as four subunits alpha1, beta1, beta2, alpha2. Tags show primary intact and the other levels lost after boiling or urea.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; content consistent with OpenStax Biology 2e, 3.4 Proteins.

ox: Not quite. α-helices and β-sheets are secondary structure: local, repeating shapes held by hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups. They depend on the sequence but aren't the sequence. A helix can unfold when heated while the order of amino acids stays exactly the same, which shows they're different levels.

Not quite. The full 3D fold of one chain is tertiary structure. It comes from how helices, sheets and loops pack together, held mostly by side-chain interactions like the water-avoiding core, hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and disulfides. Heat and urea destroy tertiary structure while the primary structure survives.

Not quite. How two or more separate chains fit together is quaternary structure, like hemoglobin's four chains (α₂β₂). Only proteins with more than one chain have it. It's about how finished chains assemble, not the order of amino acids inside one chain.

Correct. Primary structure is the order of amino acids, read from the N-terminus to the C-terminus, held together by covalent peptide bonds. The gene spells it out through the mRNA codons. Because it's covalent, it survives heat, urea or pH changes; only breaking peptide bonds changes it. Every higher level of structure follows from this sequence.

concept.t: The four levels of protein structure
p: Primary: the sequence of amino acids, held by covalent peptide bonds. Secondary: local backbone shapes, mainly α-helices and β-sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups.

Tertiary: the full 3D shape of a single chain, held mostly by side-chain interactions (the water-avoiding core, hydrogen bonds, salt bridges, disulfides). Quaternary: the arrangement of multiple chains in one protein, held by the same kinds of interactions between chains.
Denaturing a protein (with heat, urea or extreme pH) wrecks secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure but leaves primary structure intact. Only cutting peptide bonds changes the sequence.

x1A_051.trap: Primary structure is only the sequence. Any shape, even a single helix, is a higher level.

fig.cap: Top: in a helix, hydrogen-bond partners are 4 residues apart; in a sheet, strands far apart in sequence pair up. Bottom: the bond itself is backbone C=O···H–N, with side chains (R) pointing away.
fig.alt: A 30-residue chain drawn as boxes. Residues 2 to 12 form a helix with short arcs linking residue n to n plus 4. Residues 15 to 19 and 25 to 29 form sheet strands linked by long arcs. Below, two backbone chains with carbonyl oxygens of the top chain hydrogen-bonded to amide hydrogens of the bottom chain; R groups point away.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. Ionic bonds (salt bridges) form between oppositely charged side chains, like the COO⁻ of Asp or Glu and the NH₃⁺ of Lys. They help hold the overall fold and contacts between chains, but they don't define a helix or a sheet. A helix made entirely of alanine, which has no charged side chains, is still stable.

Correct. Secondary structure is held by hydrogen bonds between backbone groups: the C=O of one peptide unit bonds to the N–H of another. In an α-helix the partners are residues n and n + 4 in the same stretch; in a β-sheet they're on neighboring strands. Since every residue has the same backbone, these bonds repeat regularly, which is what gives helices and sheets their regular shapes no matter the side chains.

Not quite. Disulfide bonds are covalent S–S links made by oxidizing two cysteine SH groups. They lock parts of one chain together (tertiary) or link separate chains (quaternary), especially in proteins sent outside the cell. Only cysteine can make them, so they can't be what holds every helix and sheet.

Not quite. Peptide bonds are the covalent bonds that join one amino acid to the next along the backbone. They're primary structure, present whether the chain is folded or not, so they don't create the specific helix or sheet shape. They do supply the C=O and N–H groups that form the hydrogen bonds, which is the real answer.

p: Every amino acid in a chain contributes the same backbone pieces: an N–H and a C=O. The H on the N is slightly positive and the O on the C=O is slightly negative, so they can form a hydrogen bond.

Secondary structure is defined by these backbone-to-backbone hydrogen bonds. In an α-helix, each C=O bonds to the N–H four residues further along the same chain. In a β-sheet, bonds form between neighboring strands lying side by side.

Because these bonds don't involve side chains, almost any sequence can form helices and sheets. Side chains decide which one is more favorable, but the bonds that hold the shape are always backbone bonds.

x1A_052.trap: Secondary structure means backbone hydrogen bonds. Anything involving side chains is tertiary.

fig.cap: An ideal α-helix computed from 100° and 0.15 nm per residue. Dashed green lines join residue n to residue n + 4; one turn is 3.6 residues.
fig.alt: Side view of a helix with residues n to n plus 8 marked; dashed green hydrogen bonds connect n to n plus 4, n plus 1 to n plus 5 and so on. A bar marks one turn as 3.6 residues or 0.54 nanometers. An end-on view shows side chains R pointing outward. Tags: n to n plus 4 α-helix correct; n to n plus 3 is a 3-10 helix; n to n plus 1 or n plus 2 too close.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; residue positions computed from ideal α-helix parameters (100° and 0.15 nm per residue).

ox: Not quite. Bonding residue n to n + 2 would need a very tight loop. That only happens in rare, one-off tight turns, not in a repeating helix. If every residue did it, the backbone couldn't wind into the regular α-helix spiral.

Correct. In the α-helix, the C=O of residue n bonds to the N–H of residue n + 4. The helix rotates 100° and rises 0.15 nm per residue, so residue n + 4 sits almost right above residue n, one turn later. That lines up the C=O and N–H nearly parallel to the helix's axis. This pattern gives 3.6 residues per turn and a rise per turn of 3.6 × 0.15 nm = 0.54 nm.

Not quite. Residue n + 1 is the very next residue. Its N–H is joined to the C=O of residue n through the same flat peptide bond, so the two point away from each other and can't hydrogen-bond. Neighboring residues are covalently linked, not hydrogen-bonded.

Not quite. Hydrogen bonds to a residue on a separate, neighboring strand define a β-sheet. In a sheet the partners can be far apart in the sequence. In a helix they're always close: in the same stretch, four residues apart.

p: An α-helix is a right-handed spiral of backbone. Each residue turns the chain 100° around the axis and lifts it 0.15 nm (1.5 Å). After 3.6 residues the spiral has gone all the way around: 3.6 × 100° = 360°.

That geometry puts the C=O of residue n right below the N–H of residue n + 4. They form a hydrogen bond, and that pattern repeats down the whole helix. Every backbone C=O and N–H inside the helix is paired up.
Keep the two numbers straight: 4 is the spacing of the hydrogen bond (n to n + 4), and 3.6 is the number of residues per full turn.

x1A_053.trap: α-helix = n → n + 4 bond and 3.6 residues per turn. Don't mix up 4 (the bond spacing) with 3.6 (residues per turn).

fig.cap: The end-on view (right) shows side chains (R) radiating outward 100° apart while the backbone fills the core.
fig.alt: End-on view of an α-helix: seven backbone α-carbons near the center connected by purple lines, each with an orange stick ending in an R circle pointing outward; the helix axis is a dot at the center. A side view on the left shows hydrogen bonds from residue n to n plus 4.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; positions computed from ideal α-helix parameters (100° and 0.15 nm per residue).

ox: Not quite. The middle of an α-helix is already packed tightly with backbone atoms; there's no open channel. If side chains pointed inward, they'd crash into each other and into the backbone. Channel proteins make pores by bundling several helices together, with side chains lining the gap between helices, not inside one helix.

Not quite. Side chains alternating above and below a flat plane describes a β-strand in a sheet: each residue flips its side chain to the opposite face. A helix has no flat plane; its side chains fan out all around the axis, each about 100° from the last.

Not quite. The hydrogen bonds that hold an α-helix are between backbone groups: the C=O of residue n and the N–H of residue n + 4. Side chains aren't needed for them, which is why almost any sequence can form a helix. Side chains affect how stable the helix is, but they don't form its defining bonds.

Correct. In an α-helix the backbone forms the tightly wound core, and each side chain points outward from the axis, turned about 100° from the one before. That keeps bulky groups out of each other's way and exposes them to their surroundings. It also explains amphipathic helices: if water-avoiding residues repeat every 3 to 4 positions, they line up along one outer face.

concept.t: Where side chains go in helices and sheets
p: In an α-helix, the backbone coils into a solid rod. The side chains stick out from that rod in all directions, spiraling around it, about 100° apart from one residue to the next.

Because 3.6 residues make one turn, residues 3 or 4 apart end up on the same side of the helix. If those are all water-avoiding, the helix has one greasy face and one water-loving face. That's called an amphipathic helix, and it's common where a helix sits against the protein's core or a membrane.
In a β-sheet it's different: side chains alternate straight up and straight down from the flat sheet, every other residue on the same side.

x1A_054.trap: Helix: side chains point out like spokes. Sheet: side chains alternate up and down.

fig.cap: Two-stranded sheets seen from above. Arrows run N to C. Antiparallel neighbors point opposite ways with straight hydrogen bonds; parallel neighbors point the same way with angled ones.
fig.alt: Left panel: two strand arrows pointing in opposite directions with vertical dashed hydrogen bonds, tagged antiparallel correct. Right panel: two arrows pointing the same direction with zigzag dashed hydrogen bonds, tagged parallel. A note says hydrogen bonds join different strands and side chains point above and below the sheet.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Correct. A β-sheet is antiparallel when neighboring strands run in opposite N-to-C directions, like the two lanes of a road. That puts each C=O directly across from an N–H on the partner strand, so the hydrogen bonds go straight across and are a bit stronger. Antiparallel sheets often form from a hairpin: one strand, a short turn, then the strand coming back.

Not quite. Neighboring strands running the same N-to-C direction make a parallel β-sheet. Parallel strands can't be linked by a short turn; they need a longer connection, often a helix. Their hydrogen bonds cross at an angle instead of straight across, so parallel sheets are usually a bit less stable.

Not quite. Hydrogen bonds within a single stretch describe an α-helix (n to n + 4 along the same chain). A stretched-out β-strand can't bond to itself; its C=O and N–H groups point sideways toward neighboring strands. Every β-sheet, parallel or antiparallel, is held by bonds between strands.

Not quite. Side chains don't lie in the plane of the sheet. Because the backbone is pleated, side chains alternate above and below the sheet. The groups in the plane are the backbone C=O and N–H, which make the bonds between strands. And either way, side-chain position doesn't tell antiparallel from parallel.

p: A β-strand is a stretched-out piece of backbone. Lay two or more strands side by side and connect them with hydrogen bonds between their backbone C=O and N–H groups, and you get a β-sheet.
Each strand has a direction, from N to C. When neighbors point opposite ways, the sheet is antiparallel. When they point the same way, it's parallel. Mixed sheets have some of each.

Antiparallel sheets often form from one chain folding back on itself through a short hairpin turn, and their hydrogen bonds line up straight across. Parallel sheets need a long connection to bring the chain back to the starting end, and their hydrogen bonds are angled.

x1A_055.trap: Antiparallel and parallel refer to strand direction (N to C), not to where side chains point.

fig.cap: Edge-on view of one β-strand. Side chains alternate above (nonpolar here) and below (polar here) the sheet plane, with a two-residue repeat.
fig.alt: A zigzag backbone with black α-carbons at each pleat. Side chains Val, Ile, Phe, Leu, Val point up above the sheet plane and Ser, Thr, Asn, Gln point down below it. A bar marks a repeat of 2 residues, about 0.7 nanometers. Tags: alternating faces correct; a 3.6-residue spiral is an α-helix.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. If every side chain pointed to the same face, each residue would have to sit at the same height relative to the sheet. In fact the pleated backbone flips each residue relative to the one before, so residues 1, 3, 5 share one face and 2, 4, 6 share the other. Only every second residue points the same way.

Not quite. Side chains spiraling around with 3.6 residues per turn describes an α-helix. A β-strand is almost fully stretched out (about 0.33 to 0.35 nm per residue, versus 0.15 nm in a helix) and repeats every two residues, so its side chains can't wrap around it.

Correct. A β-strand is stretched out and pleated, like a folded paper fan. Each α-carbon sits on a fold, alternately slightly above and below the sheet, and its side chain points out on that side. So side chains alternate faces: residues i, i + 2, i + 4 on one face and i + 1, i + 3 on the other. That lets a sheet have one water-avoiding face and one water-loving face when the two kinds of residues alternate.

Not quite. What points toward the neighboring strand is the backbone C=O and N–H, which lie in the plane of the sheet and form the hydrogen bonds between strands. If side chains pointed sideways into the neighbor, they'd block those bonds. Instead, side chains stick straight out of the sheet, up or down.

p: A β-strand isn't perfectly flat; it zigzags slightly, like a pleated skirt or a folded paper fan. Each α-carbon sits at one of the folds.
Because the folds alternate up and down, so do the side chains. Every other residue points to the same face of the sheet. That's a repeat of 2.

This gives you a handy pattern to spot in a sequence. A stretch where water-avoiding residues show up every 2 positions is likely a β-strand with one greasy face. A stretch where they show up every 3 to 4 positions is likely an α-helix with one greasy face.

x1A_056.trap: Every-2 pattern = β-strand. Every-3-to-4 pattern = α-helix.

fig.cap: A four-residue β-turn with Pro at i + 1 and Gly at i + 2, closed by a C=O(i)···H–N(i + 3) hydrogen bond, plus where each answer pair usually sits in proteins.
fig.alt: A β-hairpin: two antiparallel strand arrows joined by a turn of residues i, Pro, Gly, i plus 3, with a dashed hydrogen bond between i and i plus 3. Structures of glycine and L-proline drawn with the proline ring highlighted. A table tags Gly and Pro as turn formers (correct) and Leu/Ile, Phe/Trp and Lys/Arg with their usual locations.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Not quite. Leucine and isoleucine are big, water-avoiding residues. Leucine is one of the best helix formers, and isoleucine favors β-strands; both tend to be buried in the core. Their bulky side chains block the backbone angles needed for a tight U-turn, so they're uncommon at the corners of β-turns.

Not quite. Lysine and arginine are long, positively charged residues found mostly on the protein's surface. Turns are usually on the surface too, so these can show up nearby, but charge doesn't give them the special backbone shape a tight turn needs. Lysine is actually a good helix former.

Not quite. Phenylalanine and tryptophan have big ring side chains. They prefer β-strands and buried spots, where their rings can stack and pack together. Their bulk clashes with the compact backbone of a tight turn, so they're rare in the middle of turns.

Correct. A β-turn reverses the chain over four residues, held by a hydrogen bond from the C=O of the first residue to the N–H of the fourth. Proline often sits in the second position because its ring locks the backbone into a fixed kink. Glycine often sits in the third position because, with only an H for a side chain, it can bend in ways other residues can't. Both are also known as helix breakers.

p: Proteins often need to reverse direction, for example between two strands of an antiparallel β-sheet. A β-turn does that in just four residues, with the first residue's C=O hydrogen-bonded to the fourth residue's N–H.

Such a tight bend needs backbone angles most residues can't easily reach. Two residues are especially good at it. Glycine has no real side chain, so it can bend almost any way. Proline's ring holds the backbone in a fixed kink that happens to fit the turn.
Turns are usually on the protein's surface, so polar residues like asparagine, aspartate and serine are common there too.

x1A_057.trap: Glycine and proline are opposites in stiffness (most flexible vs most rigid), yet both favor turns and both break helices.

fig.cap: Tertiary structure (third panel) is the full fold of one chain, held by side-chain interactions around a nonpolar core.
fig.alt: Four panels for primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure with the bonds that hold each. The tertiary panel shows one folded chain around an orange nonpolar core, held by hydrophobic core, hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and disulfides.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; content consistent with OpenStax Biology 2e, 3.4 Proteins.

ox: Not quite. The sequence of amino acids is primary structure. It's the covalent backbone order set by the gene, and it's where the 3D fold comes from, but it isn't the fold itself. An unfolded protein keeps its sequence while losing its tertiary structure.

Not quite. Local helices and sheets on their own are secondary structure. Tertiary structure includes them, but adds how they're arranged in space: which helices sit against which sheets, where the loops go, and which side chains are buried. Describing only the local pieces misses the overall shape.

Correct. Tertiary structure is the full 3D shape of a single chain: how its helices, sheets and loops fold and pack together. It's held mainly by side-chain interactions: water-avoiding residues buried in the core, side-chain hydrogen bonds, salt bridges, metal ions and disulfide bonds. An enzyme's active site usually forms from residues far apart in the sequence that the fold brings together.

Not quite. How two or more chains fit together is quaternary structure, found only in proteins with more than one chain, like hemoglobin. The same kinds of side-chain interactions hold the chains together, but quaternary describes contacts between chains, not the fold inside one.

p: After a chain forms local helices and sheets, those pieces fold up and pack against each other into a compact 3D shape. That overall shape of one chain is its tertiary structure.

It's held mostly by interactions between side chains. The biggest driver is the hydrophobic effect: water-avoiding side chains clump in the core, away from water. Hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and disulfide bonds add more stability.
Tertiary structure is what makes a protein work. Residues that are far apart in the sequence can end up side by side in the fold, forming a binding site or an active site.

x1A_058.trap: Tertiary = the shape of one chain. Quaternary = how several chains are arranged together.

fig.cap: Only hemoglobin, with four separate chains (α₂β₂), has quaternary structure. Myoglobin, ribonuclease A and a monomeric peptide are each a single chain.
fig.alt: Four panels: myoglobin as one blob with a red heme, tagged no quaternary; hemoglobin as four circles alpha1, beta1, beta2, alpha2, tagged quaternary; ribonuclease A as one chain with four dashed disulfides inside, tagged no quaternary; a 30-residue peptide as a single wavy line, tagged no quaternary.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. Myoglobin is a single chain of 153 residues folded around one heme. It has primary, secondary (mostly α-helix) and tertiary structure, but with only one chain it has no quaternary level. Its single binding site is why its oxygen-binding curve is a simple, non-cooperative hyperbola.

Correct. Quaternary structure is how two or more separate chains are arranged. Hemoglobin is made of two α and two β chains (α₂β₂), each folded much like myoglobin and each holding a heme. The chains are held together by noncovalent contacts. When one chain binds O₂, those contacts shift and make the others bind O₂ more easily, giving hemoglobin its S-shaped, cooperative binding curve.

Not quite. Ribonuclease A is a single chain of 124 residues held in shape by four internal disulfide bonds. Disulfides inside one chain are part of tertiary structure. Covalent links only count as quaternary when they join different chains, like in antibodies or insulin.

Not quite. By definition, a single chain can't have quaternary structure, however long it is. A 30-residue single peptide might form a helix or a small fold, but quaternary structure needs at least two chains, whether identical or different.

p: Many proteins are made of more than one chain. Each chain is a subunit, and the way the subunits fit together is the protein's quaternary structure.

Subunits can be identical or different. Hemoglobin has two α and two β chains. They're held together mostly by the same weak forces that hold a single chain's fold, and sometimes by disulfide bonds between chains.

Quaternary structure lets subunits influence each other. In hemoglobin, oxygen binding to one subunit makes the others grab oxygen more easily. That's cooperativity, and myoglobin, with just one chain, can't do it.

x1A_059.trap: Count chains, not bonds or residues. One chain means no quaternary structure.

fig.cap: Unfolded: water forms ordered cages around exposed nonpolar groups. Folded: the groups are buried and the water is released, so water's entropy rises.
