fig.alt: Left panel: an unfolded chain with five orange nonpolar groups, each surrounded by a ring of 10 blue water molecules, labeled low entropy. Right panel: a folded protein with the orange groups clustered in the core and blue water molecules scattered randomly outside, labeled entropy of water rises. A box gives ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, water entropy positive, chain entropy negative.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; schematic, not to scale.

ox: Correct. Water can't hydrogen-bond to nonpolar side chains, so the water right next to an exposed nonpolar surface gets more ordered, like a cage. That lowers water's entropy. When the protein folds and buries those side chains, the water is released and its entropy rises. That gain helps make ΔG = ΔH − TΔS negative. This is the hydrophobic effect, the main driving force for folding.

Not quite. Nonpolar side chains like leucine, valine and phenylalanine have no O–H or N–H groups and no strongly electron-pulling atoms, so they can't hydrogen-bond to each other. They do attract weakly once packed together (London dispersion forces), but that's small compared with what water gains.

Not quite. Folding does the opposite to the chain. An unfolded chain can take on a huge number of shapes, while the folded one has essentially one. So the chain's own entropy goes down when it folds, which works against folding. The favorable entropy comes from the surrounding water, not the protein.

Not quite. Disulfide bonds only form between cysteines, which make up a small share of most proteins, and they form mainly outside the cell or in the ER. Most proteins in the cytoplasm fold with no disulfides at all. Disulfides can lock a fold in place, but they don't drive nonpolar residues into the core.

p: Entropy is a measure of disorder, or how many ways molecules can arrange themselves. Processes that increase total entropy tend to happen on their own.

Water molecules normally tumble around freely, hydrogen-bonding with each other. Next to a nonpolar surface they can't do that, so they line up into an ordered cage around it. That lowers water's entropy.

When a protein folds, it hides its nonpolar side chains in the core, so much less nonpolar surface touches water. The caged water is freed, and its entropy goes up. That's the hydrophobic effect. It's the same reason oil drops in water merge into bigger drops.

x1A_060.trap: The favorable entropy belongs to the water. The protein chain itself loses entropy when it folds.

fig.cap: Free-energy contributions to folding (illustrative values, not measurements). Large favorable terms (green) are almost canceled by the chain's entropy loss (red), leaving a small net ΔG.
fig.alt: Waterfall bar chart: hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and van der Waals minus 250 kilojoules per mole; hydrophobic effect minus 300; chain conformational entropy plus 510; net folding free energy about minus 40.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph; illustrative magnitudes chosen to sum to a typical net stability, consistent with Lehninger's description of protein stability.

ox: Not quite. If folding had a positive ΔG, proteins wouldn't fold on their own. Yet most small proteins refold by themselves in a test tube with no ATP, as Anfinsen showed with ribonuclease A. Some chaperones use ATP, but that's to prevent clumping; it doesn't pay for the folded state. The folded state is already the lowest-energy state.

Not quite. Each hydrogen bond, contact or salt bridge is weak (a few kJ/mol), but a folded protein has hundreds of them, plus the big hydrophobic effect. Added up, the favorable side is hundreds of kJ/mol. So the interactions matter a lot; the real puzzle is why the net is so small anyway.

Correct. Folding takes the chain from a huge number of unfolded shapes to essentially one, so the chain loses a lot of entropy. In ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, that loss makes the −TΔS term for the chain large and positive. It cancels most of the favorable interactions and the hydrophobic effect. What's left is a small difference, typically 20 to 60 kJ/mol, which is why a single mutation or a modest temperature rise can unfold a protein.

Not quite. Folded proteins are held mostly by noncovalent forces: the hydrophobic effect, hydrogen bonds, van der Waals contacts and salt bridges. The only common covalent cross-links are disulfides, and many proteins have none. If covalent bonds held the fold, gentle heat or urea couldn't unfold proteins.

concept.t: Why proteins are only barely stable
p: ΔG (free energy change) decides whether folding happens on its own. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, where ΔH is the heat from forming or breaking interactions, T is temperature in kelvin, and ΔS is the change in entropy (disorder). A negative ΔG means folding is favorable.
Folding wins on ΔH (many new interactions) and on water's entropy (the hydrophobic effect). It loses big on the chain's own entropy, because a floppy chain becomes one fixed shape.

These huge terms nearly cancel, leaving a small net ΔG. Being only barely stable is actually useful: proteins can flex, change shape when they work, and be unfolded and broken down when the cell no longer needs them.

fx.w: ΔG = free energy change of folding (kJ/mol; negative means it happens on its own), ΔH = heat change from making interactions, T = temperature in kelvin, ΔS = entropy change of the chain plus the water. The big favorable ΔH and water entropy are mostly canceled by the chain's big entropy loss.

x1A_061.trap: A small net ΔG doesn't mean the interactions are small. It means two large terms nearly cancel.

fig.cap: Anfinsen's experiment. Removing urea and β-mercaptoethanol slowly restores full activity; oxidizing while still unfolded gives scrambled disulfides and about 1% activity.
fig.alt: Flowchart: native RNase A with 4 disulfides and 100% activity, treated with 8 M urea plus β-mercaptoethanol, becomes unfolded and reduced with 8 free thiols and 0% activity. Path 1, remove urea and reducing agent slowly then oxidize, returns to native with about 100% activity, tagged sequence encodes fold. Path 2, oxidize in 8 M urea, gives scrambled disulfides with about 1% activity. A trace of β-mercaptoethanol lets scrambled disulfides reshuffle back to native.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; content after Anfinsen's ribonuclease A experiments as described in Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry.

ox: Correct. Urea unfolded the enzyme and the reducing agent broke its disulfide bonds, leaving only the sequence. When both were slowly removed, the chain refolded, re-formed the right disulfides and got full activity back, with nothing present but its own sequence and water. So the information for the correct fold is in the primary structure. This is Anfinsen's experiment with ribonuclease A, which won the 1972 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Not quite. There were no chaperones in the test tube, yet the protein refolded fully, so chaperones can't always be required. In cells, chaperones help many proteins fold efficiently by keeping them from clumping in the crowded cytoplasm, but they don't supply the fold, and small proteins like this one fold on their own.

Not quite. The information flows the other way. The gene sets the amino acid sequence during translation, and the sequence then decides which cysteines meet and pair as the protein folds. Disulfides form during or after folding and can't specify the sequence.

Not quite. Neither urea nor a reducing agent like β-mercaptoethanol breaks peptide bonds. If the chain had been cut, simply removing the chemicals couldn't put it back together, and activity wouldn't return. Getting full activity back shows the primary structure stayed intact the whole time.

p: In the 1950s and 60s, Christian Anfinsen unfolded the enzyme ribonuclease A with urea and broke its four disulfide bonds with a reducing agent. The enzyme lost all activity.

When he slowly removed both chemicals, the enzyme refolded, its eight cysteines found their correct partners, and almost all the activity came back. Nothing was there to guide it except its own amino acid sequence.
The big lesson: a protein's sequence contains all the information needed to fold into its working shape. The folded form is simply the most stable arrangement for that sequence.

x1A_062.trap: Chaperones help folding happen efficiently. They never supply the information for the fold.

fig.cap: Path 2 (lower right) is this experiment: oxidizing in 8 M urea locks in random disulfides, so only about 1 in 105 molecules is native.
fig.alt: Flowchart of Anfinsen's experiment. Unfolded reduced RNase A oxidized while still in 8 M urea gives scrambled disulfides with about 1% activity, tagged disulfides locked before folding. A box explains 7 times 5 times 3 times 1 equals 105 possible pairings, only one native.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; content after Anfinsen's ribonuclease A experiments as described in Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry.

ox: Not quite. Urea is an unfolding agent, not something that cuts bonds with water. It breaks hydrogen bonds and weakens the hydrophobic effect, but it doesn't cut the covalent peptide bonds of the backbone, even at 8 M. The same urea in the successful refolding experiment left the enzyme fully recoverable, which proves the backbone was fine.

Not quite. Oxidizing cysteine SH groups joins two of them into a disulfide bond (S–S). It can't add carbons or turn cysteine into methionine, which would mean building a whole new side chain (methionine is CH₂–CH₂–S–CH₃). Stronger oxidation can make other sulfur acids, but never methionine.

Not quite. The primary structure, the sequence held by peptide bonds, isn't changed by urea or oxidation. The problem is a covalent mistake beyond the sequence: wrong cysteine pairs. Since the sequence is intact, adding a trace of reducing agent lets the disulfides shuffle, and the enzyme slowly regains activity. That couldn't happen if the sequence were lost.

Correct. In 8 M urea the chain is a floppy random coil, so the 8 cysteines bump into each other at random. Oxidizing at this stage locks in whatever pairs happen to form. There are 7 × 5 × 3 × 1 = 105 ways to pair 8 cysteines into 4 disulfides, and only one is right, so about 1 in 105 (roughly 1%) of molecules are correct. When urea is removed, the wrong covalent links trap the chain in shapes it can't escape, so activity stays very low.

concept.t: Why the order of folding and oxidation matters
p: Disulfide bonds are covalent links between pairs of cysteines. In a correctly folded protein, the right cysteines end up next to each other, so the right pairs form.

If you oxidize the cysteines while the chain is still unfolded, they pair up with whichever partner happens to be nearby. With 8 cysteines, there are 105 possible ways to pair them, and only one is the correct set.

Once a wrong disulfide forms, it's a covalent bond, so simply removing urea won't undo it. The chain gets trapped in a wrong shape. Adding a small amount of reducing agent lets the bonds break and re-form, so the chain can eventually find the correct pairing.

fm.f: ways to pair 2n cysteines = (2n − 1) × (2n − 3) × … × 1, where 2n = number of cysteines
fm.v: 2n = 8 cysteines (so n = 4 disulfides); correct pairings = 1; ways = ?
fm.why: Random pairing gives each of the 105 arrangements an equal chance, and only one is native.
fm.nc: The first cysteine can pair with any of the other 7; the next unpaired one with any of the remaining 5; then 3; then 1.

steps: Write the formula: ways to pair 2n cysteines = (2n − 1) × (2n − 3) × … × 1.
Write down the values: 2n = 8 cysteines, so 4 disulfides; only 1 pairing is correct.
Pick any cysteine: it can pair with any of the other 7. Then the next unpaired cysteine has 5 choices, then 3, then 1.
Fraction correct = 1 ÷ 105 ≈ 0.0095, about 1%.
The wrong disulfides are covalent, so removing urea can't fix them. Activity stays near 1%.
x1A_063.trap: Disulfides have to form after the chain folds. Oxidize first and the wrong pairs get locked in.

fig.cap: An Hsp70 chaperone binds the exposed hydrophobic patches of a folding chain and releases it (ATP-driven). With protection the chain reaches its native fold; without it, patches stick together into aggregates.
fig.alt: A chain with orange hydrophobic patches is bound by Hsp70, noncovalently, with ATP hydrolysis driving release. The released chain becomes a native fold with buried core, tagged fold set by sequence. Without a chaperone, several chains stick together in an aggregate. Bottom tags: no fold information, not covalent, do not make peptide bonds.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. The information for a protein's correct fold is in its own sequence, as Anfinsen's refolding experiments showed. Chaperones are general helpers that recognize things all unfolded chains have in common, like exposed water-avoiding stretches. They can't carry a separate blueprint for each of the thousands of proteins they help.

Correct. New or damaged chains expose water-avoiding stretches that would normally be buried. In the crowded cytoplasm these patches can stick together and form clumps. Chaperones like Hsp70 grab these exposed regions, and barrel-shaped chaperonins like GroEL/GroES give a chain a closed chamber to fold in. ATP powers cycles of grabbing and releasing, giving the chain repeated chances to fold right. The final shape is still set by the sequence.

Not quite. Chaperone binding is brief and noncovalent. Hsp70 grips the chain through water-avoiding contacts, holds on tight after it breaks down its ATP to ADP, then lets go when fresh ATP replaces the ADP. A permanent covalent bond would leave the protein stuck to the chaperone and unable to work, the opposite of what chaperones are for.

Not quite. Peptide bonds are made by the ribosome's peptidyl transferase center, which is made of rRNA (so the ribosome is a ribozyme, an RNA enzyme). Chaperones act on the chain as it comes out of the ribosome or after, helping it fold. They don't add amino acids.

p: Inside a cell, proteins are packed together tightly. A newly made chain, or one damaged by heat, has water-avoiding patches showing. Those patches are sticky and can latch onto other chains, forming useless or harmful clumps.

Chaperones prevent that. Hsp70 grabs exposed water-avoiding stretches and releases them in ATP-powered cycles. Chaperonins like GroEL/GroES build a closed chamber where a single chain can fold without bumping into anything. Many chaperones are 'heat shock proteins' (Hsp), made in larger amounts when the cell is stressed by heat.
Chaperones don't tell the protein what shape to take. They just give it a safe chance to reach the shape its sequence already specifies.

x1A_064.trap: Chaperones prevent misfolding. They don't decide the fold, form covalent bonds or make peptide bonds.

fig.cap: Urea's two denaturing actions, both noncovalent: it competes for backbone hydrogen bonds and solvates nonpolar side chains. Covalent bonds survive.
fig.alt: Structure of urea with two NH₂ groups and a C=O. Box 1: competes for hydrogen bonds, backbone C=O to urea H-N and backbone N-H to urea O=C. Box 2: solvates nonpolar side chains, weakening the hydrophobic effect. Green box: peptide bonds and disulfides survive; removing urea allows refolding. Red tags: does not hydrolyze peptide bonds, reduce S-S bonds, or add groups covalently.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

fig.cap: How common denaturing agents act. Only reducing agents break disulfides, and only hydrolysis breaks peptide bonds.
fig.alt: Table of agents (heat, urea, ethanol, SDS, strong acid or base, high salt, mercury and lead ions, β-mercaptoethanol or DTT, protease), each with its main action and whether disulfide and peptide bonds survive. All survive except disulfides with reducing agents and peptide bonds with protease.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. Cutting peptide bonds takes a protease or long heating in strong acid or base. Urea is a small, neutral molecule that can't cut the backbone. That's why urea-unfolded proteins can often refold once the urea is removed: the sequence is still there.

Correct. Urea, (NH₂)₂C=O, has two N–H groups and a C=O, so at high concentration (6 to 8 M) it hydrogen-bonds to the protein's backbone and polar side chains, replacing the protein's own internal hydrogen bonds. It also surrounds water-avoiding side chains better than water does, so hiding them in a core isn't as rewarding, which weakens the hydrophobic effect. The unfolded state becomes more favorable while covalent bonds stay intact.

Not quite. Breaking a disulfide (S–S) into two SH groups is a reduction that needs a reducing agent, like β-mercaptoethanol or DTT, to donate electrons. Urea can't do that. That's why Anfinsen had to add β-mercaptoethanol along with urea to fully unfold ribonuclease A.

Not quite. Urea works through reversible, noncovalent interactions, so removing it often lets the protein refold. Old urea solutions can slowly break down and tag lysines by accident, but that's a lab side effect, not how urea unfolds proteins.

p: Denaturing a protein means destroying its folded shape (secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure) without changing its sequence.

Urea and guanidinium chloride are chemical denaturants. At high concentrations they hydrogen-bond with the protein's backbone and make water a better solvent for water-avoiding side chains. Both effects tip the balance toward the unfolded state.
Denaturants only break noncovalent interactions. Peptide bonds and disulfide bonds survive. To break disulfides you add a reducing agent like β-mercaptoethanol or DTT.

x1A_065.trap: Urea alone never breaks disulfides. You need a reducing agent such as β-mercaptoethanol.

fig.cap: Each level of structure and what holds it. After boiling only the primary level, held by covalent peptide bonds, remains intact.
fig.alt: Four panels: primary (sequence, peptide bonds) tagged intact after boiling or urea; secondary (backbone hydrogen bonds), tertiary (side-chain interactions) and quaternary (contacts between chains) each tagged lost.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; content consistent with OpenStax Biology 2e, 3.4 Proteins.

ox: Not quite. Secondary structure is held by backbone hydrogen bonds, each worth only a few kJ/mol. Boiling easily breaks them, so helices and sheets unravel. Many proteins unfold between 40 and 70 °C, well below 100 °C. Some heated proteins later clump into new, wrong sheets, but the original secondary structure is gone.

Not quite. Tertiary structure, the 3D fold, depends on the hydrophobic effect, side-chain hydrogen bonds and salt bridges, all noncovalent. At 100 °C these are overwhelmed. The protein unfolds, its exposed sticky patches usually clump with other molecules, and the enzyme loses its active site and its activity.

Not quite. Subunits in a multi-chain enzyme are held together by the same noncovalent contacts that hold tertiary structure, so they come apart or clump randomly on boiling. Only disulfide links between chains would survive, and even then the correct arrangement is lost.

Correct. Primary structure is the sequence held by covalent peptide bonds. A peptide bond is partly double and needs an enzyme or harsh chemistry (like 6 M HCl at about 110 °C for many hours) to break at a useful rate. 10 minutes of boiling at neutral pH is enough to break weak interactions but not covalent backbone bonds, so the sequence survives while the higher levels are destroyed.

p: Proteins are held in shape mostly by weak, noncovalent interactions. Heat makes molecules jiggle harder, and eventually that motion breaks these weak contacts. The protein unfolds, which is called denaturation.
Each level of structure above primary depends on noncovalent forces: hydrogen bonds for secondary, the hydrophobic effect and salt bridges for tertiary and quaternary. So heat can destroy all three.

The sequence is held by covalent peptide bonds, which are far stronger and very slow to break without a catalyst. A boiled egg white is a good example: the proteins are unfolded and clumped, but every chain is still intact.

x1A_066.trap: Denaturing removes shape, not sequence. Boiling leaves every peptide bond in place.

fig.cap: An Asp–Lys salt bridge at three pH values. Percent charged is computed from Henderson–Hasselbalch (Asp pKₐ 3.9, Lys pKₐ 10.5). Only near neutral pH are both partners charged.
fig.alt: Three panels. pH 2: Asp side chain COOH 1% charged, Lys NH₃⁺ 100% charged, no attraction, protein strongly positive, salt bridge lost. pH 7: Asp COO⁻ and Lys NH₃⁺ both 100% charged, attraction, salt bridge holds. pH 12: Asp COO⁻ 100% charged, Lys NH₂ 3% charged, no attraction, salt bridge lost.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; charge fractions computed from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation with standard side-chain pKₐ values.

ox: Correct. A protein's fold relies on charged side chains. At very low pH (say pH 2), the COO⁻ groups of Asp and Glu (pKₐ ≈ 4) pick up protons and become neutral COOH. At very high pH (say pH 12), Lys NH₃⁺ groups (pKₐ ≈ 10.5) lose protons and become neutral NH₂. Salt bridges lose one partner's charge, hydrogen bonds shift, and the protein carries a big charge of one sign, so like charges repel. The fold falls apart even though no covalent bond breaks.

Not quite. Breaking a disulfide is a reduction that needs an electron donor like β-mercaptoethanol or DTT. Changing the H⁺ concentration doesn't provide that. Proteins with no disulfides at all are still unfolded by extreme pH, so this can't be the mechanism.

Not quite. Turning L-amino acids into D-amino acids (racemization) means pulling off the α-hydrogen. It does happen slowly in strong base or hot acid, over hours to days. pH unfolding happens in seconds to minutes and is often reversible when the pH is restored, which racemization wouldn't be.

Not quite. Acids and bases don't dry out a protein's core. Extreme pH works through charge: it changes which groups carry protons. The core is only affected indirectly, after the charges push the fold apart.

p: Some side chains carry a charge at normal pH: Asp and Glu are negative, Lys and Arg are positive, and His is partly positive. These charges form salt bridges and hydrogen bonds that help hold the fold.
Push the pH far from normal and those charges change. In strong acid, the negative groups pick up protons and go neutral. In strong base, the positive groups lose protons and go neutral.

Once the charge pattern shifts, salt bridges break and the protein is left carrying lots of the same charge, which pushes its parts apart. No covalent bonds break, so restoring the pH can sometimes let it refold.

x1A_067.trap: pH works on protonation (charge), not on covalent bonds or on L/D shape.

fig.cap: An SDS-PAGE gel with a mass ladder. Band positions are computed so that distance is linear in log(mass); smaller chains run farther.
fig.alt: Gel with a ladder lane of 250, 150, 100, 75, 50, 37, 25, 15 and 10 kilodaltons and a sample lane with bands at 120, 60 and 30 kilodaltons. A box explains that SDS unfolds proteins and gives uniform negative charge per mass, so the gel sieves by size. Tags: molecular mass correct; pI belongs to isoelectric focusing; native shape to native PAGE; intrinsic charge is swamped.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; band positions computed from a log-linear mass calibration.

ox: Not quite. The pI is what separates proteins in isoelectric focusing, where each protein moves through a pH gradient until it reaches the pH where its net charge is zero. In SDS-PAGE, SDS gives every protein a big negative charge, so they all move toward the anode no matter their pI.

Not quite. SDS, usually with heat and a reducing agent, unfolds proteins into stretched-out rods coated with SDS. That wipes out differences in folded shape, which is the whole point. Shape does matter in native PAGE, where proteins stay folded.

Correct. SDS binds proteins at a nearly constant ratio, about 1.4 g of SDS per gram of protein, so every chain gets about the same negative charge per unit mass and the same unfolded shape. The pull per unit mass is similar for all chains, and the gel acts as a sieve: smaller chains move through faster and travel farther. Distance traveled tracks the log of the mass, so a ladder of known sizes lets you estimate an unknown chain's mass.

Not quite. A protein's own net charge is tiny compared with the hundreds of negative charges from bound SDS. So its own charge is drowned out and barely matters. A protein's own charge does matter in native PAGE and ion-exchange chromatography.

p: SDS (sodium dodecyl sulfate) is a detergent with a negative charge. Heating a protein with SDS unfolds it and coats it with SDS along its whole length.
That does two things. Every protein gets about the same charge per unit mass, and every protein has the same rod-like shape. Charge and shape are no longer different between proteins.

The polyacrylamide gel is a mesh. Small chains wiggle through easily and travel far; big chains get held back. So distance depends on mass. Note that SDS-PAGE measures each separate chain, not the whole multi-chain protein.

x1A_068.trap: SDS-PAGE gives the mass of each chain, not of the whole multi-chain protein.

fig.cap: Two-state melt curves computed for Tm = 52 °C (wild type) and 44 °C (mutant). The mutant's curve is shifted 8 °C to lower temperature.
fig.alt: Fraction unfolded versus temperature from 25 to 70 degrees Celsius. Blue sigmoid for wild type crosses 0.5 at 52 degrees; red sigmoid for the mutant crosses 0.5 at 44 degrees. An arrow shows delta Tm of minus 8 degrees, less stable. A note says below its Tm the mutant is still mostly folded.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the two-state van 't Hoff model with ΔH = 300 kJ/mol and the Tm values in the question.

ox: Not quite. A stabilizing mutation makes the protein harder to unfold, so more heat is needed and the Tm goes up. Here the Tm drops from 52 °C to 44 °C, the opposite. Reading the direction of a Tm change correctly is the whole point of this kind of experiment.

Not quite. Tm measures stability (the balance between folded and unfolded), not how fast the enzyme works. Activity has to be measured separately, for example with Vₘₐₓ and Kₘ. A less stable mutant might be just as active at low temperature, or less; the melting curve alone can't tell you.

Not quite. A protein that couldn't fold at all would show no unfolding transition and no Tm. A measurable Tm of 44 °C means the mutant is folded below about 44 °C and unfolds when heated past that, just at a lower temperature than the normal protein.

Correct. Tm is the temperature where half the molecules are unfolded, where folding and unfolding are evenly balanced. A lower Tm means less heat tips the balance toward unfolded, so the folded state has less of an energy cushion. The 8 °C drop shows the mutation destabilizes the fold, maybe by removing a buried water-avoiding contact, a hydrogen bond or a salt bridge, or by putting a polar residue in the core.

p: When you slowly heat a protein, it stays folded for a while, then unfolds over a fairly narrow temperature range. The temperature at the middle of that range, where half the molecules are unfolded, is the melting temperature, Tm.
Tm is a handy measure of stability. A higher Tm means the folded state can take more heat before giving up, so it's more stable. A lower Tm means it's less stable.
Researchers compare a normal protein with mutants to see which residues matter for stability. A big drop in Tm points to a residue that was helping hold the fold together.

x1A_069.trap: Lower Tm = less stable. Don't read a lower melting point as tighter binding or higher activity.

fig.cap: Templated misfolding. Misfolded PrPˢᶜ (β-rich) converts normal PrPᶜ (α-rich) into another copy of itself, and the cycle repeats.
fig.alt: Normal PrPc drawn as an oval with helices plus misfolded PrPSc drawn as a box with β-strand arrows, templating to give two PrPSc, which leads to amyloid fibrils and neuron loss; a dashed arrow shows the cycle repeating. Bottom: same amino acid sequence, different fold; no DNA or RNA. Red tags mark wrong mechanisms: DNA or RNA genome, spreading mutations, toxic peptide fragments.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. Prions have no DNA or RNA at all; that's what made them so surprising. The prion protein is made from the host's own gene. Infectious prion material stays infectious after treatments that destroy DNA and RNA, like UV light, but loses infectivity when proteins are destroyed.

Not quite. In infectious prion disease the sequence of the prion protein doesn't change; what spreads is a folded shape. Normal and misfolded prion protein have the same sequence and differ only in how they're folded. (Some inherited prion diseases do start with a gene mutation, but that's inherited, not passed from cell to cell.)

Correct. Normal prion protein is mostly α-helix and dissolves easily. The misfolded form is rich in β-sheet. When the misfolded form meets a normal one, it acts as a template and refolds it into the bad shape, and each new bad copy can convert more. The misfolded protein stacks into tough clumps (amyloid) that enzymes can't fully break down and that damage neurons, as in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and mad cow disease.

Not quite. Prions are known for resisting breakdown: the β-sheet clumps are only partly digested by enzymes and survive normal heat sterilization. Disease comes from the misfolded protein and its clumps, not from toxic pieces made by breaking it down.

p: Most infections spread genetic material: viruses and bacteria carry DNA or RNA. Prions are different. They're made only of protein.

The prion protein normally folds mostly into α-helices. It can also fold into a very stable, β-sheet-rich shape. That misfolded shape can grab normal copies and refold them to match, like one bad apple spoiling the barrel. The number of misfolded copies grows and grows.

The misfolded copies stack into long, tough fibers called amyloid. They resist enzymes and heat, build up in the brain, and kill neurons, leaving sponge-like holes. Examples are Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in humans and mad cow disease in cattle.

x1A_070.trap: Prions pass on a shape (α-helix to β-sheet), not a gene or a mutation.

fig.cap: Left: one chain folding into two domains joined by a linker. Right: two separate chains (subunits). A domain is a folded unit within one chain.
fig.alt: Left panel: one teal chain forming two compact blobs labeled domain 1 and domain 2 joined by a linker, tagged domain, tertiary level, correct. Right panel: two separate blobs labeled chain A and chain B, tagged subunits, quaternary. A note says a primary sequence is just the residue order and a β-turn is a 4-residue reversal too small to fold on its own.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. A subunit is a separate chain in a multi-chain protein, like one α chain of hemoglobin. Subunits belong to quaternary structure. The question describes a region of a protein, part of one chain, connected to the rest of the chain by peptide bonds rather than by contacts between separate chains.

Correct. A domain is a stretch of a single chain, usually 50 to 250 residues, that folds on its own into a stable, compact 3D unit and often has its own job, like binding DNA, ATP or a membrane. Many proteins are built from several domains joined by flexible linkers, like modules. Domains are part of tertiary structure, and the same type of domain can show up in many different proteins.

Not quite. The primary sequence is just the order of amino acids along the chain. It holds the information that makes a domain fold, but it's a one-dimensional list, not a folded 3D unit with its own job.

Not quite. A β-turn is a short four-residue U-turn that reverses the chain's direction. It's a small piece of secondary structure that connects strands. It's far too small to fold on its own or do a job by itself.

p: Big proteins are often built like Lego from smaller pieces called domains. Each domain is a section of the chain that folds up on its own into a compact shape and usually has one job.
Because domains fold independently, evolution can mix and match them. The same DNA-binding or kinase domain shows up in many different proteins, combined with different partners.
A subunit is something else: a complete, separate chain. Hemoglobin has four subunits. Each of those subunits could itself contain one or more domains.

x1A_071.trap: Domain = part of one chain. Subunit = a separate chain.

fig.cap: The reducing cytosol keeps cysteines as thiols; the oxidizing ER lumen (with PDI) forms disulfides, which persist after secretion.
fig.alt: Schematic cell. Cytosol labeled reducing, GSH to GSSG above 30 to 1, cysteines as free SH, few disulfides. ER lumen labeled oxidizing, GSH to GSSG about 1 to 1 to 3 to 1, Ero1 and PDI make S-S bonds, tagged secretory pathway. An arrow labeled secretion leads outside, where S-S bonds stay intact. The reaction 2 Cys-SH gives Cys-S-S-Cys plus 2 H⁺ plus 2 electrons is shown as an oxidation.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; redox ratios from standard cell biology texts (Alberts, Molecular Biology of the Cell).

ox: Correct. Forming a disulfide is an oxidation: 2 Cys–SH → Cys–S–S–Cys + 2 H⁺ + 2 e⁻. The cytosol is kept strongly reducing by glutathione (reduced glutathione outnumbers its oxidized form by more than 30 to 1) and by the thioredoxin system, which break any disulfides that form. The ER is much more oxidizing, and enzymes like protein disulfide isomerase form and rearrange disulfides in proteins headed for secretion. Outside the cell is oxidizing too, so the bonds stay intact.

Not quite. Cytosolic proteins have plenty of cysteines. They're kept as free SH groups, which matter in active sites (cysteine proteases), in holding metals (zinc fingers) and in sensing oxidation. The difference between compartments is how oxidizing they are, not whether cysteine is present.

Not quite. Temperature doesn't decide whether disulfides form. The cytosol and the ER of the same cell are at the same temperature, yet one forms disulfides and the other doesn't. What matters is the balance of oxidizing and reducing molecules in each compartment.

Not quite. All ribosomes use the same genetic code and read the cysteine codons UGU and UGC. Secreted proteins are made by the same kind of ribosome as cytosolic ones; it just docks on the rough ER and feeds the growing chain inside. Where the protein ends up, not which ribosome made it, decides whether disulfides form.

p: A disulfide bond (S–S) joins two cysteines. Making one is an oxidation, because the two SH groups lose electrons. Breaking one is a reduction.

Different parts of the cell have different chemistry. The cytosol is reducing: it's full of glutathione, which donates electrons and keeps cysteines as SH. The ER lumen is oxidizing, and it has enzymes like protein disulfide isomerase that help form the right disulfides.

Proteins that are secreted or sit on the cell surface pass through the ER, pick up disulfides there, and keep them in the oxidizing space outside the cell. That's why antibodies, insulin and many hormones have disulfides, while most cytosolic proteins don't.

x1A_072.trap: Disulfide formation is an oxidation, so it happens in oxidizing places (the ER and outside the cell), not in the reducing cytosol.

fig.cap: Attraction between a +1 and a −1 charge in water computed with Debye–Hückel screening. At 0.4 nm, 1 M NaCl cuts the attraction from −4.3 to −1.2 kJ/mol.
fig.alt: Attraction energy versus distance from 0.3 to 1.5 nanometers for no salt, 0.01 M, 0.15 M and 1 M NaCl. Higher salt curves are much shallower. An annotation at 0.4 nanometers gives minus 4.3 kilojoules per mole with no salt and minus 1.2 with 1 M NaCl, a 73% reduction.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from Coulomb's law with Debye–Hückel screening (relative permittivity 80, 25 °C).

ox: Not quite. Peptide bonds are covalent bonds in the backbone. Breaking them takes an enzyme or long heating in strong acid. Dissolved Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions can't do that, so 1 M NaCl leaves the sequence untouched.

Not quite. Disulfide bonds are covalent S–S bonds, and only a chemical reduction breaks them, using a reducing agent like β-mercaptoethanol or DTT. NaCl isn't a reducing agent, so disulfides are unaffected.

Correct. A salt bridge is an attraction between opposite charges, like Lys NH₃⁺ and Glu COO⁻. In 1 M NaCl, free Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions gather around each charge and muffle it. The distance over which charges can still feel each other (the Debye length) shrinks from about 3 nm in 0.01 M salt to about 0.3 nm in 1 M. A salt bridge spans about 0.4 nm, so its attraction drops by roughly 70%. That's also why high salt is used to wash proteins off ion-exchange columns.

Not quite. The hydrophobic effect depends on how water is organized, and many salts actually make it stronger. That's the idea behind salting out. So moderate NaCl tends to leave water-avoiding packing intact or slightly stronger, not weaker.

p: Opposite charges attract. In a protein, a positive side chain (like lysine) and a negative one (like glutamate) can pair up into a salt bridge that helps hold the fold.

Dissolved salt is full of free ions. Negative Cl⁻ ions cluster near positive side chains, and positive Na⁺ ions cluster near negative ones. This cloud of ions muffles each charge, a process called screening. The more salt, the shorter the distance over which two charges can still feel each other.
Screening only affects interactions based on charge. Covalent bonds (peptide bonds, disulfides) are untouched, and water-avoiding interactions in the core aren't weakened by moderate salt.

fm.f: λD ≈ 0.304 nm ÷ √I, where λD = Debye screening length (how far a charge's pull reaches in salty water at 25 °C), I = ionic strength in mol/L (for NaCl, equal to its concentration)
fm.v: I = 1 M; λD = ?
fm.why: More salt means a shorter reach for each charge.

fm.f: screening factor = e raised to the power (−r ÷ λD), where r = distance between the two charges, λD = Debye length
fm.v: r ≈ 0.4 nm (typical salt bridge); λD ≈ 0.30 nm; screening factor = ?
fm.s: r ÷ λD = 0.4 ÷ 0.304 ≈ 1.3; e raised to the power −1.3 ≈ 0.27
fm.why: This tells you what fraction of the attraction is left after screening.
fm.nc: 0.27 left means about 1 − 0.27 = 0.73, or 73%, is lost.

steps: Write the formula: λD ≈ 0.304 nm ÷ √I, then screening factor = e raised to the power (−r ÷ λD).
Write down the values: 1 M NaCl, so I = 1 M; a salt bridge spans r ≈ 0.4 nm.
Find the screening length: √1 = 1, so λD ≈ 0.304 ÷ 1 ≈ 0.30 nm.
Divide the distance by the screening length: 0.4 ÷ 0.304 ≈ 1.3.
Screening factor = e raised to the power −1.3 ≈ 0.27, so only about 27% of the attraction is left: a loss of about 100% − 27% = 73%.
Peptide and disulfide bonds are covalent and unaffected; water-avoiding packing is, if anything, slightly strengthened.
x1A_073.trap: Salt targets charge-based interactions. It can't break covalent bonds and tends to strengthen water-avoiding ones.

fig.cap: Schematic Ramachandran plot. Shaded areas are the sterically allowed φ/ψ regions; dots mark standard α-helix and β-sheet angles.
fig.alt: Plot of psi against phi from minus 180 to plus 180 degrees. Shaded allowed regions in the upper left (β-sheet, with antiparallel at minus 139, plus 135 and parallel at minus 119, plus 113), the lower left (α-helix at minus 57, minus 47) and a small upper-right region (left-handed helix, mostly glycine). White areas are disallowed steric clashes.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; schematic allowed regions and standard angles after Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry.

ox: Correct. The backbone can twist at two bonds per residue: φ around N–Cα and ψ around Cα–C. The peptide bond itself is flat and doesn't twist. A Ramachandran plot graphs φ against ψ and shades the combinations where atoms don't collide. The allowed regions match real secondary structures: the right-handed α-helix near φ = −57°, ψ = −47°, and β-sheets near φ = −120° to −140°, ψ = +115° to +135°. Glycine can reach extra regions, and proline is restricted.

Not quite. Absorbance plotted against wavelength is an absorption spectrum. Proteins absorb at 280 nm because of tryptophan and tyrosine, which is used to measure protein concentration, but that says nothing about which backbone angles are allowed.

Not quite. Reaction speed plotted against substrate concentration is a Michaelis-Menten plot. It curves up and levels off at Vₘₐₓ, reaching half of Vₘₐₓ when [S] = Kₘ. It describes how fast an enzyme works, not the shape of the backbone.
Not quite. pH plotted against added base (or net charge against pH) is a titration curve, which shows pKₐ values and the pI. It's about groups gaining and losing protons, not backbone shape.

p: Each residue in a protein chain has two backbone bonds that can twist: φ (around N–Cα) and ψ (around Cα–C). The peptide bond between residues is flat and stiff, so it doesn't count.
If you try every possible pair of φ and ψ, most of them make atoms bump into each other. A Ramachandran plot is a map with φ on one axis and ψ on the other, with the allowed pairs shaded in.

The allowed islands line up with the structures we actually see: one island for α-helices and one for β-sheets. Glycine, with no real side chain, can go almost anywhere on the map. Proline, locked by its ring, is stuck in a small area.

x1A_074.trap: φ and ψ twist. The peptide bond (ω) doesn't, because it's flat.

fig.cap: Solubility versus ionic strength computed with illustrative constants: solubility rises slightly at low salt (salting in) and then falls steadily at high salt (salting out).
fig.alt: Graph of log relative solubility against ionic strength from 0 to 8 molar. The curve rises to a maximum near 0.6 molar (salting in, ions shield surface charges) and then falls linearly (salting out, ions bind the water needed to hydrate the protein, so proteins aggregate and precipitate).
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Debye–Hückel salting-in term plus the Cohn salting-out equation with illustrative constants (A = 1.2, Ks = 0.25 L/mol).

ox: Not quite. Salting in happens at low salt: a few ions muffle charged patches on the protein surface, so the proteins attract each other less and dissolve better. That's the opposite of what's described here, where the protein comes out of solution at high salt. Salting in and salting out are two ends of the same curve.

Not quite. Ammonium sulfate doesn't break peptide bonds, and salting out isn't really denaturation. Most proteins precipitated this way keep their fold and dissolve again, fully active, once the salt is removed. That's exactly why it's a standard first step in purifying proteins.

Not quite. In sulfate (SO₄²⁻), sulfur is already as oxidized as it can get, so it can't donate electrons and isn't a reducing agent. Breaking disulfides takes something like β-mercaptoethanol or DTT. Salting out has nothing to do with disulfides.

Correct. At high concentration the salt ions hold onto lots of water, tying up most of the available water molecules. Too little is left to surround the protein's surface, so its water-avoiding patches stick to each other instead, and the proteins clump and precipitate. Ammonium sulfate is used because it dissolves extremely well. Different proteins precipitate at different salt levels, which lets you separate them.

p: A protein stays dissolved when water molecules surround its surface. How much salt is around changes that.
At low salt, adding a little helps: ions muffle the charged patches on proteins so they don't stick to each other, and solubility goes up. That's salting in.

At high salt, the ions grab so much water that the proteins don't have enough left. Their sticky patches find each other, and they precipitate. That's salting out. It's gentle and reversible, so labs use it (often with ammonium sulfate) to pull proteins out of a mixture in steps.

fx.f: log S = log S₀ + A·√I ÷ (1 + √I) − Ks·I
fx.w: S = protein solubility, S₀ = solubility in pure water, I = ionic strength (M), A and Ks = constants for a given protein and salt. The middle term makes solubility rise at low salt (salting in); the last term makes it fall at high salt (salting out).

x1A_075.trap: Low salt: salting in (more soluble). High salt: salting out (precipitates).

fig.cap: Net charge of a model protein computed from Henderson–Hasselbalch for each ionizable group. Net charge crosses zero at the pI (about 6.1), where solubility is lowest.
fig.alt: Curve of net charge against pH from 1 to 13, falling from about plus 25 to minus 29. It crosses zero at pH 6.1, highlighted as the pI where the protein is least soluble. Points mark pI minus 2 with net charge plus 12 and pI plus 2 with net charge minus 3. Below the pI the region is labeled net positive; above it, net negative.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for a model protein (10 Asp, 12 Glu, 4 His, 2 Cys, 6 Tyr, 12 Lys, 8 Arg plus termini) with standard pKₐ values.

ox: Not quite. Two pH units below its pI, a protein has picked up extra protons and carries a clear positive charge. Every molecule is positive, so neighbors push each other away and stay spread out in solution. It's more soluble here than at the pI.

Correct. At the pI the protein's positive and negative charges balance, so its net charge is zero. With no net charge, the molecules don't repel each other, and their sticky spots (water-avoiding patches, hydrogen bonds, small areas of opposite charge) let them clump and precipitate. This is how milk curdles when it's acidified to about pH 4.6, the pI of its main protein, casein.

Not quite. Two pH units above the pI, the protein has lost protons and carries a negative charge. All the molecules are negative and push each other apart, so they stay dissolved. It's more soluble here than at the pI, just as it is below the pI.

Not quite. pH 7 is special for water (neutral), not for proteins. Each protein has its own pI based on its amino acids, from below 2 (pepsin) to above 10 (lysozyme). A protein is least soluble at its own pI, which can be far from 7.

p: Proteins stay dissolved partly because they carry a net charge. Molecules with the same charge repel each other, which keeps them from clumping.
At the pI, the net charge is zero. The protein still has plenty of charged groups, but the positives and negatives cancel. With no overall repulsion, the molecules can stick together and precipitate.

So solubility is lowest at the pI and rises as you move the pH away from it in either direction. That's the idea behind isoelectric precipitation, used to separate proteins and seen every time milk curdles.

x1A_076.trap: Least soluble at the pI, not at pH 7. Zero net charge doesn't mean no charged groups.

fig.cap: A size-exclusion column and its elution profile computed from a log-linear calibration. The 440 kDa protein elutes first (9.5 mL) and the 12 kDa protein last (20.0 mL).
fig.alt: Left: column of porous beads; large purple proteins pass between beads while small orange proteins enter pores. Right: absorbance against elution volume with peaks at 9.5 mL (440 kilodaltons), 12.7 mL (150), 16.2 mL (45) and 20.0 mL (12), after a void volume at 8 mL. Tag: largest elutes first. Note: separation by size only; charge and pI do not matter.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; peaks computed from Ve = V₀ + Kav(Vt − V₀) with an illustrative log-linear Kav calibration.

ox: Not quite. The smallest protein comes out last, not first. Small molecules can enter the pores in the beads, so they explore more of the column (inside the beads and between them) and take a longer path.

Correct. Size-exclusion chromatography uses porous beads. Proteins too big to enter the pores stay in the space between beads and get swept straight through, so they come out first. Smaller proteins spend time inside the pores and are delayed. How late a protein comes out tracks the log of its mass, so the column can estimate a protein's full folded mass, including all its subunits.

Not quite. Separating by charge is what ion-exchange chromatography does, using charged beads that grab oppositely charged proteins. Size-exclusion beads aren't charged, so a protein's charge has basically no effect on when it comes out; only its size matters.

Not quite. The pI sets a protein's charge at a given pH, which matters in ion-exchange chromatography and isoelectric focusing. Size exclusion doesn't use charge, so the protein with the lowest pI doesn't come out in any special order.

p: In size-exclusion (gel filtration) chromatography, a column is filled with beads full of tiny pores. A protein mixture is poured in and washed through with buffer.

Big proteins can't fit into the pores, so they rush through the spaces between beads and come out first. Small proteins duck in and out of the pores, taking a longer, winding path, so they come out later.
Because proteins stay folded, this measures the size of the whole assembled protein, including all its subunits. Compare that with SDS-PAGE, which measures each chain separately.

x1A_077.trap: Gel filtration: big comes out first. SDS-PAGE: small runs farthest. Both involve pores, but the visible result looks opposite.

fig.cap: The same three proteins on a native gel (illustrative positions that depend on charge, size and shape) and on an SDS gel (positions computed from mass). Proteins B and C both run at 30 kDa in SDS.
fig.alt: Two gels. Native PAGE lanes A, B, C: compact very negative 60 kilodalton monomer A runs farthest; weakly charged 60 kilodalton dimer B stays near the top; elongated 30 kilodalton monomer C is in the middle. SDS-PAGE: A at 60 kilodaltons, B and C both at 30 kilodaltons. Tags: native separates by size plus charge plus shape (correct); mass alone is SDS; pI alone is isoelectric focusing.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; SDS band positions computed from a log-linear mass calibration, native positions schematic.

ox: Not quite. Separating by mass alone is what SDS-PAGE does: SDS unfolds proteins and gives them the same charge per unit mass, wiping out differences in shape and charge. Native PAGE keeps those differences, so two proteins with the same mass can end up in very different spots.

Not quite. Separating by pI alone is isoelectric focusing, where proteins move through a pH gradient and stop where their net charge is zero. Native PAGE uses one pH throughout, and proteins keep moving based on their charge at that pH, plus their size and shape.

Not quite. Native PAGE is designed to keep proteins folded: no SDS, no reducing agent, no boiling. That's its whole advantage. Enzymes can still work in the gel and multi-chain complexes stay together. The denaturing version is SDS-PAGE.

Correct. Without SDS, each protein keeps its fold, its own net charge at the gel's pH, and any partner chains. How far it moves depends on its charge relative to its mass (which drives it) and its size and shape (which slow it through the gel's pores). A compact, highly charged protein runs far; a big or stretched-out, weakly charged complex runs a short way.

p: Both methods pull proteins through a gel with an electric field. The difference is whether SDS is added.

SDS-PAGE: SDS unfolds proteins and coats them evenly with negative charge. Every chain has the same charge per mass and the same rod shape, so it separates by mass alone. Multi-chain proteins fall apart into single chains.

Native PAGE: no SDS. Proteins keep their natural fold, charge and partners. Separation depends on charge, size and shape all at once. It's less useful for measuring mass but great for studying active enzymes and intact complexes.

x1A_078.trap: Native PAGE isn't separation by mass alone. Only SDS-PAGE strips away charge and shape differences.

fig.cap: Charge at pH 7 for each protein. Only the pI 9.5 protein is positive and sticks to the negative cation-exchange bead.
fig.alt: A pI number line from 3 to 11 with buffer pH 7 marked. Proteins at pI 4.5 and 5.5 are red (net negative), pI 7.0 gray (about zero), pI 9.5 green (net positive). Below, a bead covered in negative charges holds a positive protein (pI 9.5) while negative proteins (pI 4.5 and 5.5) wash through. Elution is by raising salt or pH. Tag: binds most strongly, pI 9.5.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Correct. A protein is positive when the pH is below its pI. At pH 7, the protein with pI 9.5 is 9.5 − 7 = 2.5 units below its pI, so it has a clear positive charge and binds tightly to the negative beads. It stays on the column while the others wash through. You get it off later by adding more salt (Na⁺ competes for the beads) or raising the pH above 9.5.

Not quite. With pI 4.5, pH 7 is 7 − 4.5 = 2.5 units above the pI, so this protein is negative. The negative beads push it away and it flows straight through. It would bind to an anion-exchange column instead, which has positive beads.

Not quite. With pI 7.0, this protein has almost no net charge at pH 7, so there's little to attract it to the beads. A few positive patches might hold it slightly, but it'll come off long before a strongly positive protein.

Not quite. With pI 5.5, pH 7 is 7 − 5.5 = 1.5 units above the pI, so the protein is negative and isn't held by the negative beads. It's less negative than the pI 4.5 protein, but still the wrong sign to stick.

p: Ion-exchange chromatography separates proteins by charge. The column is packed with charged beads. Proteins with the opposite charge stick; proteins with the same charge, or no charge, wash through.
The names describe what the beads grab. A cation exchanger has negative beads and grabs cations (positive proteins). An anion exchanger has positive beads and grabs anions (negative proteins).
To predict a protein's charge, compare the buffer pH to its pI. pH below pI: positive. pH above pI: negative. Stuck proteins are released later by adding salt, whose ions compete for the beads.

x1A_079.trap: Cation exchanger = negative beads that grab cations (positive proteins, where pH is below pI).

fig.cap: Predicted results for each answer compared with the observed data (150 kDa native; 50 kDa on SDS-PAGE with or without reducing agent). Only the noncovalent trimer matches.
fig.alt: Table with columns gel filtration, SDS-PAGE without reducing agent and SDS-PAGE with β-mercaptoethanol. Observed: 150, 50, 50 kilodaltons. Noncovalent trimer of 3 times 50: 150, 50, 50, check. Disulfide-linked trimer: 150, 150, 50, cross. 150 kilodalton monomer: 150, 150, 150, cross. Noncovalent dimer of 2 times 75: 150, 75, 75, cross.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. If the three 50 kDa chains were joined by disulfides, SDS without reducing agent couldn't separate them, because SDS only breaks noncovalent interactions. The gel without reducing agent would show 150 kDa, and only adding reducing agent would give 50 kDa. Since 50 kDa shows up either way, there are no disulfides between chains.

Not quite. A single 150 kDa chain would run at about 150 kDa on SDS-PAGE, with or without reducing agent, because SDS can't cut peptide bonds. The 50 kDa band shows the 150 kDa protein must be made of smaller chains.

Correct. Gel filtration measures the folded, assembled mass: 150 kDa. SDS-PAGE measures each separate chain: 50 kDa. So 150 ÷ 50 = 3 chains, and since there's only one band they're the same size (likely identical). SDS alone, without reducing agent, already separates them, so they're held together only by noncovalent interactions. It's a noncovalent trimer of 50 kDa chains.

Not quite. Two 75 kDa chains would give the right total (2 × 75 = 150 kDa), but on SDS-PAGE they'd run as a 75 kDa band. The band here is at 50 kDa, so the chain size and the number of chains don't match.

p: Gel filtration (size-exclusion chromatography) keeps proteins folded and together, so it measures the mass of the whole protein, all subunits included.

SDS-PAGE unfolds proteins and separates their chains, so it measures each chain. Running it with and without reducing agent tells you whether chains are linked by disulfides: if the size only drops when reducing agent is added, they were.
Put the two together: whole mass ÷ chain mass = number of chains. The reducing test then tells you whether they're held together by disulfides or only by noncovalent contacts.

steps: Write the formula: number of subunits = native mass ÷ subunit mass.
Write down the values: native mass (gel filtration) = 150 kDa; subunit mass (SDS-PAGE) = 50 kDa, one band.
One band means all subunits are the same size.
Plug in: 150 kDa ÷ 50 kDa = 3 subunits.
The 50 kDa band appears even without reducing agent, so SDS alone separates the subunits: no disulfides between chains.
Conclusion: a noncovalent trimer of three 50 kDa subunits.
x1A_080.trap: SDS only breaks noncovalent contacts. A band that changes only with reducing agent means disulfides.

fig.cap: Heat and urea (top two rows) disrupt noncovalent forces but leave both disulfide and peptide bonds intact; only reducing agents or proteases break those.
fig.alt: Table of denaturing agents with their main action and whether disulfide and peptide bonds survive. Heat: breaks hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic packing, both covalent bonds survive. Urea: hydrogen-bonds to backbone and solvates nonpolar groups, both survive. β-mercaptoethanol or DTT breaks disulfides; protease breaks peptide bonds.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. Hydrogen bonds are among the first interactions lost, not the last ones standing. Each is weak (a few kJ/mol), heat easily breaks them, and urea competes directly for the same C=O and N–H groups. So the protein's backbone and side-chain hydrogen bonds are broken here.

Not quite. Disulfide bonds do survive, because they're covalent and no reducing agent was added. But salt bridges are noncovalent attractions between charged side chains. Once the protein unfolds, the partners drift apart and get surrounded by solvent, so the salt bridges are lost. Only half of this pair is right.

Not quite. Peptide bonds survive, but water-avoiding interactions don't. Urea surrounds water-avoiding side chains and weakens the hydrophobic effect, and heat breaks up the packed core further, so those buried residues get exposed. Pairing a covalent bond with a noncovalent force makes this only half right.

Correct. Heat and urea only act on noncovalent interactions: hydrogen bonds, the hydrophobic effect, salt bridges and van der Waals packing. Peptide bonds (the covalent backbone) and disulfide bonds (covalent S–S links) need specific chemistry to break: hydrolysis for peptide bonds and a reducing agent like β-mercaptoethanol or DTT for disulfides. With no reducing agent, both survive, so the sequence and any disulfide links stay intact.

concept.t: What denaturing conditions can and can't break
p: Proteins are held together by two kinds of bonds. Covalent bonds (peptide bonds and disulfides) are strong and need specific chemical reactions to break. Noncovalent interactions (hydrogen bonds, salt bridges, the hydrophobic effect, van der Waals contacts) are weak and easy to disrupt.
Heat, urea, extreme pH and detergents like SDS all go after the noncovalent interactions. They unfold a protein but leave its covalent bonds alone.
To break disulfides you need a reducing agent such as β-mercaptoethanol or DTT. To break peptide bonds you need a protease or harsh acid hydrolysis.

x1A_081.trap: Urea and heat never break disulfides. You need a reducing agent for that.

fig.cap: Helical wheel for an 18-residue helix with Leu at positions 1, 4, 5, 8, 11, 12, 15 and 18, each residue placed 100° from the last. All eight leucines cluster on one face.
fig.alt: Helical wheel with 18 residues around a circle. Leucines at positions 1, 4, 5, 8, 11, 12, 15 and 18 occupy one shaded arc labeled hydrophobic face; lysines and glutamates occupy the other side. Tags: amphipathic helix correct; transmembrane helix needs about 20 nonpolar residues; β-strand repeat is 2.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; residue angles computed at 100° per residue (3.6 residues per turn).

ox: Not quite. A helix that crosses a membrane has to be water-avoiding all the way around, because the whole thing sits in the oily middle of the membrane. It needs about 20 mostly water-avoiding residues in a row. Charged residues on most of its surface would be very unfavorable inside the membrane, so this helix can't cross one.

Not quite. Leucine is one of the best helix formers, and charged residues like Lys and Glu fit in helices too; they can even pair up into salt bridges that steady the helix. The helix breakers are proline and, to a lesser extent, glycine, and neither is mentioned here.

Correct. An α-helix has 3.6 residues per turn, so each residue is 100° around from the last. Residues 3 apart are 3 × 100° = 300° around, and 4 apart are 4 × 100° = 400° around. Those land just 60° or 40° from the starting spot, so they're on nearly the same side. Leucines at that spacing form a water-avoiding stripe on one face, and the charged residues fill the opposite face. Helices like this pack against other helices (leucine zippers) or lie on membrane surfaces.

Not quite. In a β-strand, side chains flip sides every residue, so the water-avoiding repeat would be every 2 residues (positions 1, 3, 5...). A spacing of 3 to 4 matches the 3.6-residue repeat of an α-helix. Also, the question already tells you it's a helix.

p: Amphipathic means having two sides with opposite personalities: one water-avoiding, one water-loving.

In an α-helix, each residue sits 100° around from the previous one, and 3.6 residues make a full circle. So residues at positions i, i + 3, i + 4 and i + 7 cluster on the same face. If you put water-avoiding residues at those spots, you get a greasy stripe down one side of the helix.

Amphipathic helices are everywhere: lying on membrane surfaces with the greasy face dipped into the lipids, or pairing with another helix greasy-face to greasy-face. A leucine zipper, found in some DNA-binding proteins, is two such helices zipped together by their leucines.

x1A_082.trap: Every 3 to 4 residues = one face of a helix. Every 2 residues = one face of a β-strand.

fig.cap: Edge-on view of stacked silk β-sheets. Glycine H atoms point to one face and alanine CH₃ groups to the other, so sheets interlock closely (about 0.35 nm and 0.57 nm apart).
fig.alt: Five blue zigzag β-sheets seen edge-on and stacked vertically. In each sheet, small H labels point to one face and orange methyl circles to the other. Gly faces meet about 0.35 nanometers apart and Ala faces about 0.57 nanometers apart. Tags: no sulfur, no charge; β-sheet not α-helix.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; intersheet spacings after Marsh, Corey and Pauling's silk fibroin structure as summarized in Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry.

ox: Not quite. Disulfide bonds only form between cysteine SH groups. Glycine's side chain is an H and alanine's is a CH₃, so neither has sulfur. Silk's strength comes from tightly packed β-sheets held by hydrogen bonds and close contacts, not covalent cross-links.

Correct. In a β-strand, side chains alternate faces, so in a Gly-Ala repeat every glycine (H) points to one face and every alanine (CH₃) to the other. These tiny side chains let sheets stack very closely: glycine face against glycine face (about 0.35 nm apart) and alanine face against alanine face (about 0.57 nm apart), with many close contacts. That dense packing makes silk strong and hard to stretch, since the strands are already fully extended.

Not quite. Glycine and alanine have uncharged, water-avoiding side chains (H and CH₃), so they can't form salt bridges. Salt bridges need charged residues like Lys, Arg, Asp or Glu. The forces between stacked silk sheets are close contacts (van der Waals forces) between the small side chains.

Not quite. The question says fibroin forms β-sheets, and this sequence suits sheets, not helices. Glycine actually weakens helices because it's too floppy. Helix-based fibers, like α-keratin in hair, have very different sequences.

p: Silk fibroin is mostly β-sheets stacked on top of each other. Its sequence is dominated by a simple repeat: Gly-Ala-Gly-Ala (often with some Ser).

In a β-strand, side chains alternate faces. So in this repeat, all the glycines point one way and all the alanines point the other. Both side chains are tiny, so the sheets are nearly flat on both faces.

Flat sheets can stack almost like sheets of paper, held by hydrogen bonds within each sheet and close contacts between sheets. The strands are already stretched out, so silk resists further stretching and is very strong for its weight.

x1A_083.trap: Glycine and alanine have no sulfur and no charge. Their advantage is simply being small.

fig.cap: Folding releases ordered water from nonpolar surfaces. A less polar solvent such as ethanol solvates those surfaces, so burying them pays less and the fold weakens.
fig.alt: Left: unfolded chain with nonpolar groups each surrounded by an ordered ring of water molecules. Right: folded protein with a buried nonpolar core and free water outside. Text box: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; water entropy increases on folding; a less polar solvent such as ethanol solvates nonpolar groups so burying them pays less.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; schematic, not to scale.

fig.cap: Ethanol's row: it lowers solvent polarity and weakens the hydrophobic effect; disulfide and peptide bonds survive.
fig.alt: Table of denaturing agents with main actions and whether disulfide and peptide bonds survive; the ethanol row reads less polar solvent, weakens hydrophobic effect, both covalent bonds survive.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Correct. Ethanol is less polar than water and has a greasy ethyl group, so it can surround water-avoiding side chains much better than water can. The hydrophobic effect depends on how badly the solvent tolerates exposed water-avoiding surfaces. In water-ethanol mixtures, unfolding exposes the core at a smaller energy cost, so the folded state isn't favored anymore and the protein unfolds. That's why 70% ethanol works as a disinfectant.

Not quite. Cutting a peptide bond takes a protease or long heating in strong acid or base. Ethanol is a neutral alcohol and can't cut amide bonds under normal conditions. Ethanol-unfolded proteins keep their full sequence, which is why some can refold after the ethanol is removed.
Not quite. Ethanol doesn't oxidize cysteine SH groups under these conditions; making disulfides takes an oxidizing agent. And extra disulfides would tend to hold a protein together, not unfold it.

Not quite. Chelators like EDTA pull metal ions out by gripping them with several atoms at once. Ethanol has just one OH group and isn't a chelator. Some metal-dependent proteins are switched off by chelators, but that's a different mechanism from how ethanol unfolds proteins.

p: Proteins fold largely because of the hydrophobic effect: water dislikes touching water-avoiding side chains, so those side chains get tucked into the core.
Organic solvents like ethanol are less polar than water. They're comfortable around water-avoiding side chains. Mixing ethanol into water makes exposed water-avoiding surfaces much less costly.

So the reason to stay folded weakens, and the protein unfolds. This kills bacteria by unfolding their proteins, which is why alcohol is used as a disinfectant. It's also used in labs to precipitate proteins.

x1A_084.trap: Ethanol weakens the hydrophobic effect. It doesn't cut, oxidize or chelate anything.

fig.cap: Two cysteine thiols bind Hg²⁺ to form a Cys–S–Hg–S–Cys bridge (L-cysteine is R), distorting the protein's fold.
fig.alt: Structure of L-cysteine with its SH highlighted, plus mercury(II), losing 2 protons to give two cysteines bridged through S-Hg-S, highlighted. A box explains that soft metal ions bind soft thiol sulfur tightly, bridging cysteines, blocking active sites and displacing zinc. Red tags: peptide bonds cut, lysine turned into arginine, pH pushed above 12; none of these happen.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Not quite. Heavy-metal ions at toxic levels don't cut the protein backbone. Their damage comes from binding to side chains, mainly cysteine sulfur, and warping the fold. Cutting peptide bonds takes proteases or harsh acid or base, which metal salts don't provide.

Not quite. A metal ion can't rebuild one amino acid's side chain into another's. Turning lysine into arginine would mean adding carbon and nitrogen atoms through a dedicated building reaction. Metals act by binding to existing side chains, not by changing what they are.

Correct. Hg²⁺ and Pb²⁺ are 'soft' metal ions, and cysteine's sulfur is a 'soft' partner, so they bind each other very tightly (the mercury-sulfur bond is one of the strongest metal bonds in biology). The metal can bridge two cysteines, block a key SH group in an active site, or push Zn²⁺ out of zinc-binding sites. Each of these warps the fold or blocks function. That's why heavy-metal poisoning shuts down many enzymes at once.

Not quite. Metal salts like HgCl₂ or Pb(NO₃)₂ make water slightly acidic, if anything, not strongly basic. Reaching pH 12 would need a strong base like NaOH. pH isn't how heavy metals switch proteins off.

p: Some metal ions are 'soft': big, with electrons that are easy to push around. Mercury (Hg²⁺), lead (Pb²⁺) and cadmium (Cd²⁺) are examples. Soft metals bind most strongly to soft partners, and sulfur is the softest common atom in proteins.

Cysteine's SH group is the main target. When a heavy metal grabs it, it can block a working SH group in an active site, cross-link the wrong cysteines, or replace zinc in proteins that need zinc to hold their shape.
Because cysteines are found in many enzymes, one heavy metal can disrupt lots of proteins at once. Treatments for metal poisoning use chelators with SH groups that grab the metal away from proteins.

x1A_085.trap: Heavy metals target sulfur (cysteine SH groups). Think soft metal binding soft sulfur.

fig.cap: Heat unfolds compact egg-white proteins; their exposed hydrophobic patches stick together into an opaque network that cannot refold on cooling.
fig.alt: Native compact soluble globular proteins, heated, become unfolded chains with orange hydrophobic patches exposed, which stick together into an aggregated network gel that scatters light. A dashed red cooling arrow back to native is blocked because chains are tangled. Red tags: hydrolyzed, made carbohydrate, new peptide bonds; none of these happen.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Correct. Heat unfolds egg-white proteins like ovalbumin, exposing water-avoiding side chains that were buried in their cores. Exposed patches on neighboring chains stick together (and some new disulfides form), building a tangled 3D network. The network scatters light, so the white turns opaque and solid. On cooling, the chains are stuck in the tangle and can't reach their original folds, so the change is effectively permanent even though the sequences are intact.

Not quite. Cooking doesn't break peptide bonds; that takes proteases (as in digestion) or long boiling in strong acid. And free amino acids are small and dissolve in water, so if the proteins had really been broken down, you'd get a clear liquid, not an opaque solid.

Not quite. Heat can't turn one kind of biomolecule into another. Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds; carbohydrates are chains of sugars joined by glycosidic bonds. Cooking changes how proteins are folded and how they clump, not what they're made of.

Not quite. Making new peptide bonds takes energized amino acids and a ribosome (or special chemistry); heat alone doesn't join protein chains end to end. The clumps in cooked egg are held mostly by noncovalent water-avoiding contacts, plus some disulfide shuffling, not new peptide bonds.

p: Some unfolded proteins can refold once conditions return to normal. Others can't, because something else happens while they're unfolded: they clump together.

When a protein unfolds, its water-avoiding core is exposed. In a crowded solution, these sticky patches find other unfolded chains and tangle together. Once tangled, the chains can't get free to refold.

That's why a cooked egg never uncooks. The sequence is unchanged, but the proteins are locked in a clumped network. The same kind of clumping causes trouble in diseases where misfolded proteins pile up.

x1A_086.trap: Irreversible doesn't mean the backbone broke. It means the unfolded chains clumped together.

fig.cap: E1, E2 and E3 attach a chain of four or more ubiquitins to a misfolded protein; the 26S proteasome then degrades it into short peptides. Other modifications have different jobs.
fig.alt: Flow: E1 activates ubiquitin using ATP, E2 carries it, E3 ligase recognizes the misfolded protein; the protein gets a chain of at least 4 Lys48-linked ubiquitins and goes to the 26S proteasome, which releases short peptides and recycles ubiquitin. Tag: cytosolic quality control. Box: phosphorylation switches activity, not disposal; mannose-6-phosphate is added in Golgi for lysosomes; glycosylation happens in ER and Golgi.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. Phosphorylation by kinases is a reversible on/off switch: adding a phosphate changes a protein's activity, partners or location. It isn't a general disposal tag and doesn't send proteins out of the cell. (Sometimes a phosphate signals that a protein should then get ubiquitin, but ubiquitin is the actual destruction tag.)

Not quite. Mannose-6-phosphate is added in the Golgi to sugar chains on lysosomal enzymes, and it sends them to lysosomes, not mitochondria. It only applies to proteins in the secretory pathway, not misfolded proteins in the cytosol. Mitochondrial proteins are sent by a signal sequence at their N-terminus.

Not quite. Most glycosylation happens inside the ER and Golgi, on proteins in the secretory pathway. A cytosolic protein never goes there. Sugar chains do help with folding checks in the ER, but they aren't the cytosol's destruction tag.

Correct. Misfolded cytosolic proteins are spotted, often with help from chaperones, by ubiquitin ligases. A three-enzyme relay (E1 activates ubiquitin using ATP, E2 carries it, E3 attaches it to a lysine on the target) builds a chain of at least four ubiquitins. The 26S proteasome recognizes that chain, unfolds the protein using ATP, and cuts it into short peptides, while the ubiquitin gets recycled.

p: Cells constantly check their proteins. Ones that are misfolded, damaged or no longer needed get destroyed so they don't clump up or cause trouble.

In the cytosol and nucleus, the 'destroy me' tag is ubiquitin, a small protein. A team of enzymes (E1, E2 and E3) attaches a chain of ubiquitins to a lysine on the target. E3 is the part that picks which protein gets tagged.

The tagged protein goes to the proteasome, a large barrel-shaped complex. It unfolds the protein, feeds it into the barrel, and chops it into small peptides. Don't confuse this with lysosomes, which digest material brought in from outside or from inside membranes, and which receive enzymes tagged with mannose-6-phosphate.

x1A_087.trap: Ubiquitin = destroy (via the proteasome). Mannose-6-phosphate = go to the lysosome. Phosphate = switch on or off.

fig.cap: An ideal α-helix computed from 100° and 0.15 nm per residue: one turn spans 3.6 residues and 0.54 nm, while hydrogen bonds link residues n and n + 4.
fig.alt: Side view of a helix with residues n through n plus 8; a bar marks one turn as 3.6 residues equals 0.54 nanometers; dashed hydrogen bonds connect each residue to the one 4 later. End-on view shows side chains pointing outward.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; residue positions computed from ideal α-helix parameters (100° and 0.15 nm per residue).

ox: Not quite. About two residues per repeat describes a stretched-out β-strand, where side chains alternate sides and the pattern repeats every two residues (about 0.7 nm). An α-helix is far more compact, with each residue rising only 0.15 nm, so more residues fit in each turn.

Correct. Each residue in an α-helix turns 100° around the axis and rises 0.15 nm. A full 360° turn takes 360° ÷ 100° = 3.6 residues, and each turn rises 3.6 × 0.15 nm = 0.54 nm. Because 3.6 isn't a whole number, the side-chain pattern doesn't repeat exactly each turn, which is why residues i, i + 3, i + 4 and i + 7 line up on one face.

Not quite. 4.0 is tempting because the hydrogen bonds join residue n to residue n + 4. But the bond spacing and the residues per turn are different numbers. With 3.6 residues per turn, residue n + 4 is at 4 × 100° = 400°, just past one full turn, close enough for its N–H to reach the C=O of residue n.

Not quite. About 10 (really about 10.5) is the number of base pairs per turn of B-DNA, a different double helix with a rise per turn of about 3.4 nm. A protein α-helix is much tighter, with only 3.6 residues per turn.

p: Three numbers describe the α-helix. Each residue rotates 100° around the axis. Each residue rises 0.15 nm (1.5 Å) along the axis. And the hydrogen bonds link residue n to n + 4.
From those you get the rest. Residues per turn = 360° ÷ 100° = 3.6. Rise per full turn (the pitch) = 3.6 × 0.15 nm = 0.54 nm.
Keep the look-alikes straight: 3.6 is residues per turn, 4 is the hydrogen-bond spacing, 2 is the repeat of a β-strand, and about 10.5 is base pairs per turn of DNA.

fm.f: residues per turn = 360° ÷ rotation per residue, where rotation per residue = how far each residue turns around the helix axis
fm.v: rotation per residue = 100°; residues per turn = ?
fm.why: A full turn is 360°, so divide it by how much each residue contributes.
fm.nc: 360 ÷ 100 = 3.6 (move the decimal point two places left).

fm.f: pitch = residues per turn × rise per residue, where pitch = how far the helix climbs in one full turn
fm.v: residues per turn = 3.6; rise per residue = 0.15 nm; pitch = ?
fm.why: Each residue climbs 0.15 nm, and a turn holds 3.6 residues.

steps: Write the formula: residues per turn = 360° ÷ rotation per residue.
Write down the values: rotation per residue = 100°; rise per residue = 0.15 nm.
Plug in: residues per turn = 360° ÷ 100° = 3.6.
Find the rise per turn: pitch = 3.6 × 0.15 nm.
x1A_088.trap: 4 is the hydrogen-bond spacing (n to n + 4). 3.6 is residues per turn.

fig.cap: Along one chain, helix hydrogen bonds join residues 4 apart (short arcs), while sheet hydrogen bonds join strands far apart in sequence (long arcs). Both are backbone C=O···H–N bonds.
fig.alt: A 30-residue chain drawn as boxes. Residues 2 to 12 form a helix with short purple arcs linking each residue to the one 4 later. Residues 15 to 19 and 25 to 29 form two strands linked by long orange arcs. Below, a diagram of two backbone chains joined by C=O to H-N hydrogen bonds, with R groups pointing away, labeled noncovalent.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. Both the α-helix and the β-sheet are held by hydrogen bonds between backbone groups: the C=O of one peptide unit and the N–H of another. Side chains aren't involved in either, which is why these shapes can form from so many different sequences. Side-chain hydrogen bonds belong to tertiary structure.

Correct. In an α-helix every hydrogen bond is local: residue n bonds to residue n + 4 in the same stretch.
