In a β-sheet the bonds link strands lying side by side, and those strands can be close in sequence (a hairpin), dozens or hundreds of residues apart, or even on different chains. So sheet bonds can connect distant parts of the sequence, while helix bonds always join near neighbors.

Not quite. Hydrogen bonds are noncovalent in both structures. They're an attraction between an H on a nitrogen (N–H) and a lone pair on an oxygen (O=C), worth only a few kJ/mol each. Nothing about a β-sheet makes them covalent, and their weakness is why both helices and sheets come apart when heated.

Not quite. The fixed n to n + 4 pattern is what defines the α-helix. In a β-sheet, the partner residues depend on how the strands line up next to each other, so there's no fixed spacing, and the partners are usually much farther apart than four residues.

p: Secondary structure is held together by hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups. Both helices and sheets use these same bonds.
In an α-helix, the chain coils on itself, and each C=O bonds to the N–H just four residues later. Everything stays local, within one continuous stretch.

In a β-sheet, stretched-out strands lie side by side and bond across to each other. The strands can come from very different parts of the chain, so sheets often bring distant regions together into one structure.

x1A_089.trap: Helix bonds are local (n to n + 4). Sheet bonds join separate strands that can be far apart.

fig.cap: Net charge versus pH computed for two model proteins of similar size. The Lys/Arg-rich protein crosses zero near pH 12; the Asp/Glu-rich one near pH 3.6.
fig.alt: Two net-charge curves against pH from 1 to 14. Blue curve for a Lys/Arg-rich protein (32 basic, 6 acidic) is strongly positive at pH 7 (about plus 26) and crosses zero near pH 12. Red curve for an Asp/Glu-rich protein (6 basic, 34 acidic) is strongly negative at pH 7 and crosses zero near pH 3.6.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation using standard side-chain pKₐ values for the stated compositions.

ox: Not quite. A pI well below 7 belongs to a protein rich in acidic residues (Asp, Glu). Their COO⁻ groups make the protein negative at neutral pH, so you'd have to lower the pH to add protons before the charge hits zero. This protein is the opposite, so its pI is high, not low.

Correct. Lys (side-chain pKₐ ≈ 10.5) and Arg (pKₐ ≈ 12.5) are positive at pH 7, and with few acidic residues to balance them, the protein has a big positive charge at neutral pH. To reach net zero, the pH has to rise until many of these groups lose their protons, which only happens well above 7. Real basic proteins like histones and lysozyme (pI ≈ 11) behave this way.

Not quite. pH 7 is neutral for water, not a default pI for proteins. A pI of exactly 7 would need the positive and negative charges to balance at pH 7, which a protein with lots of Lys and Arg and few Asp and Glu doesn't do. Protein pI values range from below 2 to above 11.

Not quite. Composition is exactly what lets you estimate the pI: count the acidic groups (Asp, Glu, C-terminus) and the basic groups (Lys, Arg, His, N-terminus) and compare. Software predicts pI from sequence this way, usually to within about one pH unit.

p: A protein's pI depends on which charged groups it has. Acidic side chains (Asp, Glu) are negative at neutral pH. Basic side chains (Lys, Arg, and partly His) are positive.

If acidic groups outnumber basic ones, the protein is negative at pH 7, and you'd have to lower the pH to reach zero charge. That means a low pI. If basic groups outnumber acidic ones, the protein is positive at pH 7, and you'd have to raise the pH. That means a high pI.
DNA-binding proteins like histones are packed with Lys and Arg, giving them high pI values and a strong positive charge that grips negatively charged DNA.

x1A_090.trap: More basic residues means a higher pI, because you need a higher pH to strip their protons.

fig.cap: Net charge of a model protein versus pH, computed from Henderson–Hasselbalch. Left of the pI (pH < pI) the curve is above zero: net positive.
fig.alt: Net charge against pH from 1 to 13 for a model protein; the curve is positive (shaded red, labeled pH below pI, net positive) at low pH, crosses zero at the pI of about 6.1, and is negative (shaded blue, labeled net negative) above it. pI minus 2 gives net plus 12.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for a model protein with standard pKₐ values.

ox: Not quite. A protein is net negative when the pH is above its pI. Then there are fewer H⁺ ions around than needed to keep its groups protonated, so COO⁻ groups stay negative and some amines lose their protons, tipping it negative. This choice flips the rule.

Not quite. A net charge of zero happens only when the pH equals the pI; that's what the pI means. Zero net charge doesn't mean no charged groups, just that the positives and negatives balance. Any pH below the pI gives a nonzero, positive charge.

Not quite. Net charge depends on how many groups are protonated at a given pH, which is set by each group's pKₐ compared with the pH, not by the protein's mass. Two proteins of the same mass can have opposite charges at pH 7 if one is rich in Lys and Arg and the other in Asp and Glu.

Correct. When the pH is below the pI, there are more H⁺ ions around than at the pI, so more of the protein's groups are protonated. COO⁻ groups pick up H⁺ and go neutral, while amines and histidines stay or become positive. The result is a net positive charge, and the further below the pI, the more positive. Such a protein moves toward the cathode in electrophoresis and sticks to cation-exchange columns.

p: Every protein has a pI, the pH where its net charge is zero. You don't need to count individual groups to know its charge at another pH; just compare.
pH below pI: there are lots of protons around, the protein soaks them up, and it's positive. pH above pI: protons are scarce, the protein gives them up, and it's negative.
This rule shows up again and again: which way a protein moves in electrophoresis, whether it sticks to a cation or anion exchanger, and where it stops in isoelectric focusing.

x1A_091.trap: pH below pI → positive (think 'protons pile on'). pH above pI → negative.

fig.cap: Uversky's charge–hydropathy plot. Sequences with low mean hydropathy and high net charge (upper left) are disordered; hydrophobic, weakly charged sequences (lower right) fold.
fig.alt: Plot of mean net charge per residue against mean hydropathy with a straight boundary line H equals (R plus 1.151) divided by 2.785. The upper-left region is labeled intrinsically disordered: low hydropathy, high net charge. The lower-right region is labeled folded: hydrophobic enough to form a core.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph of the boundary equation from Uversky, Gillespie and Fink (2000).

ox: Correct. Intrinsically disordered regions are rich in charged and polar residues (Glu, Lys, Arg, Ser, Gln, Pro) and poor in bulky water-avoiding ones (Leu, Ile, Val, Phe, Trp). Without enough water-avoiding side chains there's no core to bury, so the hydrophobic effect can't drive folding. A high net charge also makes the chain repel itself and stay stretched out. Low water-avoidance plus high charge is the classic recipe for disorder.

Not quite. Leucine, isoleucine and phenylalanine are the bulky water-avoiding residues that build protein cores. A stretch rich in them strongly wants to bury them, so it tends to fold (or clump if it can't fold properly). That's the makeup of ordered domains, the opposite of disordered regions.

Not quite. Disulfide bonds are covalent cross-links that limit how a chain can move and lock in a folded shape. A region full of disulfides would be more rigid, not floppy. Many small proteins outside the cell, like some toxins, owe their rigid shapes to dense disulfides.

Not quite. Glycine is common in flexible regions, but real disordered regions have mixed compositions dominated by charged, polar and proline residues. A pure glycine stretch is an unusual, poorly soluble sequence, not the typical makeup of disordered proteins.

p: Not every part of a protein folds into one fixed shape. Intrinsically disordered regions stay floppy, constantly shifting between many shapes.

The reason is their composition. Folding is driven mostly by burying water-avoiding side chains. Disordered regions have few of those and lots of charged and polar residues, so there's nothing to bury, and same-sign charges push the chain apart.

Being floppy is often useful. Many disordered regions act like flexible arms that can grab different partners, folding into a shape only once they bind. They're common in signaling proteins and transcription factors.

fx.w: An observed dividing line (from Uversky): ⟨R⟩ = average net charge per residue, ⟨H⟩ = average water-avoidance score (0 to 1). A sequence whose water-avoidance falls below this line for its charge tends to be disordered.

x1A_092.trap: Disorder comes from few water-avoiding residues and many charges, not from glycine alone or from cross-links.

fig.cap: Heat partly unfolds proteins, which pull Hsp70/Hsp90 away from HSF1; HSF1 then turns on heat shock genes, making more chaperones, and excess free Hsp70 shuts the response off.
fig.alt: Flowchart: temperature rises; proteins partly unfold exposing hydrophobic patches; Hsp70 and Hsp90 bind them, releasing HSF1; HSF1 trimer enters the nucleus and binds heat shock elements; transcription of HSP genes gives more chaperones; chaperones refold or prevent aggregation, tagged the real job. A dashed feedback loop shows excess free Hsp70 binding HSF1 again. Red tags: heat shock proteins do not make heat, form from other proteins, or repair or digest DNA.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. Heat shock proteins are chaperones, not heat-making enzymes. Body heat comes mostly from metabolism (and in brown fat, from a protein called UCP1). The name refers to when they're made, after a heat shock, not to what they do.

Not quite. Heat doesn't turn one protein into another. Each heat shock protein has its own gene, and their levels rise because the cell reads those genes more. Heat only partly unfolds proteins that already exist.

Correct. Higher temperature partly unfolds many proteins and exposes their water-avoiding patches, which risk clumping. Chaperones like Hsp70 and Hsp90 grab these patches, which frees a transcription factor called HSF1 they normally hold onto. HSF1 then switches on the heat shock genes, so the cell makes more chaperones to refold damaged proteins, prevent clumping, or send hopeless ones to the proteasome. Once things are fixed, free Hsp70 grabs HSF1 again and the response shuts off.

Not quite. Heat shock proteins act on proteins, not DNA. DNA damage is handled by DNA repair systems, and DNA is broken down by nucleases. Chaperones recognize the exposed water-avoiding surfaces of partly unfolded protein chains.

p: Proteins are only barely stable, so even a modest temperature rise makes some of them start to unfold. Partly unfolded proteins expose sticky water-avoiding patches and can clump together.

Cells have a built-in alarm. Normally, chaperones like Hsp70 hold onto a transcription factor called HSF1 and keep it inactive. When unfolded proteins pile up, the chaperones get pulled away to deal with them, HSF1 is set free, and it switches on genes for more chaperones.
The extra chaperones help refold damaged proteins and keep them from clumping. Once the crisis passes, chaperones are free again, they grab HSF1, and production drops back to normal.

x1A_093.trap: 'Heat shock' describes when they're made, not what they do. They're chaperones for proteins.

fig.cap: Unfolding curves computed from ΔG = ΔG(H₂O) − m[urea] with m = 5 kJ/mol per M. Wild type is half unfolded at 4.0 M; the mutant at 2.0 M.
fig.alt: Fraction unfolded against urea concentration from 0 to 8 molar. Red mutant curve crosses 0.5 at 2.0 molar; blue wild-type curve crosses 0.5 at 4.0 molar. An arrow labeled less urea needed, less stable points from the wild-type midpoint to the mutant midpoint. Legend: wild type ΔG in water 20 kilojoules per mole, mutant 10.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the linear extrapolation model (two-state, 25 °C) with the midpoints in the question.

ox: Not quite. A more stable folded state resists unfolding, so it would need more urea to reach the midpoint, not less. Here the mutant is half unfolded at 2.0 M while the wild type needs 4.0 M, which means the mutant is the less stable one.

Not quite. Urea works through weak, noncovalent interactions: it hydrogen-bonds with the backbone and surrounds water-avoiding side chains. It doesn't form covalent bonds with proteins to unfold them, and this experiment measures how stable the fold is, not any chemical reaction with urea.

Not quite. A point mutation changes one residue, so the mutant is the same length as the wild type. Anyway, chain length doesn't set the midpoint in a simple way. The midpoint reflects the energy difference between the folded and unfolded states.

Correct. At the midpoint, half the molecules are unfolded and the energy change for unfolding is zero. In the simple model, ΔG(unfolding) = ΔG(water) − m × [urea], so at the midpoint ΔG(water) = m × midpoint. If both proteins have a similar m (say 5 kJ/mol per M), the wild type has about 5 × 4.0 = 20 kJ/mol of stability and the mutant about 5 × 2.0 = 10 kJ/mol. The mutation roughly halved the stability, so less urea tips it over.

p: One way to measure how stable a protein is: add more and more urea and watch it unfold. The urea concentration where half the molecules are unfolded is the midpoint, often written Cm.
A higher midpoint means the protein needs more urea to unfold, so it's more stable. A lower midpoint means it's less stable. It works just like melting temperature: lower Tm, less stable.

The unfolding energy drops in a straight line as urea is added: ΔG(unfolding) = ΔG(water) − m × [urea]. At the midpoint ΔG is zero, so ΔG(water) = m × Cm. That lets you turn a midpoint into an actual stability number.

fm.f: ΔG(unfolding) = ΔG(water) − m × [urea], where ΔG(water) = stability with no urea (kJ/mol), m = how sensitive unfolding is to urea (kJ/mol per M), [urea] = urea concentration (M)
fm.v: at the midpoint ΔG(unfolding) = 0; m ≈ 5 kJ/mol per M (a typical value, assumed the same for both); Cm(wild type) = 4.0 M; Cm(mutant) = 2.0 M; ΔG(water) = ?
fm.s: 0 = ΔG(water) − m × Cm → ΔG(water) = m × Cm. Wild type: 5 × 4.0 = 20 kJ/mol. Mutant: 5 × 2.0 = 10 kJ/mol.
fm.why: At the midpoint, folded and unfolded are balanced, so the stability equals m times the urea it took to get there.
fm.nc: Difference: 20 − 10 = 10 kJ/mol less stable for the mutant.

steps: Write the formula: ΔG(unfolding) = ΔG(water) − m × [urea].
Write down the values: at the midpoint ΔG(unfolding) = 0; m ≈ 5 kJ/mol per M (assumed the same for both); wild-type midpoint = 4.0 M; mutant midpoint = 2.0 M.
Set ΔG(unfolding) to 0 and rearrange: ΔG(water) = m × midpoint.
Wild type: 5 × 4.0 = 20 kJ/mol.
Mutant: 5 × 2.0 = 10 kJ/mol.
Compare: 20 − 10 = 10 kJ/mol, so the mutant's folded state is about 10 kJ/mol less stable.
x1A_094.trap: Lower denaturant midpoint = less stable, just like a lower Tm = less stable.

fig.cap: Proinsulin (86 residues, one chain) is cut at two dibasic sites, releasing the C-peptide and leaving insulin's A and B chains held by disulfides: a change in primary structure.
fig.alt: Bar diagram of proinsulin: B chain 30 residues, Arg-Arg, C-peptide 31 residues, Lys-Arg, A chain 21 residues, with scissors at the two cleavage sites. An arrow labeled hydrolysis of peptide bonds leads to insulin: B chain and A chain joined by two disulfide bonds, and released C-peptide. Tag: primary structure changed. Note: heat, urea and pH change only the fold.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; residue counts for human proinsulin.

fig.cap: Only the primary level is held by peptide bonds; heat, urea and pH affect the other three levels.
fig.alt: Four panels for primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure with the bonds that hold each; primary tagged intact after boiling or urea, others lost.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; content consistent with OpenStax Biology 2e, 3.4 Proteins.

ox: Not quite. Heat breaks noncovalent interactions (hydrogen bonds, the hydrophobic effect, salt bridges), unfolding secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure. Peptide bonds are covalent and don't break during ordinary heating, so the sequence stays the same even when the protein is fully unfolded.

Not quite. 6 M urea unfolds proteins by hydrogen-bonding to the backbone and surrounding water-avoiding side chains. Those are noncovalent effects, so the sequence and its peptide bonds stay intact, which is why urea-unfolded proteins can often refold once the urea is removed.

Correct. Primary structure is the covalent sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds, so only breaking or making peptide bonds changes it. Proteolytic cleavage cuts specific peptide bonds. Proinsulin (one chain of 86 residues) is cut to remove the C-peptide, leaving insulin's A and B chains (21 and 30 residues) held together by disulfides. Zymogens like trypsinogen are activated the same way. The products have different sequences from the starting protein.

Not quite. Dropping the pH from 7 to 3 adds protons to COO⁻ groups, changing charges and breaking salt bridges, which can unfold the protein. But that's a reversible acid-base change, not a change to the backbone. The order of amino acids stays the same.

p: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence, held by covalent peptide bonds. It's the only level of structure that denaturing conditions can't touch.
Heat, urea, detergents and pH changes all break noncovalent interactions. They wreck the 3D shape but leave every peptide bond in place.

To change the sequence itself, peptide bonds have to be cut or made. Cells do this on purpose with proteases. Many proteins are made as longer, inactive precursors, like proinsulin or the zymogen trypsinogen, and are switched on by cutting off a piece.

x1A_095.trap: Denaturing changes shape. Only cutting or making peptide bonds changes the sequence.

fig.cap: Helix-turn-helix bound to DNA: helix 1 and the recognition helix (helix 2) are joined by a turn within one chain, and helix 2 sits in the major groove.
fig.alt: DNA double helix drawn as two blue and teal strands with base-pair rungs. An orange helix 1 connects through a short turn to a red helix 2 lying in the major groove. Text: recognition helix sits in the major groove and reads bases through side-chain hydrogen bonds, noncovalent. Bottom tags: one chain, not 4 subunits; sequence varies; no covalent bond to DNA.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; schematic, not to scale.

ox: Not quite. Motifs are defined by a recurring 3D arrangement of helices and strands, not by an identical sequence. Different helix-turn-helix proteins (like the lac repressor and λ repressor) have quite different sequences that fold into the same pattern, and their recognition helices differ so each binds a different DNA sequence.

Correct. A helix-turn-helix is a motif: two α-helices joined by a short turn, about 20 residues in all, within one chain. The second helix, the recognition helix, fits into the DNA's major groove, where its side chains form hydrogen bonds and close contacts with the edges of specific base pairs. The first helix helps hold it in position. Many bacterial repressors and eukaryotic homeodomain proteins use this motif.

Not quite. Quaternary structure is the assembly of separate chains. A helix-turn-helix forms within one chain, from back-to-back segments of it. Many of these proteins do bind DNA as pairs, but the motif itself belongs to one chain's fold.

Not quite. Transcription factors bind DNA reversibly through noncovalent interactions: hydrogen bonds to the bases, salt bridges between Lys or Arg and the negative phosphate backbone, and close contacts. A covalent link would make regulation impossible, because the factor couldn't let go when conditions change.

p: Between secondary structure (single helices and sheets) and tertiary structure (the whole fold) sits an in-between level: motifs, also called supersecondary structure. A motif is a small, recognizable combination of a few helices or strands.

The same motif can appear in many unrelated proteins, usually doing a similar job. Examples include the helix-turn-helix, the zinc finger and the leucine zipper, all common in DNA-binding proteins, and the β-α-β unit found in many enzymes.
In the helix-turn-helix, one helix lies in the major groove of DNA, where the edges of the base pairs are exposed. Its side chains read the bases, letting the protein find its specific DNA sequence.

x1A_096.trap: A motif is a recurring shape within one chain. It isn't a fixed sequence and isn't a multi-chain assembly.

fig.cap: A Cys₂His₂ zinc finger: Zn²⁺ is held tetrahedrally by two Cys from the β-hairpin and two His from the α-helix, acting as the core of this tiny fold.
fig.alt: Schematic of a β-hairpin with two cysteines and an α-helix with two histidines, all four bound by dashed lines to a central zinc ion, labeled 4 ligands, tetrahedral, 2 Cys S, 2 His N. Text: about 30 residues, too small for a real hydrophobic core, zinc acts as the core. Tags: structural, not catalytic (correct); zinc makes peptide bonds (wrong); S-S between metals (wrong).
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; schematic, not to scale.

ox: Correct. A classic zinc finger is only about 30 residues: a β-hairpin followed by an α-helix. That's too small to bury a real water-avoiding core, so a Zn²⁺ ion takes its place. The zinc is gripped by the sulfur atoms of two cysteines in the hairpin and the nitrogen atoms of two histidines in the helix, tying the two pieces together. Pulling the zinc out (for example with EDTA) unfolds the finger. The zinc is structural, not catalytic.

Not quite. Peptide bonds are made by the ribosome during translation, linking one amino acid's carboxyl to the next one's amino group. Metal ions don't make peptide bonds. The zinc in a zinc finger forms coordinate bonds with side-chain sulfur and nitrogen atoms.

Not quite. A disulfide is a covalent S–S bond between the sulfurs of two cysteines. It can't form between two metal atoms. In a zinc finger, the cysteines bind the zinc instead of pairing with each other, and there's only one zinc per finger.

Not quite. The zinc in a zinc finger is structural: it holds the fold together and doesn't speed up any reaction. Without it the finger can't fold, because it's too small to have enough water-avoiding packing. Catalytic zinc is found in other proteins, like carbonic anhydrase, where it helps activate water.

p: Most proteins hold their shape by burying water-avoiding side chains in a core. Very small domains don't have enough residues to build a good core, so they need another way to stay folded.

A zinc finger solves this with a metal ion. A Zn²⁺ is held by four side chains, typically two cysteines and two histidines, at a spot where the hairpin and helix meet. The zinc acts like a staple, clamping the small fold together.

Zinc fingers are very common in DNA-binding proteins. The helix fits into the DNA's major groove and reads a few base pairs, and proteins often string several fingers together to recognize longer sequences.

x1A_097.trap: The zinc in a zinc finger is a structural staple, not a catalyst, and it isn't part of any S–S bond.

fig.cap: A serine residue becomes phosphoserine (the α-carbon is S in both). The side chain goes from neutral to about −2 at pH 7.4.
fig.alt: Structure of a serine residue (capped) with its CH₂OH side chain highlighted, an arrow labeled kinase plus ATP minus ADP, and phosphoserine with the CH₂-O-PO₃ 2- group highlighted. Note: phosphate pKa2 about 5.8, about 98% minus 2 at pH 7.4; α-carbon stays S. Green box: new electrostatic contacts with Arg and Lys rearrange loops and domains; phosphatases reverse it. Red tags: changes α-carbon configuration, breaks peptide bond, adds positive charge.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app. Dianion fraction computed from Henderson–Hasselbalch.

ox: Not quite. Phosphorylation adds a phosphate to serine's side-chain oxygen (CH₂–OH becomes CH₂–O–PO₃²⁻). No bond to the α-carbon is made or broken, so its 3D arrangement stays the same: it's L-serine before and after. Changing that would mean breaking a bond to the α-carbon, which kinases don't do.

Not quite. Kinases move the last phosphate of ATP onto the serine's OH. The peptide bonds on either side of the serine aren't touched, so the chain stays intact. If phosphorylation cut the chain, a phosphatase couldn't undo it just by removing the phosphate.

Correct. The added phosphate's second pKₐ is about 5.8, so at pH 7.4 it's about 98% in the −2 form. A neutral OH becomes a bulky, strongly negative group. It can form new salt bridges with nearby Arg or Lys, push away nearby Asp or Glu, and add hydrogen bonds, which can rearrange loops or whole domains. That shape change switches activity on or off, as in glycogen phosphorylase and many kinases.

Not quite. A phosphate group is negative (−2 at body pH, −1 below about pH 5.8). It attracts positive groups like Arg and Lys, and it would push away COO⁻ groups. A positive charge would come from protonated amines, not phosphate.

p: Kinases add phosphate groups to the OH side chains of serine, threonine and tyrosine. Phosphatases take them off. This is one of the cell's main on/off switches.
The phosphate is big and carries about two negative charges at body pH. Dropping that onto a neutral OH changes which nearby groups are attracted or repelled.

The protein may shift a loop to pair the phosphate with a positive Arg or Lys, or swing a region away to escape a negative neighbor. That shape change can open or close an active site, or create a docking spot for another protein.

x1A_098.trap: Phosphate is negative (about −2 at pH 7.4). It pairs with Lys and Arg, not with COO⁻ groups.
mem: Polar uncharged: S, T, C, N, Q, Y
Kinases phosphorylate S, T and Y (the OH side chains)
Phosphate adds a bulky negative charge (about −2 at pH 7.4)
x1A_098.sc: Phosphate = negative = new salt bridges with Lys/Arg, or pushing away Asp/Glu.
x1A_098.mn: STC NQY for the polar uncharged ones: Stick To Courses; Never Quit Yelling.
x1A_098.plain: Serine's OH is like a handle. A kinase hangs a heavy, negatively charged backpack (the phosphate) on it, and the protein shifts its shape to deal with the new weight and charge.

fig.cap: Free-energy levels of native (N) and unfolded (U) states for each change (illustrative values, kJ/mol). The engineered disulfide raises U and widens the gap; the other three changes narrow it, drawn here as a less stable native state.
fig.alt: Energy-level diagram with five columns. Wild type: gap 30. Plus engineered S-S bond: U raised, gap 42, tagged more stable. Buried Leu to Asp: N raised, gap 15. Gly in mid-helix: gap 22. Surface salt bridge removed: gap 26. These three tagged less stable.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; illustrative free-energy values.

ox: Correct. Stability is the energy gap between the unfolded and folded states. A disulfide between two residues that are already close in the folded protein doesn't strain the folded state, but it ties the unfolded chain into a loop, removing many of its possible shapes. Lowering the unfolded state's entropy raises its energy, which widens the gap, so the protein's stability and melting temperature go up. This is a common protein-engineering trick, and it's also why secreted proteins often have disulfides.

Not quite. Leucine buried in the core helps drive folding through the hydrophobic effect. Swapping it for aspartate puts a charged COO⁻ in the oily interior, where there's no water and no partner for it. That costs a lot of energy, making the folded state much less stable.

Not quite. Glycine has no real side chain, so it's very floppy. Locking it into a helix costs more freedom than locking other residues, and it adds no side-chain packing. Several glycines in the middle of a helix weaken the helix and lower overall stability. Glycine fits better in turns and loops.

Not quite. A surface salt bridge, say between Lys and Glu, adds a modest attraction that helps the folded state. Changing both to alanine removes it, so the folded state loses some support. The effect is usually small, because water and ions partly muffle surface salt bridges, but it lowers stability, not raises it.

p: Stability is the energy difference between the folded and unfolded states. You can raise it by making the folded state more comfortable, or by making the unfolded state less comfortable.

A well-placed disulfide works mainly the second way. An unfolded chain is stable partly because it has so many possible shapes (high entropy). A disulfide ties two parts of the chain together, cutting down those options, so unfolding isn't as attractive.
Changes that usually hurt stability: putting a charged or polar residue in the core, adding glycine or proline in the middle of a helix, or removing a salt bridge or hydrogen bond.

x1A_099.trap: A good disulfide stabilizes mostly by making the unfolded state less favorable (lowering its entropy).

fig.cap: Heme iron's coordination in globins: four porphyrin nitrogens in the plane, the proximal His (F8) imidazole below as the fifth ligand, and O₂ at the sixth site above, hydrogen-bonded by the distal His (E7).
fig.alt: Perspective drawing of a porphyrin plane with Fe²⁺ at the center bonded to four nitrogens. Below, a histidine imidazole ring binds the iron through its unprotonated nitrogen, labeled proximal His F8, 5th coordination site. Above, O=O binds the 6th site on the distal side; distal His E7 hydrogen-bonds to O₂ but is not bonded to iron. Tags: His (globins) correct; Cys (P450s), Lys, Glu wrong.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; schematic, not to scale.

ox: Not quite. A cysteine is the heme iron's partner in cytochrome P450 enzymes, where its strong electron donation helps activate O₂ for oxidation reactions. Globins need to carry O₂ without reacting with it, and their iron partner is histidine, not cysteine.

Not quite. Lysine's side chain ends in an amine that's protonated (NH₃⁺) at body pH, so its lone pair isn't free to bind iron. Lysines near the heme can attract the heme's negative side groups, but they don't bind the iron in globins.

Not quite. Glutamate's COO⁻ can bind some metal ions, like in certain non-heme iron or calcium sites, but it isn't the heme partner in globins. A negative oxygen partner would also tend to push the iron to Fe³⁺ (methemoglobin), which can't carry O₂.

Correct. In myoglobin and in each hemoglobin chain, the heme iron (Fe²⁺) is held by the four nitrogens of the ring and by a nitrogen on the proximal histidine below the ring, making five bonds. O₂ binds at the sixth spot on the other side, where the distal histidine hydrogen-bonds to it without touching the iron. When O₂ binds, the iron moves into the plane of the ring and tugs the proximal histidine and its helix. That shift helps trigger hemoglobin's cooperative switch to its high-affinity shape.

concept.t: How heme iron is held in globins
p: Heme is a flat ring (a porphyrin) with an iron ion in the middle. Four nitrogens in the ring hold the iron from four sides. The iron can make two more bonds, one above the ring and one below.

In myoglobin and hemoglobin, one of those spots is taken by the proximal histidine, which anchors the heme to the protein. The other spot is where O₂ binds. On the O₂ side, the distal histidine doesn't bond to the iron; it hydrogen-bonds to O₂ and helps keep carbon monoxide from binding as easily.

The iron must stay Fe²⁺ to carry oxygen. When O₂ binds, the iron slides into the ring's plane and pulls the proximal histidine with it. In hemoglobin, that small movement spreads to the other chains and helps them grab oxygen more easily.

x1A_100.trap: Globins: the proximal histidine binds the iron; the distal histidine only hydrogen-bonds to O₂. Cysteine belongs to P450 enzymes.

fig.cap: In every Gly-X-Y repeat, glycine (G) points into the crowded axis of the triple helix, where only a hydrogen side chain fits; X and Y residues face outward.
fig.alt: Sequence strip Gly-Pro-Hyp-Gly-Pro-Ala-Gly-Lys-Hyp-Gly with glycines highlighted, and a cross-section of three chains with a glycine from each chain touching the central axis. Labels mark the correct reason (only glycine fits) and the three wrong reasons.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. A disulfide bond is a sulfur-to-sulfur link, and it only forms between two cysteines, the amino acid with an -SH group. Glycine's side chain is a single hydrogen, so there's no sulfur to bond with. Collagen fibers are cross-linked, but through modified lysines, not through glycine.

Correct. The three chains wind so tightly that every third position (the Gly in Gly-X-Y) faces the center of the rope, where the chains touch. Only a hydrogen atom fits there, and glycine is the only amino acid whose side chain is just H. Even alanine, with a small CH₃, would bump into the other chains. That's why swapping out one of these glycines can cause brittle bones.

Not quite. A salt bridge is an attraction between a positive side chain and a negative one, like lysine (+) and aspartate (−). Glycine's side chain is just a hydrogen, which is neither acidic nor basic, so it carries no charge. Glycine is there because it's small, not because of charge.

Not quite. In collagen, the amino acids that get an -OH group added (hydroxylated) are proline, which becomes hydroxyproline, and lysine, which becomes hydroxylysine. Glycine has no carbon side chain to put an -OH on. Hydroxyproline does help hold the helix together, but that's a separate fact from why every third spot must be glycine.

concept.t: How collagen's triple helix is built
p: Collagen is the most common protein in your body. It's the tough, rope-like protein in skin, tendons, bone and cartilage. Each collagen chain repeats the same three-amino-acid pattern over and over: Gly-X-Y. X is often proline and Y is often hydroxyproline (a proline with an extra -OH).

Three of these chains wrap around each other to make a triple helix. Because of the way they twist, the first spot of every triplet ends up in the very center, squeezed between the other two chains. Only glycine, whose side chain is a lone hydrogen atom, is small enough for that spot. The stiff ring shapes of proline and hydroxyproline in the other two spots help lock the twist in place.

For the MCAT, link collagen with three things: glycine (small size), vitamin C (needed to add the -OH groups to proline and lysine), and a structural job rather than a catalytic one. Don't mix up collagen's triple helix with an α helix, which is a single coiled chain.

x1A_101.trap: Picking a reason based on charge, sulfur or hydroxylation. Glycine is there only because it's tiny: its side chain is just H.

fig.cap: Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases add OH groups (shaded) to proline and lysine. Ascorbate keeps their iron as Fe²⁺; without it, collagen lacks Hyp and Hyl.
fig.alt: Proline converted to 4-hydroxyproline by prolyl 4-hydroxylase, and lysine converted to 5-hydroxylysine by lysyl hydroxylase, with a note that ascorbate re-reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺. A red box explains the effects of scurvy, with tags marking the correct and incorrect choices.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Not quite. Collagen chains are built only from amino acids. Vitamin C never becomes part of the chain. It helps the enzymes that modify the chain, and you only need a little of it, because it gets reused instead of being built in.

Correct. Prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase add -OH groups to proline and lysine while collagen is being made in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Both enzymes hold an iron atom that must stay as Fe²⁺, and vitamin C puts it back into that form when it gets oxidized. Without vitamin C, too little hydroxyproline forms, so the triple helix falls apart at body temperature, and too little hydroxylysine forms, so fewer cross-links can be made.

Not quite. Peptide bonds in collagen, like in every protein, are made on the ribosome. That step needs no vitamin. People with scurvy make normal collagen chains. What fails is the step that comes after the chains are made, when the -OH groups get added.

Not quite. The cross-links between collagen molecules are made by a different enzyme, lysyl oxidase, which needs copper. Vitamin C doesn't form cross-links itself. Low vitamin C cuts cross-linking only indirectly, because fewer hydroxylysines are around to be linked.

p: Collagen is first made as a longer version called procollagen on ribosomes attached to the rough ER. Before the three chains twist together, enzymes called hydroxylases add -OH groups to some prolines and lysines. These enzymes use iron (Fe²⁺), oxygen and a molecule called α-ketoglutarate. Vitamin C's job is to keep the iron in its working Fe²⁺ form.

Hydroxyproline is what keeps the triple helix stable at body temperature. Hydroxylysine gives attachment points for the cross-links that make collagen fibers strong. So without vitamin C, collagen is weak wherever the body needs to keep making it: gums bleed, bruises appear easily, blood vessels get fragile and wounds heal poorly.

This is the MCAT's go-to example of a vitamin working as an enzyme helper (a cofactor), not as a building block. Keep the steps in order: ribosome makes the chain, hydroxylases add -OH (needs vitamin C), the chains twist together, and later lysyl oxidase cross-links them outside the cell.

x1A_102.trap: Thinking vitamin C is part of collagen or is the cross-linker. It's a helper for the hydroxylase enzymes.

fig.cap: Top: reducing cystine gives two cysteines, and oxidation re-forms the S–S bond. Bottom: the three steps of a perm, ending with disulfides between new partner cysteines.
fig.alt: Cystine and two cysteine molecules linked by a two-way arrow labeled reduce and oxidize. Below, three panels show two keratin strands with S–S bridges, the bridges broken into SH groups, and new S–S bridges after the strands have slid.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

ox: Not quite. Peptide bonds are the bonds in a protein's backbone. Mild reducing lotions don't break them. You'd need strong acid, strong base or digestive enzymes. And if peptide bonds were cut, the keratin chains would fall apart and the hair would be ruined, not reshaped.

Not quite. Hydrogen bonds do help hold hair's shape, but they're weak and they reset with nothing more than water. That's why a blow-dry style disappears on a humid day. A perm uses reduce-then-oxidize chemistry, which only works on bonds that can gain and lose electrons, and hydrogen bonds can't. A perm lasts for weeks because it locks the shape with covalent bonds.

Not quite. Glycosidic bonds link sugar units together, like in starch and cellulose. α-Keratin is a protein, so its chains are held together by peptide bonds and by disulfide cross-links. Glycosidic bonds aren't broken by reducing agents anyway.

Correct. α-Keratin has lots of cysteine, and neighboring chains are tied together by disulfide (S–S) bonds. The reducing lotion adds hydrogen and splits each S–S into two -SH groups, so the strands can shift while the hair is held on a curler. The oxidizing lotion (often hydrogen peroxide) then pulls those hydrogens off, and new S–S bonds form between cysteines that now sit side by side. The curl is locked in.

concept.t: Disulfide bonds: made by oxidation, broken by reduction
p: A disulfide bond is a covalent S–S link between the -SH groups of two cysteines. Forming it is an oxidation (electrons are removed). Breaking it is a reduction (electrons are added). Disulfides help hold the folded shape of many proteins, especially ones outside cells, like antibodies, insulin and keratin.

Because they're covalent, disulfides survive things that easily break weaker attractions like hydrogen bonds. That's why a perm survives washing. It's also why scientists add a reducing agent, such as β-mercaptoethanol, when they want to pull disulfide-linked protein chains apart in the lab.

The MCAT likes to match each bond with what breaks it. Hydrogen bonds: water or heat. Salt bridges: changes in pH or salt. Disulfides: reducing agents. Peptide bonds: hydrolysis by acid, base or protein-cutting enzymes. Reducing agents leave the amino acid sequence untouched.

x1A_103.trap: Mixing up which bonds respond to redox. Reduction breaks S–S bonds and oxidation forms them; peptide bonds need hydrolysis.

fig.cap: The three cytoskeletal filaments compared by subunit, size, nucleotide, motors and jobs. Microfilaments are made of actin.
fig.alt: Table comparing microfilaments (G-actin, about 7 nm, ATP, myosins), microtubules (α/β tubulin, about 25 nm, GTP, kinesins and dyneins) and intermediate filaments (keratins, vimentin, lamins, about 10 nm, no nucleotide, no motors). A note says collagen is extracellular, not cytoskeleton.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; values from standard cell biology texts.

ox: Correct. Microfilaments are the thinnest cytoskeletal filaments, about 7 nm wide, and they're made of actin. Single G-actin units bind ATP and join into a two-stranded chain called F-actin. Microfilaments form the thin filaments in muscle, help cells crawl and pinch in two during division, and serve as tracks for myosin motors.

Not quite. Tubulin builds microtubules, the widest cytoskeletal filaments, about 25 nm across and hollow. Microtubules form the spindle that pulls chromosomes apart, the core of cilia and flagella, and the tracks for kinesin and dynein. The names sound alike, which is the trap here.

Not quite. Keratin is one family of intermediate filament proteins, the middle-sized filaments at about 10 nm. They're found in skin cells, hair and nails, and their main job is resisting stretching. Other intermediate filament proteins include vimentin and the nuclear lamins.

Not quite. Collagen isn't part of the cytoskeleton. Cells make it and push it outside, where it forms fibers in the extracellular matrix (the material between cells). It's a fibrous structural protein like the cytoskeletal ones, which makes it tempting, but it lives in a completely different place.

p: Cells with a nucleus have three filament systems inside them. Microfilaments are made of actin (about 7 nm), use ATP, and work with myosin motors for muscle contraction, cell crawling and cell division. Microtubules are made of tubulin (about 25 nm, hollow), use GTP, and work with kinesin and dynein motors to move cargo, build the spindle and power cilia. Intermediate filaments (keratins, vimentin, lamins, about 10 nm) use no nucleotide and mainly resist tension.

An easy way to keep them straight: by size, microfilaments are smallest, intermediate filaments are in the middle, and microtubules are biggest. By fuel, actin goes with ATP, tubulin with GTP, and intermediate filaments with nothing.

MCAT questions often pair each filament with its motor (myosin on actin; kinesin and dynein on microtubules) or a job (spindle = microtubules, ring that pinches a dividing cell = actin, lining of the nucleus = lamins). Collagen and elastin are outside the cell, not part of the cytoskeleton.

x1A_104.trap: Mixing up microfilaments and microtubules. Microfilament = actin; microtubule = tubulin.

fig.cap: GTP-bound tubulin (green β subunits) adds to the plus end and forms a stabilizing cap. Once the cap is lost, the GDP lattice peels apart (catastrophe).
fig.alt: Side view of a microtubule with GDP-tubulin in gray and a GTP cap in green at the plus end, free GTP-tubulin dimers adding to the tip, and below, a capless microtubule with curling protofilaments and GDP-tubulin falling off. Tags: GTP correct; ATP, cAMP and NADH incorrect.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. ATP is what actin binds, and actin builds microfilaments. Actin follows a pattern a lot like tubulin's: it joins the filament carrying ATP and breaks it down afterward. That similarity makes ATP tempting, but tubulin uses GTP. Pair them up: actin with ATP, tubulin with GTP.

Not quite. Cyclic AMP (cAMP) is a second messenger, a small signaling molecule a cell makes when certain hormones bind outside. It turns on an enzyme called protein kinase A. It floats freely in the cell and doesn't build or power microtubules.

Correct. Each tubulin pair binds GTP. Soon after a pair joins the plus end, the β-tubulin turns its GTP into GDP. Pairs holding GTP stick on well, so a cap of GTP-tubulin keeps a growing end stable. When the breakdown catches up and the cap disappears, the GDP-tubulin peels away and the microtubule shrinks quickly. This growing-and-shrinking cycle is called dynamic instability.

Not quite. NADH is an electron carrier. It picks up electrons in glycolysis and the citric acid cycle and drops them off at the electron transport chain. It doesn't bind cytoskeletal proteins and doesn't power filament building. Picking it mixes up metabolism with the cytoskeleton.

p: A microtubule is a hollow tube made of 13 strands, and each strand is a head-to-tail chain of α/β-tubulin pairs. Since every pair points the same way, the tube has two different ends: a fast-growing plus end and a slower minus end. In most cells, the minus ends are anchored near the nucleus at the centrosome.

Free tubulin pairs carry GTP. After a pair joins the plus end, the GTP on its β-tubulin gets turned into GDP. If new pairs keep adding faster than that happens, the end stays capped with GTP-tubulin and keeps growing. If the cap is lost, the tube unravels quickly. This lets microtubules in a dividing cell keep reaching out until they find and grab chromosomes.

Some drugs work by jamming this cycle. Colchicine blocks microtubules from forming, and taxol keeps them from coming apart. Both stop cell division. On the MCAT, pair actin with ATP and tubulin with GTP.

x1A_105.trap: Swapping the nucleotides. Actin binds ATP; tubulin binds GTP.

fig.cap: In an axon, microtubule minus ends face the cell body. Kinesin carries cargo out to the terminal; dynein carries it back to the soma.
fig.alt: Neuron with a cell body on the left, an axon with a microtubule marked minus at the soma and plus at the terminal, a green arrow labeled kinesin anterograde pointing right and a red arrow labeled dynein retrograde pointing left. Tags mark dynein as correct and kinesin, myosin II and tubulin as incorrect.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. Most kinesins walk toward the plus end of a microtubule. In an axon, the plus ends are all at the terminal, so kinesin carries cargo out from the cell body toward the terminal. That's anterograde transport, the opposite of what the question asks.

Not quite. Myosin II walks on actin filaments. It makes up the thick filaments in muscle and helps pinch a cell in two during division. Long-distance transport down an axon runs on microtubules, so myosin II is the wrong motor on the wrong track.

Not quite. Tubulin is the protein that microtubules are built from. It's the road, not the vehicle. Tubulin doesn't grab cargo or walk anywhere. The question asks for the motor protein that walks along the road.

Correct. Axon microtubules all have their minus ends at the cell body and their plus ends at the terminal. Dynein walks toward the minus end, so it brings cargo from the terminal back to the cell body. That's retrograde transport. Rabies virus and tetanus toxin hijack this route to reach the brain and spinal cord.

concept.t: Motor proteins and which way they walk
p: Motor proteins burn ATP to walk along a filament in one direction, carrying cargo. Two families walk on microtubules: kinesins, which mostly head to the plus end, and dyneins, which head to the minus end. Myosins walk on actin instead.

Which way the cargo actually goes in the cell depends on how the track is laid down. In axons, minus ends sit at the cell body and plus ends at the terminal. So kinesin carries cargo out (anterograde) and dynein carries it back (retrograde). In most other cells, minus ends cluster near the nucleus, so kinesin carries things outward and dynein carries them inward.

A memory trick: kinesin goes out to the plus end, dynein comes back down. Dynein also makes cilia and flagella beat. Keep the motors (kinesin, dynein, myosin) separate from the tracks (microtubules built from tubulin, microfilaments built from actin).

x1A_106.trap: Getting the direction backward. Kinesin goes out to the plus end; dynein comes back toward the minus end and the cell body.

fig.cap: The cross-bridge cycle. The highlighted step is ATP binding, which releases the myosin head from actin.
fig.alt: Four-state cycle: rigor (head bound to actin), ATP bound (head released), ADP and Pi (head re-cocked), and ADP-Pi head bound to actin, with arrows labeled ATP binds and detach, ATP hydrolysis, binds actin, and Pi release power stroke. The ATP-binding arrow is green.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; cycle as taught in standard physiology texts.

ref.t: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 10.3 Muscle Fiber Contraction and Relaxation

ox: Not quite. The power stroke happens later in the cycle. First the cocked head, holding ADP and Pi, grabs actin. Then Pi leaves, and that's what swings the head and pulls the thin filament. ATP binding does the opposite of pulling: it makes the head let go.

Not quite. Whether Ca²⁺ sits on troponin depends on how much Ca²⁺ is in the cell fluid. That's controlled by the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR), the muscle cell's calcium storage tank, which releases Ca²⁺ and pumps it back. The pump does use ATP, but that's a different protein. ATP binding to the myosin head doesn't change troponin.

Correct. In the 'rigor' state, a myosin head is clamped tightly to actin with nothing bound to it. When ATP binds the head, the head's grip on actin drops sharply and it lets go. The head then splits ATP into ADP and Pi, which re-cocks it for the next pull. After death, ATP runs out, so the heads stay clamped, and the muscles stiffen (rigor mortis).

Not quite. The thin filaments (actin plus tropomyosin and troponin) stay intact the whole time a muscle contracts. Muscle shortens because the thick and thin filaments slide past each other. Actin breaking down and rebuilding matters when a cell crawls, not in the cross-bridge cycle.

p: A muscle contracts as myosin heads on the thick filament grab, pull and release the actin thin filament over and over. Start with a head clamped to actin, with nothing bound (the rigor state). ATP binds, and the head lets go. ATP is split into ADP + Pi, which cocks the head. The cocked head grabs actin. Pi leaves, which fires the power stroke. ADP leaves, and the head is back in rigor.

Calcium is the on switch. When a nerve signal reaches the muscle, the SR releases Ca²⁺. Ca²⁺ binds troponin, which slides tropomyosin off the spots on actin where myosin grabs. With no Ca²⁺, the heads can't grab, the cycle stops and the muscle relaxes.
For the MCAT: ATP is needed to let go (no ATP means rigor mortis), splitting ATP cocks the head, Pi release fires the stroke, and Ca²⁺ controls whether myosin can reach actin at all.

x1A_107.trap: Thinking ATP binding causes the pull. ATP is needed to let go of actin; with no ATP, the muscle locks in rigor.

fig.cap: The cross-bridge cycle. The highlighted step, Pi release from the actin-bound head, triggers the power stroke.
fig.alt: Four-state cross-bridge cycle with the arrow from the ADP-Pi head bound to actin to the rigor state highlighted green and labeled Pi release, power stroke, then ADP leaves. Tags mark Pi release as correct and ATP binding and hydrolysis as incorrect.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; cycle as taught in standard physiology texts.

ref.t: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 10.3 Muscle Fiber Contraction and Relaxation

ox: Not quite. ATP binding is the step that makes the myosin head let go of actin. It ends a pull instead of making one. That's why running out of ATP after death leaves the heads stuck to actin (rigor mortis) instead of causing extra contraction.

Correct. After ATP is split, the head holds ADP and Pi in a cocked, high-energy shape. Once Ca²⁺ has uncovered the binding spots and the head grabs actin, Pi leaves. That release triggers the head to swing, pulling the thin filament toward the middle of the sarcomere (the basic contracting unit of muscle). The energy from splitting ATP was stored in the cocked head and gets spent right here.

Not quite. ATP is split while the head is detached from actin. That step re-cocks the head into its ready position and stores energy in its shape, but nothing gets pulled yet. It's easy to assume force happens the moment ATP is split, but splitting and pulling are separate steps.

Not quite. When Ca²⁺ leaves troponin (because the SR pumps it back into storage), tropomyosin slides back over actin's binding spots, so myosin heads can't grab anymore. That stops the cycle and the muscle relaxes. It's an on/off switch, not a step in the head's movement.

p: Myosin is an enzyme that splits ATP, and its shape changes depending on what's bound to it. Each cycle: ATP binds, the head lets go. ATP is split (head still free), the head re-cocks and stores energy. The head, holding ADP + Pi, grabs actin. Pi leaves, and the head swings (power stroke). ADP leaves, and the head is back to clamped.

This order means the head only grabs actin once it's ready to pull. Calcium and the troponin–tropomyosin complex decide whether the binding spots on actin are open, so they decide whether cycling happens at all. They don't move the head themselves.

MCAT questions test what happens if you block each step. Block ATP binding: the muscle freezes in rigor. Block ATP splitting: heads stay detached and uncocked. Low Ca²⁺: the muscle relaxes. 'ATP powers the stroke' is loosely true overall, but the step tied to the stroke itself is Pi release.

x1A_108.trap: Mixing up the steps. Splitting ATP cocks the head, Pi release fires it, and ATP binding lets it go.

fig.cap: Binding curves computed from the Hill equation: myoglobin (n = 1, P50 ≈ 3 mmHg) is hyperbolic; hemoglobin (n ≈ 2.8, P50 ≈ 26 mmHg) is sigmoidal.
fig.alt: Graph of O₂ saturation against PO₂ from 0 to 100 mmHg. The myoglobin curve rises steeply and hyperbolically, reaching 50 percent near 3 mmHg; the hemoglobin curve is S-shaped, reaching 50 percent at 26 mmHg. Notes explain cooperativity and that myoglobin has the higher affinity.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Hill equation, Y = Pⁿ/(P50ⁿ + Pⁿ), with standard textbook P50 and n values.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 39.4 Transport of Gases in Human Bodily Fluids

ox: Correct. Hemoglobin is made of four chains (two α and two β), each with a heme. When O₂ binds one heme, it shifts the contacts between the chains from the low-grip T state toward the high-grip R state, so the remaining hemes bind O₂ more easily. That makes saturation climb steeply over a narrow range of O₂ pressure, which gives the S shape. Myoglobin is one chain with one heme, so it has no partners and its curve is a plain hyperbola.

Not quite. It's the reverse: myoglobin holds O₂ more tightly. Its P50, the O₂ pressure where it's half full, is about 2 to 3 mmHg, compared with about 26 mmHg for hemoglobin. Higher grip would slide a curve to the left, but it wouldn't change its shape from a bend to an S.

Not quite. Myoglobin does have heme: one per chain. That's where O₂ binds, and it's why muscle looks red. A protein with no heme couldn't bind O₂ at all. The two curves differ because of how many subunits work together, not because one protein lacks heme.

Not quite. In both proteins, O₂ attaches to the iron by a bond that easily comes apart again. It has to, because both proteins need to let go of O₂ in tissues. If O₂ were stuck permanently, neither protein would be any use. The S shape comes from the subunits working together.

p: A protein with one binding site, like myoglobin, gives a hyperbolic curve: it fills up quickly at first and then levels off. A protein with several sites that affect each other, like hemoglobin, can show cooperativity, where filling one site changes how easily the others fill. Positive cooperativity gives an S-shaped (sigmoidal) curve.

Hemoglobin flips between the T state (low grip, favored by H⁺, CO₂ and a molecule called 2,3-BPG) and the R state (high grip, favored by O₂ itself). The steep middle of its S curve sits between tissue O₂ pressure (about 40 mmHg) and lung O₂ pressure (about 100 mmHg). So a small drop in O₂ pressure in the tissues makes hemoglobin release a lot of O₂. Myoglobin, with its very low P50, stays almost full in tissues and acts as an O₂ storage tank in muscle.

MCAT questions often ask which protein holds O₂ more tightly (myoglobin) and what P50 means (the O₂ pressure at 50% full; lower means a tighter grip). Cooperativity is about sites helping each other, not about how strong any one bond is.

x1A_109.trap: Thinking hemoglobin's S shape means it holds O₂ more tightly. Myoglobin holds it more tightly; hemoglobin's S shape comes from cooperativity.

fig.cap: Hill-equation curves for normal blood (P50 26 mmHg) and an illustrative right-shifted curve for active muscle (P50 32 mmHg). At a muscle PO₂ of 20 mmHg the shifted curve releases more O₂.
fig.alt: Two sigmoidal O₂ saturation curves; the green active-muscle curve lies to the right of the blue normal curve. At PO₂ 20 mmHg the green curve is at about 21 percent and the blue at about 32 percent; unloading from 100 to 20 mmHg is 65 percent normally versus 75 percent when shifted.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Hill equation (n = 2.8; P50 26 mmHg normal, 32 mmHg illustrative right shift).

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 39.4 Transport of Gases in Human Bodily Fluids
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 22.5 Transport of Gases

ox: Not quite. A drop in temperature makes hemoglobin hold O₂ more tightly and shifts the curve to the left, so less O₂ comes off. Working muscle actually gets warmer, which shifts the curve right. This choice names the right factor but the wrong direction.

Not quite. Active muscle makes more CO₂, not less. CO₂ loosens hemoglobin's grip in two ways: it attaches to hemoglobin directly, and it makes acid (H⁺) when it reacts with water. A fall in CO₂ would shift the curve left and make hemoglobin hold O₂ more tightly.

Correct. Working muscle makes CO₂ and lactic acid, which lower the pH nearby. The extra H⁺ attaches to certain spots on hemoglobin and favors its low-grip T state. This is the Bohr effect. The O₂ curve shifts right, so at the same O₂ pressure in the tissue, hemoglobin releases more O₂, right where it's needed.

Not quite. 2,3-BPG (2,3-bisphosphoglycerate) is a small molecule in red blood cells that sits in a pocket of hemoglobin and favors the low-grip T state. Less 2,3-BPG means a tighter grip and a left shift. In fact, 2,3-BPG goes up, not down, when the body is short on O₂, such as at high altitude.

concept.t: Right and left shifts of the hemoglobin curve
p: Anything that loosens hemoglobin's grip on O₂ shifts the curve to the right (a higher P50), so more O₂ comes off at a given O₂ pressure. The classic list: more CO₂, more acid (lower pH, the Bohr effect), higher temperature and more 2,3-BPG. All of these push hemoglobin into its low-grip T state. They're exactly the conditions in busy tissue, so O₂ gets delivered where it's needed most.

The opposite changes (less CO₂, higher pH, cooler temperature, less 2,3-BPG), along with fetal hemoglobin and carbon monoxide, shift the curve to the left (a lower P50). A left shift helps hemoglobin pick up O₂ but makes it worse at dropping O₂ off.

A common memory aid for a right shift is 'CADET, face right': CO₂, Acid, 2,3-DPG (another name for BPG), Exercise and Temperature. In the lungs the reverse happens: CO₂ is breathed out, pH rises, and hemoglobin grabs O₂ more easily.

x1A_110.trap: Mixing up the direction. Everything that rises in working tissue (CO₂, H⁺, temperature, 2,3-BPG) shifts the curve right; a fall in any of them shifts it left.

fig.cap: Hill-equation curves for HbF (P50 ≈ 19 mmHg) and HbA (P50 ≈ 26 mmHg). At a placental PO₂ of 30 mmHg, HbF is about 78% saturated versus 60% for HbA.
fig.alt: Two sigmoidal curves of O₂ saturation against PO₂; the fetal hemoglobin curve lies to the left of the adult curve. At 30 mmHg the fetal curve reads 78 percent and the adult 60 percent. A note explains that γ chains bind 2,3-BPG weakly.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Hill equation, Y = Pⁿ/(P50ⁿ + Pⁿ), with standard textbook P50 and n values.

ref.t: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 22.5 Transport of Gases

ox: Correct. 2,3-BPG fits in a pocket between the two β chains of adult hemoglobin, held there by positively charged amino acids, and it favors the low-grip T state. In fetal hemoglobin, the γ chains have an uncharged amino acid (serine) at one of those spots, so the pocket holds 2,3-BPG less well. With less 2,3-BPG bound, fetal hemoglobin grips O₂ more tightly (P50 about 19 mmHg versus about 26 for adult). So O₂ moves from the mother's blood to the baby's.

Not quite. Fetal hemoglobin (two α and two γ chains) and adult hemoglobin (two α and two β) both have four chains with one heme each, so each can carry up to four O₂. More hemes would raise how much O₂ the blood can carry, not how tightly each heme holds it.

Not quite. In both kinds of hemoglobin, O₂ binds the iron by a bond that comes apart easily. If fetal hemoglobin stuck to O₂ permanently, it could never deliver O₂ to the baby's tissues, which would defeat the whole point. Its tighter grip is just a modest shift to the left.

Not quite. Fetal hemoglobin is still four chains working together, with an S-shaped curve. The curve simply sits to the left of the adult curve. Losing cooperativity would make the curve a simple bend, which would actually make loading and unloading O₂ less efficient.

p: A fetus gets its O₂ from the mother's blood across the placenta, where the O₂ pressure is fairly low (about 30 to 40 mmHg). To take O₂ away from the mother's hemoglobin, the fetus needs hemoglobin that grips O₂ more tightly. Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) uses two γ chains in place of β chains, and its P50 is about 19 mmHg, versus about 26 mmHg for adult hemoglobin.

The difference comes from 2,3-BPG, a by-product of glucose breakdown in red blood cells. One 2,3-BPG molecule sits in the central pocket of hemoglobin and holds it in the low-grip T state. The γ chains of HbF are missing one of the positive charges that holds 2,3-BPG in place, so HbF binds it weakly and stays in its high-grip form more often.

For the MCAT, these all shift the curve left (tighter grip, lower P50): fetal hemoglobin, carbon monoxide, less 2,3-BPG, less CO₂, higher pH and lower temperature. Also remember that 2,3-BPG rises at high altitude, which helps adults release O₂ to tissues.

x1A_111.trap: Thinking fetal hemoglobin has extra hemes. It has the same four; it grips O₂ tighter because it binds 2,3-BPG weakly.

fig.cap: Hill-equation curves (n = 2.8) for normal hemoglobin (P50 26 mmHg) and the mutant (P50 12 mmHg). Between 100 and 40 mmHg the mutant releases about 3% of its O₂ versus 21% for normal.
fig.alt: Two sigmoidal O₂ saturation curves; the red mutant curve lies left of the blue normal curve, crossing 50 percent at 12 versus 26 mmHg. A dotted line at 40 mmHg shows the mutant still near 97 percent saturated.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Hill equation, Y = Pⁿ/(P50ⁿ + Pⁿ), with standard textbook P50 and n values.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 39.4 Transport of Gases in Human Bodily Fluids

ox: Not quite. P50 is the O₂ pressure where hemoglobin is half full. If the mutant held O₂ more weakly, it would need more pressure to get half full, so its P50 would be higher than 26 mmHg. A P50 of 12 mmHg means the opposite: a tighter grip.

Not quite. P50 measures how tightly O₂ is held, not how much can be carried. Every hemoglobin has four hemes and carries at most four O₂ molecules, whatever its P50. Carrying twice as much would need twice as many binding sites, and P50 says nothing about that.

Not quite. P50 is a single point on the curve. It tells you where the curve sits, not how it's shaped. Cooperativity shows up as how steep and S-shaped the curve is, which is measured by the Hill coefficient. A low P50 could come with or without cooperativity.

Correct. The mutant is half full at 12 mmHg, less than half the 26 mmHg that normal hemoglobin needs, so its curve is shifted left and it grips O₂ more tightly. It fills up fine in the lungs, but it stays nearly full in tissues. Using the Hill equation with n = 2.8, normal hemoglobin releases about 21% of its O₂ between 100 and 40 mmHg, and the mutant releases only about 3%.

concept.t: P50 and what curve shifts mean
p: P50 is the O₂ pressure at which a binding protein is 50% full. It works backward from what you might expect: a low P50 means a high affinity (a tight grip) and a curve shifted left. A high P50 means a looser grip and a curve shifted right. Normal adult hemoglobin has a P50 of about 26 mmHg; myoglobin's is about 2 to 3 mmHg.

What really matters for the body is how much O₂ comes off between the lungs (about 100 mmHg) and the tissues (about 40 mmHg at rest). A left-shifted hemoglobin loads well but unloads poorly. A right-shifted one unloads more. Normal hemoglobin strikes a balance between the two.

Keep three ideas separate. Affinity is how tightly O₂ is held (shown by P50). Capacity is how much O₂ can be carried (number of sites and amount of hemoglobin). Cooperativity is how S-shaped the curve is (the Hill coefficient).

fm.f: Y = Pⁿ ÷ (P50ⁿ + Pⁿ), where Y = fraction of hemoglobin filled with O₂, P = O₂ pressure, P50 = pressure at half full, n = Hill coefficient
fm.v: n = 2.8 (hemoglobin); normal P50 = 26 mmHg; mutant P50 = 12 mmHg; lung P = 100 mmHg; tissue P = 40 mmHg; Y = ?
fm.why: The amount of O₂ delivered is the drop in fullness between lung pressure and tissue pressure.
fm.nc: At P = P50, r = 1 and Y = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5 exactly, which is the definition of P50. The powers of 2.8 need a calculator; on the test day only the direction matters.

steps: Write the formula: Y = Pⁿ ÷ (P50ⁿ + Pⁿ). Dividing the top and bottom by P50ⁿ turns it into Y = r ÷ (1 + r), where r = (P ÷ P50)ⁿ.
Write down the values: n = 2.8, normal P50 = 26 mmHg, mutant P50 = 12 mmHg, lungs P = 100 mmHg, tissues P = 40 mmHg.
Read the P50 first: 12 mmHg is lower than 26 mmHg, so the mutant is half full at a lower pressure. That means a tighter grip and a left shift.
Normal hemoglobin in the lungs: 100 ÷ 26 ≈ 3.85, and 3.85 raised to the 2.8 power ≈ 43.5. Y = 43.5 ÷ (1 + 43.5) = 43.5 ÷ 44.5 ≈ 0.977, about 98% full.
Normal hemoglobin in the tissues: 40 ÷ 26 ≈ 1.54, and 1.54 raised to the 2.8 power ≈ 3.34. Y = 3.34 ÷ 4.34 ≈ 0.770, about 77% full. It releases 0.977 − 0.770 ≈ 0.21, about 21% of its O₂.
Mutant in the lungs: 100 ÷ 12 ≈ 8.33, and 8.33 raised to the 2.8 power ≈ 379. Y = 379 ÷ 380 ≈ 0.997, about 99.7% full.
Mutant in the tissues: 40 ÷ 12 ≈ 3.33, and 3.33 raised to the 2.8 power ≈ 29.1. Y = 29.1 ÷ 30.1 ≈ 0.967, about 97% full. It releases 0.997 − 0.967 = 0.03, only about 3%.
Conclusion: the mutant grips O₂ more tightly and releases much less in the tissues.
x1A_112.trap: Reading a smaller P50 as weaker binding. A low P50 means a HIGH affinity: half full at a lower pressure.

fig.cap: Three binding curves with the same P50 (26) computed from the Hill equation with n = 2.8, 1 and 0.5. Only n = 1 gives a simple hyperbola.
fig.alt: Graph of saturation against PO₂ with three curves crossing at 50 percent and 26 mmHg: a sigmoidal blue curve for n = 2.8, a hyperbolic green curve for n = 1, and a flatter orange curve for n = 0.5. A note says n is not the number of sites.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Hill equation with P50 = 26 and n = 2.8, 1 and 0.5.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 39.4 Transport of Gases in Human Bodily Fluids

ox: Not quite. Positive cooperativity means filling one site makes the others fill more easily. That gives a Hill coefficient bigger than 1 and an S-shaped curve. Hemoglobin is the classic example, with n ≈ 2.8. A value of exactly 1.0 means no such effect.

Correct. The Hill coefficient measures how much filling one site affects the others. When n = 1, each site binds on its own, no matter whether the others are filled, and the curve is a simple hyperbola like myoglobin's. That's true whether the protein has one site or several independent ones.

Not quite. Negative cooperativity means filling one site makes the others harder to fill. That gives a Hill coefficient less than 1, and the curve rises fast at first and then flattens out more than a simple hyperbola. A value of exactly 1.0 rules it out.

Not quite. The Hill coefficient doesn't count binding sites. A protein with four independent sites still has n = 1, and hemoglobin has four sites but n ≈ 2.8. The number of sites sets the highest n could ever be, but n itself measures how the sites interact.

p: The Hill equation describes what fraction of a protein's binding sites are filled at a given amount of the molecule it binds (the ligand). The exponent in it, n, is called the Hill coefficient. It sums up cooperativity in one number: n > 1 means positive cooperativity, n = 1 means none, and n < 1 means negative cooperativity.

Positive cooperativity makes an S-shaped curve that acts like a switch: a small change in ligand near the middle causes a big change in how full the protein is. That's what lets hemoglobin load O₂ in the lungs and unload it in tissues. With n = 1 the curve is a simple bend, the same shape you see for a simple enzyme in Michaelis–Menten kinetics.

n can't be bigger than the number of sites, but it isn't equal to it: hemoglobin has 4 sites and n ≈ 2.8. Some enzymes regulated by other molecules (allosteric enzymes) show S-shaped curves too, and the MCAT may ask you to spot cooperativity from a curve's shape.

x1A_113.trap: Reading n = 1 as 'one binding site.' It means no cooperativity, however many sites there are.

fig.cap: O₂ content curves: normal blood, blood with half the Hb (normal shape), and blood with 50% COHb, whose remaining hemes are left-shifted (illustrative P50 12 mmHg, n 1.8). From 100 to 40 mmHg they release about 21, 10 and 4 units.
fig.alt: Graph of O₂ content as percent of normal capacity against PO₂. The normal curve rises to about 98; a dashed anemia curve rises sigmoidally to about 49; the CO curve reaches about 45 already at 40 mmHg and flattens near 49, so it releases very little between 100 and 40 mmHg.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Hill equation (normal: P50 26 mmHg, n 2.8; 50% COHb modeled with illustrative P50 12 mmHg, n 1.8 for the remaining hemes).

ref.t: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 22.5 Transport of Gases

ox: Not quite. CO binds the iron in its normal Fe²⁺ form, the same form that binds O₂. It doesn't oxidize the iron. Iron turned into Fe³⁺ makes a different molecule, methemoglobin, which is caused by things like nitrites or certain drugs, not CO.

Correct. CO binds heme about 200 to 250 times more tightly than O₂, so it takes up seats and cuts how much O₂ the blood can carry. On top of that, CO-bound hemes push the four-chain protein toward its high-grip R state. The hemes still holding O₂ then grip it more tightly, the curve shifts left, and less O₂ comes off in the tissues. Two problems at once.

Not quite. CO doesn't break hemoglobin into separate chains. Hemoglobin with CO bound still has its four chains. In fact, the extra harm depends on the chains staying together, because their teamwork is what passes the high-grip state from the CO-bound hemes to the O₂-bound ones.

Not quite. If the remaining hemes held O₂ more loosely, they'd release it more easily, which would partly make up for the lost seats. CO does the opposite: it makes the remaining hemes grip O₂ more tightly. That's why CO poisoning is worse than an anemia that removes the same amount of hemoglobin.

p: Carbon monoxide binds the Fe²⁺ in heme, in the same spot as O₂, but about 200 to 250 times more tightly. Hemoglobin with CO on it is called carboxyhemoglobin. CO hurts O₂ delivery in two ways. First, each heme holding CO can't carry O₂, so capacity drops. Second, because the four chains work together, CO pushes hemoglobin into its high-grip R state, so the remaining hemes hold their O₂ tighter and release less in the tissues.

Compare two people: one with half their hemes blocked by CO, and one with anemia (half the normal amount of hemoglobin). The anemic person's remaining hemoglobin still drops O₂ off normally, so they're better off. Also, the O₂ dissolved in blood plasma is normal in CO poisoning, so a blood test of arterial O₂ pressure can look fine. Treatment is pure O₂, sometimes under high pressure, which pushes CO off the heme faster.
Don't mix up CO poisoning with methemoglobin (iron oxidized to Fe³⁺, which can't bind O₂) or with cyanide poisoning (which blocks the last step of the electron transport chain in mitochondria).

x1A_114.trap: Forgetting CO's second effect. It takes up seats AND makes the remaining hemes hold O₂ tighter, so they release less.

fig.cap: IgG schematic. The variable domains of the heavy and light chains (green) at each arm tip form the antigen-binding sites; the hinge and Fc are constant heavy-chain regions.
fig.alt: Y-shaped antibody with two heavy chains in blue forming the stem and inner arms, two light chains in orange on the outer arms, green variable regions at all four arm tips with red antigens bound, and black disulfide bonds at the hinge and between heavy and light chains. Labels identify variable regions, constant regions, hinge and Fc.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. The constant region of the heavy chains, especially the stem of the Y (Fc), is the same for every antibody of one class. It doesn't bind the target. It decides the antibody's class (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE or IgD) and connects to immune cells and other defense proteins. It decides what happens after the target is caught, not what gets caught.

Not quite. The hinge is the bendy stretch where the two arms meet the stem, held together by disulfide bonds. It lets the arms swing to reach targets at different distances, but it has no binding surface of its own.

Not quite. The light-chain constant region comes in only two types (κ and λ) and is the same across many different antibodies. A part that doesn't change can't give the variety needed to recognize millions of different targets. It helps build the arm but doesn't touch the target.

Correct. The binding site sits at the tip of each arm and is built from the variable region of one heavy chain and one light chain together. Each variable region has three extra-variable loops, so six loops together form a surface that fits one specific epitope. B cells create this variety by shuffling gene pieces (VDJ recombination) and by later mutations.

p: An IgG antibody is a Y made of two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains, held together by disulfide bonds. Each arm of the Y (called Fab, for 'fragment, antigen-binding') holds a whole light chain and the front part of a heavy chain. The stem (called Fc) is made of the back parts of the two heavy chains.

The tips of the arms are the variable regions, and they differ from antibody to antibody. A heavy-chain and a light-chain variable region together make one binding site, so each IgG has two identical sites. The constant regions are the same within a class and decide what the antibody does: the Fc stem binds receptors on immune cells and turns on complement, a set of defense proteins in blood.

MCAT takeaways: variable = what it binds, constant = what it does. When a B cell switches class (say from IgM to IgG), it swaps the heavy-chain constant region but keeps the same variable region, so it still binds the same target.

x1A_115.trap: Thinking one chain alone forms the binding site, or that the constant region binds the target. The variable regions of BOTH a heavy and a light chain do it.

fig.cap: Three things bound antibodies do. In opsonization (green), the exposed Fc tails are gripped by macrophage Fc receptors, triggering engulfment.
fig.alt: Three panels: neutralization shows antibodies surrounding a virus so it cannot attach to a host cell membrane; agglutination shows antibodies bridging four bacteria into a clump; opsonization shows a bacterium coated with antibodies whose Fc tails face an engulfing macrophage. A note explains class switching.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Correct. Opsonization means coating a target to make it easier to eat. IgG antibodies grab the bacterium with their tips, so their stems (Fc regions) point outward. Macrophages and neutrophils have Fc receptors that latch onto those stems, and that triggers them to swallow the bacterium (phagocytosis). A complement protein called C3b can coat targets the same way.

Not quite. Neutralization happens when antibodies cover the parts of a virus or toxin that it uses to attach to your cells, so it can't get in or do damage. It works even without any eating cells. It's an important antibody job, for example against tetanus toxin, but the question describes cells eating the bacterium more easily.

Not quite. Agglutination is clumping. Each antibody has at least two arms, so it can grab two targets at once and link them together (IgM, with 10 arms, is great at this). Clumping can help clear germs and is the basis of blood typing, but the key idea in the question is eating cells recognizing bound antibody.

Not quite. Class switching is a genetic change inside an activated B cell. It swaps which stem its antibodies have, for example from IgM to IgG or IgE, while keeping the same tips and the same target. It changes which antibody gets made. It isn't something antibodies do to a bacterium.

concept.t: What antibodies do after they bind
p: Once an antibody binds its target, the result depends on what its stem recruits and how many targets it grabs. Neutralization: antibodies block the parts a germ or toxin uses to attach. Agglutination: antibodies with several arms link targets into clumps. Opsonization: eating cells recognize the antibody stems and swallow the target. Complement activation: IgM and IgG turn on blood defense proteins that coat targets or punch holes in them.
A related idea: natural killer (NK) cells can grab the stem of IgG on an infected cell and kill that cell. And IgE sitting on mast cells makes them release histamine in allergies.

MCAT questions usually describe a result and ask for the name. Coat to eat = opsonization. Block = neutralization. Clump = agglutination. Class switching and affinity maturation are changes inside B cells, not actions antibodies take.

x1A_116.trap: Mixing up the three. Opsonization is coating for eating; neutralization is blocking; agglutination is clumping.

fig.cap: Four ways membrane proteins respond to signals. Only the ligand-gated channel, such as the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, is both receptor and pore.
