fig.alt: Membrane schematic with four panels: a ligand-gated channel with two acetylcholine molecules bound and ions flowing through its pore; a closed voltage-gated channel; a seven-helix GPCR with a G protein underneath; and a receptor tyrosine kinase dimer with phosphorylated tails. Tags mark the ligand-gated channel as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 9.1 Signaling Molecules and Cellular Receptors

ox: Not quite. A voltage-gated channel opens when the voltage across the membrane changes. It has a built-in voltage sensor and doesn't need a chemical to bind. The nicotinic receptor opens when acetylcholine binds, whatever the voltage. Its opening does change the voltage, which then opens nearby voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, but it isn't one itself.

Not quite. A G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) is a single protein that crosses the membrane seven times and switches on a G protein inside the cell. It has no pore. Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors are GPCRs, which is where this trap comes from, but nicotinic receptors are channels. GPCR responses are slower because they go through several steps.

Correct. The nicotinic receptor is five subunits arranged in a ring around a central pore. When two acetylcholine molecules bind its outer surface, the protein changes shape and the pore opens within about a millisecond, letting Na⁺ in and some K⁺ out. Since the chemical itself opens the gate, it's a ligand-gated ion channel, like the GABA-A and NMDA receptors in the brain.

Not quite. Receptor tyrosine kinases, like the insulin receptor, cross the membrane once. When their ligand binds, they pair up and add phosphate groups to tyrosines inside the cell, which starts a chain of signals. They don't form a pore, so they can't let ions through directly.

concept.t: Kinds of receptors on the cell surface
p: Receptors on the cell surface are sorted by how they pass a signal inward. Ligand-gated ion channels are a receptor and a pore in one: the ligand binds and the channel opens, so the response takes milliseconds. G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) cross the membrane seven times and switch on G proteins, which then control enzymes and small messenger molecules inside the cell. Enzyme-linked receptors, like receptor tyrosine kinases, have an enzyme built into their inside part.

Voltage-gated channels aren't receptors for chemicals at all. They open when the membrane's voltage changes. And some receptors sit inside the cell: steroid and thyroid hormones slip through the membrane and bind receptors that turn genes on or off.

Acetylcholine is the MCAT's favorite example of one messenger with two receptor types. Nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated channels, found where nerves meet skeletal muscle. Muscarinic receptors are GPCRs, found on targets of the parasympathetic nervous system like the heart and glands.

x1A_117.trap: Mixing up the two acetylcholine receptors. Nicotinic = ion channel; muscarinic = GPCR.

fig.cap: Adhesion molecules sorted by partner. Cadherins (green) bind identical cadherins on the neighboring cell and need bound Ca²⁺ (orange dots).
fig.alt: Two cells side by side above an extracellular matrix layer. Between the cells: a gap-junction connexon pair, green cadherin rods from each cell meeting in the middle with calcium ions, and a selectin binding sugar ligands on the second cell. An integrin connects the first cell to the matrix and to actin. Tags mark cadherins as correct and integrins, selectins and aquaporins as incorrect.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 4.6 Connections between Cells and Cellular Activities

ox: Not quite. Integrins are made of two different chains (α and β), and they mostly bind proteins in the extracellular matrix, the material around cells, like fibronectin and collagen. Some bind molecules on other cells, but never an identical integrin. They do use metal ions like Mg²⁺, which makes this tempting.

Not quite. Selectins do need Ca²⁺, which makes this a strong distractor. But they bind specific sugar groups on another cell's surface proteins, not identical selectins. They create the brief, slippery contacts that let white blood cells roll along blood vessel walls.

Not quite. Aquaporins are channel proteins that let water cross membranes quickly, for example in the kidney under the control of ADH (antidiuretic hormone). They don't bind neighboring cells at all, so they aren't adhesion molecules.

Correct. Cadherins (the name comes from 'calcium-dependent adhesion') bind identical cadherins on the next cell, like hands clasping matching hands. Ca²⁺ ions sit between the segments of their outer part and make it stiff enough to bind. If you remove the Ca²⁺ with a chemical like EDTA, the cells fall apart. Losing E-cadherin helps cancer cells break away and spread.

p: Four families of adhesion molecules show up on the MCAT. Cadherins: need Ca²⁺ and bind identical cadherins on neighboring cells, in adherens junctions and desmosomes. Integrins: bind the extracellular matrix (the protein mesh around cells) and connect to the actin skeleton inside. Selectins: need Ca²⁺ and bind sugars, making brief contacts between white blood cells and blood vessel walls. Immunoglobulin-family molecules (like ICAM-1): don't need Ca²⁺.
The easiest way to sort them is by what they grab. Same molecule: cadherin. Matrix: integrin. Sugar: selectin.
Lab clue: if cells come apart when Ca²⁺ is removed, and only stick back to cells of their own type, the molecules holding them together are cadherins.

x1A_118.trap: Picking selectins because they also need Ca²⁺. Selectins bind sugars; only cadherins bind identical cadherins.

fig.cap: Adhesion molecules sorted by partner. Integrins (green) span the membrane, binding matrix proteins outside and actin inside.
fig.alt: Two cells above an extracellular matrix layer. A green integrin pair crosses the bottom membrane of the first cell into the matrix, connected to actin inside. Between the cells are cadherins, a selectin and a gap junction made of connexins. Tags mark integrins as correct and cadherins, selectins and connexins as incorrect.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 4.6 Connections between Cells and Cellular Activities

ox: Not quite. Cadherins connect a cell to its neighbor by binding identical cadherins, and inside the cell they do link to actin. But they bind other cells, not matrix proteins like fibronectin.

Not quite. Selectins bind sugar groups on other cells and make brief, weak contacts, like white blood cells rolling along a vessel wall. They don't bind fibronectin and aren't the main link between the matrix and the cell's skeleton.

Correct. Integrins cross the membrane and are made of an α chain and a β chain. Their outer heads grab matrix proteins such as fibronectin, often at a short Arg-Gly-Asp (RGD) sequence. Their inner tails connect through helper proteins (like talin and vinculin) to actin filaments, at spots called focal adhesions. They signal both ways: matrix contact sends signals in, and signals inside can switch integrins to grip harder.

Not quite. Connexins team up to form gap junctions, tiny channels that connect the insides of two neighboring cells. Ions and small molecules pass straight through, which lets an electrical signal spread across heart muscle, for example. They don't bind the matrix.

concept.t: Integrins link the matrix to the cell skeleton
p: Integrins are the main way cells hold onto the extracellular matrix, the mesh of proteins around them. Each integrin is a pair of chains, α and β. Different pairs grab different matrix proteins, like fibronectin, laminin or collagen. Inside the cell, helper proteins connect integrins to actin filaments.

Integrins also carry signals. Grabbing the matrix switches on enzymes inside the cell that control growth, survival and movement (outside-in signaling). Signals inside the cell can also switch integrins into a stronger grip (inside-out signaling). That's how white blood cells suddenly stick firmly to a blood vessel wall during inflammation, and how platelets stick together when blood clots.
Sort adhesion molecules by what they grab: cadherins grab cadherins (cell to cell, need Ca²⁺), integrins grab the matrix, selectins grab sugars, and connexins form channels between cells.

x1A_119.trap: Mixing up cell-to-matrix and cell-to-cell. Cell-to-matrix = integrins; cell-to-cell, like-to-like = cadherins.

fig.cap: Steps of leukocyte extravasation. Rolling (step 1) depends on selectins binding sugar ligands; integrins act later in firm arrest.
fig.alt: A vessel wall with four leukocytes left to right: rolling on selectin tethers, activation by chemokines, flattened firm arrest via integrins and ICAM-1, and transmigration between endothelial cells. A box explains that selectins are lectins binding sialylated carbohydrates.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; steps as described in standard immunology texts.

ref.t: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 21.2 Barrier Defenses and the Innate Immune Response

ox: Not quite. Cadherins hold cells of the same tissue together by binding identical cadherins, protein to protein. They don't bind sugars, and white blood cells floating in blood don't use them to latch onto vessel walls.

Correct. Selectins are sugar-binding proteins (lectins). E-selectin and P-selectin appear on the walls of inflamed blood vessels, and L-selectin sits on white blood cells. They bind certain sugar groups on the other cell's proteins. These bonds form and break quickly under the push of flowing blood, so the white blood cell tumbles slowly along the wall. That buys it time to pick up signals telling it where to go.

Not quite. Integrins (like LFA-1 on white blood cells) handle the next step: the firm stop. Signals called chemokines switch them on, and then they bind proteins like ICAM-1 on the vessel wall tightly enough to halt the cell. They bind proteins, not sugars, so they don't explain the rolling.

Not quite. Collagen is a structural protein in the extracellular matrix, including the thin layer under the vessel wall. It isn't a receptor on the surface of white blood cells or vessel-lining cells, so it can't create the rolling contacts in flowing blood.

concept.t: How white blood cells leave the blood
p: To reach infected tissue, white blood cells leave the bloodstream in steps. Rolling: selectins bind sugar groups with bonds that form and break quickly, so the cell slows and rolls along the vessel wall. Activation: signals called chemokines on the vessel wall switch on the white blood cell's integrins. Firm stop: switched-on integrins bind proteins like ICAM-1 on the wall and hold the cell in place. Squeezing out: the cell slips between the wall cells into the tissue.

Each step uses the right kind of grip for its job: weak, quick sugar bonds for rolling, and strong, controllable protein bonds for stopping. Inflammation signals like histamine make the vessel wall put out more selectins and ICAM-1.

Real-world link: people born without a key integrin (leukocyte adhesion deficiency) get repeated infections without pus, because their white blood cells roll but can't stop. On the MCAT, the word 'carbohydrate' points to selectins.

x1A_120.trap: Picking integrins for rolling. Rolling uses selectins binding sugars; integrins do the firm stop afterward.

fig.cap: Ligand binding brings two RTK chains together; each kinase domain phosphorylates its partner's tyrosines, and SH2-domain proteins dock on the phosphotyrosines.
fig.alt: Four stages across a membrane: two separate receptor monomers with a ligand above, a ligand-bound dimer, the dimer with phosphate groups on both cytoplasmic tails, and an SH2 protein docking on a phosphotyrosine with the downstream pathways Grb2-Sos-Ras-MAPK and PI3K-Akt listed. Tags mark dimerization and tyrosine phosphorylation as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 9.2 Propagation of the Signal

ox: Correct. Growth factors like EGF and PDGF bind the outside of RTKs and bring two receptor chains together. (The insulin receptor is already a pair, and binding rearranges it.) Side by side, each kinase adds phosphates to tyrosines on its partner. These phosphotyrosines become docking spots for proteins like Grb2, which connects to Sos and Ras and then a chain of kinases (the MAP kinase cascade), or for PI3K, which switches on Akt.

Not quite. Swapping GDP for GTP on a three-part (heterotrimeric) G protein is how G protein-coupled receptors signal. RTKs do eventually switch on a small GTP-binding protein called Ras, but only indirectly, through Grb2 and Sos after the tyrosines get phosphates. And Ras is a single small protein, not a three-part G protein.

Not quite. Opening a pore so Na⁺ can flow in describes a ligand-gated ion channel, like the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. Each RTK chain crosses the membrane only once and doesn't make a channel. It signals by enzyme activity inside the cell.

Not quite. Receptors that move into the nucleus and turn genes on or off are inside-the-cell receptors for fat-soluble messengers, like steroid and thyroid hormones. RTKs stay in the membrane. They change gene activity only indirectly, through a chain of kinases that eventually reaches gene-controlling proteins.

p: Receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) cross the membrane once. The outside part binds a growth factor, and the inside part is a kinase that adds phosphates to tyrosines. When the growth factor binds, two receptors pair up. Each one then adds phosphates to its partner's tyrosines, which fully switches on both kinases and creates docking spots.

Signaling proteins latch onto those phosphotyrosine spots and pass the message on. Grb2 and Sos switch on Ras, which starts the Raf → MEK → ERK chain (the MAP kinase cascade) that drives cell division. PI3K makes a lipid messenger that switches on Akt, which helps the cell grow and survive. The insulin receptor uses this same family of tricks to tell cells to take up glucose.
On the MCAT, recognize RTKs by these words: growth factor, dimerization, autophosphorylation, tyrosine, Ras, MAP kinase. Mutations that leave an RTK or Ras stuck 'on' can cause cancer.

x1A_121.trap: Mixing up RTKs and GPCRs. RTKs pair up and add phosphates to each other; GDP-for-GTP swapping on a three-part G protein belongs to GPCRs.

fig.cap: The G-protein cycle. The highlighted step is the ligand-bound receptor acting as an exchange factor: GDP leaves Gα and GTP enters.
fig.alt: Four boxes in a cycle: inactive Gα-GDP bound to Gβγ; ligand-bound receptor acting as GEF so GDP leaves and GTP enters (highlighted green); active Gα-GTP separated from Gβγ regulating an effector; Gα GTPase hydrolyzing GTP back to GDP. Tags mark GDP to GTP exchange as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 9.1 Signaling Molecules and Cellular Receptors

ox: Not quite. GPCRs don't add phosphates to their G proteins. Some GPCRs get phosphates added to themselves later, by other enzymes, and that's actually how the signal gets shut down. Adding phosphates to tyrosines is the trademark of receptor tyrosine kinases, a different kind of receptor.

Not quite. Breaking GTP down to GDP turns the G protein off, and Gα does that itself, with its own built-in GTPase activity. If the receptor did it, the receptor would be switching the G protein off, not on.

Correct. When a messenger binds, the GPCR changes shape and acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF), meaning it opens Gα's pocket so GDP falls out. There's much more GTP than GDP in the cell, so GTP fills the pocket. GTP-bound Gα changes shape, lets go of Gβγ, and both can switch on targets like adenylyl cyclase or phospholipase C until Gα breaks down its GTP.

Not quite. Nothing gets cut. The three-part G protein just separates into Gα (with GTP) and Gβγ by changing shape, and they rejoin after GTP is broken down, so the cycle can repeat many times. Turning a protein on by cutting it is how inactive enzyme forms like trypsinogen work, not G proteins.

p: Three-part G proteins (Gα, Gβ, Gγ) are switches. Off: Gα holds GDP and stays stuck to Gβγ. On: an active GPCR makes Gα drop GDP and pick up GTP, and then Gα separates from Gβγ. Gα with GTP (and sometimes Gβγ) switches on target proteins. Off again: Gα breaks down its GTP to GDP and rejoins Gβγ.

The signal lasts as long as Gα keeps its GTP. So anything that blocks Gα from breaking down GTP leaves the switch stuck on (cholera toxin does this to Gαs). One active receptor can switch on many G proteins, which makes the signal bigger.
Vocabulary to know: a GEF turns a G protein on by swapping GDP for GTP; a GTPase (the protein's own, or a helper called a GAP) turns it off. The small G protein Ras follows the same rules.

x1A_122.trap: Mixing up the on and off steps. The receptor swaps GDP for GTP (on); Gα breaks down its own GTP (off).

fig.cap: The three classic Gα pathways. Gq (green) activates phospholipase C, which makes IP₃ (Ca²⁺ release) and DAG (PKC activation).
fig.alt: Three columns of flowchart boxes: Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP and PKA; Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase, lowering cAMP; Gq activates phospholipase C-β, PIP₂ is cleaved to IP₃ and DAG, IP₃ releases ER calcium, DAG and calcium activate PKC. Example receptors are listed under each.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 9.2 Propagation of the Signal

ox: Correct. Active Gαq switches on phospholipase C-β, which cuts the membrane lipid PIP₂ into two messengers. IP₃ dissolves in the cell fluid, travels to the ER and opens Ca²⁺ channels there, so Ca²⁺ rises in the cell. DAG stays in the membrane and, with Ca²⁺, switches on protein kinase C (PKC). The α₁-adrenergic receptor is a classic Gq receptor.

Not quite. Switching on adenylyl cyclase, which turns ATP into cAMP and switches on protein kinase A, is the Gs pathway. β-adrenergic and glucagon receptors use it. Gq doesn't act on adenylyl cyclase.
Not quite. Blocking adenylyl cyclase to lower cAMP is the Gi pathway, used by α₂-adrenergic and M2 muscarinic receptors. It's the opposite of Gs, but it's still not Gq.

Not quite. A ligand-gated Na⁺ channel is its own receptor: the messenger binds and the channel opens, with no G protein involved. Gq signals through an enzyme, phospholipase C. Any effect it has on channels comes later, through Ca²⁺ and PKC.

p: Which Gα a receptor uses decides which enzyme it controls. Gs turns adenylyl cyclase up, so more cAMP is made and protein kinase A (PKA) turns on. Gi turns adenylyl cyclase down, so cAMP falls. Gq turns on phospholipase C, which cuts PIP₂ into IP₃ and DAG. IP₃ releases Ca²⁺ from the ER, and DAG plus Ca²⁺ switches on PKC.

These small messengers (second messengers) make the signal bigger and spread it through the cell. Adrenergic receptors use all three: β receptors use Gs, α₂ uses Gi, and α₁ uses Gq. A popular memory aid is 'QISS': α₁ = Gq, α₂ = Gi, β₁ = Gs, β₂ = Gs.
On the MCAT, any mention of IP₃, DAG, PIP₂, phospholipase C or Ca²⁺ release from the ER points to Gq. Any mention of cAMP points to Gs or Gi.

x1A_123.trap: Linking Gq to cAMP. IP₃ and DAG come from the Gq → phospholipase C branch; cAMP is the Gs/Gi branch.

fig.cap: Cholera toxin blocks step 4 (Gα's GTPase), so Gαs·GTP stays active and cAMP stays high, driving CFTR Cl⁻ secretion.
fig.alt: G-protein cycle with the off-switch step crossed out in red and dashed. A box beneath traces the consequences: toxin ADP-ribosylates Gαs, no GTPase, adenylyl cyclase stays on, cAMP high, PKA opens CFTR, chloride, sodium and water enter the gut lumen. Tags mark cAMP staying high as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 9.2 Propagation of the Signal

ox: Not quite. Gαs turns adenylyl cyclase up. It's Gαi that turns it down. Cholera toxin locks Gαs on, so the enzyme is pushed harder and cAMP rises. This choice mixes up Gs with Gi.
Not quite. Phospholipase C and IP₃ belong to the Gq pathway. Cholera toxin acts on Gαs, whose target is adenylyl cyclase, so the messenger that stays high is cAMP, not IP₃.

Not quite. The toxin never touches the receptor. Part of it enters the cell and tags Gαs itself. The receptor can still bind its messenger normally. The problem is that Gαs stays switched on even when no messenger is around.

Correct. Cholera toxin adds an ADP-ribose tag to Gαs, which disables its ability to break down GTP. Gαs stays in the GTP-bound 'on' form and keeps pushing adenylyl cyclase, so cAMP stays high. In intestinal cells, cAMP switches on protein kinase A, which opens CFTR chloride channels. Cl⁻, then Na⁺ and water, flow into the gut, causing the massive watery diarrhea of cholera.

p: A G protein stays on as long as Gα holds GTP. So if you block Gα from breaking down GTP, the switch gets stuck on. Cholera toxin does exactly this to Gαs. Adenylyl cyclase keeps running and cAMP stays high. In the small intestine, that opens CFTR chloride channels, and salt and water pour out into the gut. Treatment is drinking a mix of water, salt and glucose, which uses a Na⁺-glucose transporter the toxin doesn't affect to pull water back in.

Pertussis toxin (whooping cough) tags Gαi instead, so Gi can't be switched on by its receptor. Gi normally turns adenylyl cyclase down, so cAMP also ends up high, by a different route. Blocking an off switch and blocking a brake give the same result.
MCAT approach: figure out which Gα is hit, which enzyme it controls, and whether the toxin locks it on or off. Then predict what happens to the messenger.

x1A_124.trap: Thinking that blocking GTP breakdown shuts the pathway down. It keeps Gαs ON, so cAMP rises.

fig.cap: Left: the 9 + 2 axoneme with dynein arms (red) on each doublet. Right: dynein makes doublets slide, and because nexin links tie them together, sliding becomes bending.
fig.alt: Cross-section of an axoneme showing nine microtubule doublets in a ring, each with red dynein arms and gray radial spokes, and a central pair. On the right, two parallel doublets connected by dynein arms with an arrow for sliding, and below them a bent pair of doublets. A box notes that bacterial flagella are rotary motors.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. Myosin pulling on actin powers muscle contraction, cell crawling and cell division. But the core of a cilium or flagellum, the axoneme, is built from microtubules, not actin. Myosin plays no part in making it bend.

Correct. The axoneme has nine microtubule doublets around a central pair (9 + 2). Dynein arms anchored on one doublet use ATP to walk along the next doublet. The doublets are tied together by linking proteins, so they can't slide apart, and the sliding force turns into bending. Dynein working on one side and then the other makes the cilium whip back and forth.

Not quite. A spinning motor powered by protons flowing into the cell is how a bacterial flagellum works. It's a stiff corkscrew made of a protein called flagellin, turned like a propeller. Eukaryotic cilia and flagella are covered by the cell membrane, are powered by ATP, and bend instead of spin.

Not quite. Most kinesins walk toward the plus end, not the minus end. And kinesins carry cargo; they don't bend the axoneme. Some kinesins do carry supplies up and down inside a cilium, but the motor that makes it bend is dynein.

p: Eukaryotic cilia and flagella share the same core, the axoneme: nine microtubule doublets around two single microtubules (9 + 2), wrapped in the cell membrane. At the base sits a basal body, built like a centriole with nine triplets. Dynein arms on each doublet use ATP to walk on the next doublet, and linking proteins turn that sliding into bending.

Cilia sweep fluid across surfaces, like mucus up your airways or an egg along the oviduct. A sperm cell swims with a single flagellum. When dynein arms are defective (primary ciliary dyskinesia, also called Kartagener syndrome), people get constant lung infections, male infertility and, in about half of cases, organs flipped left to right.

Contrast with bacteria: a bacterial flagellum is made of flagellin, sits outside the membrane, and spins like a propeller powered by H⁺ flow. Also remember which motor goes with which track: dynein and kinesin on microtubules, myosin on actin.

x1A_125.trap: Thinking eukaryotic flagella spin. They bend, because dynein slides microtubule doublets; only bacterial flagella spin.

fig.cap: Typical plasma concentrations: albumin about 4.2 g/dL, IgG about 1.1, fibrinogen about 0.3, and free hemoglobin near zero.
fig.alt: Horizontal bar chart of typical plasma protein concentrations: albumin 4.2 g/dL in green with a note that it supplies 75 to 80 percent of oncotic pressure and is a carrier; immunoglobulin G 1.1, fibrinogen 0.3 and free hemoglobin about zero in red with notes on their roles.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest chart; mid-range adult reference values from standard physiology texts.

ref.t: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 18.1 An Overview of Blood

ox: Not quite. Hemoglobin is packed inside red blood cells, not dissolved in plasma. Free hemoglobin in plasma is normally close to zero, and if red cells burst, it gets mopped up quickly. Hemoglobin carries O₂ and CO₂, not fatty acids and drugs.

Correct. Albumin is made by the liver and is the most plentiful plasma protein, about 3.5 to 5 g/dL, roughly 55 to 60% of all plasma protein. Oncotic pressure depends on the number of particles that can't leave the capillaries, so this common, fairly small protein makes most of it, about 75 to 80%. Albumin also has pockets that carry fatty acids, bilirubin, thyroid hormone, calcium and many drugs. Low albumin, from liver disease, poor nutrition or kidney loss, causes edema.

Not quite. Fibrinogen is a clotting protein that the enzyme thrombin turns into fibrin threads. There's only about 0.2 to 0.4 g/dL of it, far less than albumin, so it adds little to oncotic pressure. Serum is what you get when you take plasma and remove fibrinogen and the other clotting factors.

Not quite. IgG is the most common antibody, at about 1 g/dL. It fights infection and crosses the placenta to protect a baby. But there's several times less of it than albumin, and it isn't a general carrier for fatty acids and drugs.

p: Plasma holds about 6 to 8 g of protein in every 100 mL (6 to 8 g/dL). The main groups are albumin (the biggest share), globulins (including antibodies) and fibrinogen (for clotting). The liver makes most of them. Antibodies are the exception: immune cells called plasma cells make those.

Blood pressure pushes water out of capillaries into the tissues. Oncotic pressure pulls it back in. It comes from proteins that are too big to leave the capillaries, and it depends on how many of them there are. Since albumin is the most common plasma protein, it supplies most of this pull. When albumin drops, the push wins, water collects in the tissues, and you get swelling (edema).

Albumin is also blood's main carrier for things that don't dissolve well in water, like fatty acids and unconjugated bilirubin, plus calcium and many drugs. That matters for medicine: only the part of a drug that isn't stuck to albumin is free to act.

x1A_126.trap: Thinking the biggest or most famous protein makes oncotic pressure. It depends on particle count, so the most plentiful plasma protein, albumin, wins.

fig.cap: A Ca²⁺ rise fills calmodulin's four EF hands; the shape change lets it bind and activate target enzymes. Pumps lower Ca²⁺ to switch it off.
fig.alt: Flowchart: a signal raises cytosolic calcium from about 0.1 to 1 micromolar; apo-calmodulin binds four calcium ions and changes shape; calcium-calmodulin activates targets such as CaM kinase II, myosin light-chain kinase, calcineurin and phosphodiesterase. A side box describes pumps switching it off. Tags mark the adaptor role as correct and pump, kinase and GTP roles as incorrect.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 9.2 Propagation of the Signal

ox: Not quite. Ca²⁺ is removed from the cell fluid by separate pumps and exchangers built into membranes. Calmodulin is a small protein floating in the cell fluid with no part that crosses a membrane, so it can't pump anything. It can switch one of those pumps on, though.

Not quite. Calmodulin has no enzyme activity of its own. It switches on kinases, such as CaM kinase II and myosin light-chain kinase, and those kinases do the job of adding phosphates. Treating the go-between as the enzyme is the mistake here.

Not quite. Using GTP breakdown as a timer is how G proteins work. Calmodulin doesn't bind GTP or any nucleotide. Whether it's on or off depends only on whether Ca²⁺ is bound, which follows how much Ca²⁺ is in the cell.

Correct. Calmodulin has four Ca²⁺-binding spots called EF hands. When Ca²⁺ in the cell climbs from about 0.1 μM to about 1 μM, the spots fill and calmodulin changes shape, exposing greasy patches that wrap around target proteins. Ca²⁺-calmodulin then switches on enzymes like CaM kinase II and, in smooth muscle, myosin light-chain kinase. When Ca²⁺ is pumped away, calmodulin lets go.

p: Ca²⁺ is a second messenger, a small signal molecule inside the cell. Pumps keep Ca²⁺ in the cell fluid very low, about 10⁻⁷ M. When a signal arrives, channels open in the cell membrane or the ER (for example, opened by IP₃) and Ca²⁺ rises for a short time. Cells read this rise with Ca²⁺-binding proteins, and the most common one is calmodulin.

When Ca²⁺ binds, calmodulin changes shape and can now grab and switch on dozens of different target proteins. In smooth muscle, Ca²⁺-calmodulin switches on myosin light-chain kinase, which starts contraction. In neurons, CaM kinase II helps strengthen connections between cells, which is part of learning. Troponin C, the Ca²⁺ sensor in skeletal muscle, is a close cousin of calmodulin.
Keep the jobs straight: channels and IP₃ raise Ca²⁺, calmodulin senses it, kinases and other enzymes act on it, and pumps remove Ca²⁺ to end the signal.

x1A_127.trap: Treating calmodulin as an enzyme or pump. It's a Ca²⁺-switched helper that turns other enzymes on.

fig.cap: Reaction-coordinate diagram (illustrative values). The enzyme lowers Ea from 100 to 60 kJ/mol, while reactants and products, and so ΔG (−30 kJ/mol), stay the same.
fig.alt: Free energy against reaction progress: a red uncatalyzed curve peaking at 100 and a lower green enzyme-catalyzed curve peaking at 60, both starting at 0 and ending at −30. Arrows mark each activation energy and the unchanged ΔG.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; curves drawn to scale from the stated illustrative energies.

ox: Correct. How fast a reaction goes depends on how many molecules have enough energy to reach the transition state, the top of the energy hill. The enzyme's active site holds the transition state tightly, using hydrogen bonds, charge attractions and well-placed chemical groups, which lowers the hill. Even a smaller hill makes a huge difference: enzymes often speed reactions up by a factor of a million or far more.

Not quite. ΔG is the difference in free energy between the products and the starting molecules. It depends only on where you start and where you end, not on the path. An enzyme doesn't change either end, so it can't make ΔG more negative or turn an unfavorable reaction into a favorable one. To do that, a cell has to pair the reaction with a favorable one, like breaking down ATP.

Not quite. Enzymes are catalysts, not heaters. They work at the steady temperature of the cell. Heating would speed reactions up, but that isn't how enzymes do it, and too much heat would actually unfold (denature) most enzymes.

Not quite. A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions by the same amount, so the equilibrium position stays the same. Enzymes just help a reaction reach equilibrium sooner. Moving the equilibrium would mean changing ΔG°, and catalysts can't do that.

p: Every reaction passes through a high-energy, in-between arrangement called the transition state. The energy needed to reach it from the starting molecules is the activation energy (Ea). Only molecules with enough energy get over the hill, and that fraction shrinks very fast as Ea grows. So even a modest drop in Ea gives a big jump in speed. Enzymes give the reaction an easier path with a lower hill, mainly by holding the transition state tightly.

Enzymes use several tricks: holding molecules close together in the right direction, lending or borrowing H⁺ (acid–base help), forming a short-lived bond with the substrate, using metal ions, and squeezing the substrate toward the transition state shape.

What enzymes don't change: ΔG, ΔH, the equilibrium constant, or how much product you end with. They aren't used up either. On an energy diagram, the enzyme's curve has a lower peak, but the same starting and ending heights.

x1A_128.trap: Thinking enzymes change ΔG. They lower the height of the hill (Ea), never the difference between start and finish.

fig.cap: A ⇌ B with Keq = 3, computed from first-order rate laws. With or without enzyme (rates ×100), the product fraction settles at 0.75; adding enzyme at equilibrium changes nothing.
fig.alt: Graph of fraction as product B against time from 0 to 400 minutes. The green curve with enzyme jumps to 0.75 almost immediately; the red uncatalyzed curve rises gradually to the same 0.75 plateau. An arrow at 300 minutes marks enzyme being added at equilibrium with no change.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from reversible first-order kinetics with kf = 0.02 per min and kr = 0.0067 per min (enzyme: both ×100).

ox: Not quite. Making more product would mean a new ratio of product to reactant, which needs a different equilibrium constant (Keq). Keq depends only on ΔG° and temperature, and an enzyme changes neither. The enzyme speeds up making product and breaking it down equally, so there's no net change.

Not quite. Making more reactant would also mean a new ratio, just tilted the other way. Catalysts don't favor either direction. It's tempting to think the enzyme might push things backward once equilibrium is reached, but it speeds both directions by the same factor.

Correct. At equilibrium, the forward and backward rates are already equal. Both directions go through the same transition state, so when the enzyme lowers it, both rates rise by the same factor and stay equal. The amounts of reactant and product don't change. An enzyme can only help a system that isn't at equilibrium yet get there faster.

Not quite. Equilibrium is dynamic: molecules keep converting in both directions at equal rates, so the reaction never stops. There's just no overall change. Adding an enzyme makes both directions faster, but the amounts still stay the same.

p: Where a reaction's equilibrium sits is set by energy: ΔG° = −RT ln Keq, where Keq is the equilibrium constant, R is the gas constant and T is temperature. A catalyst changes the path the reaction takes (how fast it goes), not the energy of the starting molecules or products. So Keq and the final amounts don't change. Because the forward and backward reactions share one transition state, lowering it speeds both by the same factor.
If a mixture starts away from equilibrium, an enzyme just gets it to the same final ratio sooner. If a mixture is already at equilibrium, adding an enzyme changes nothing you can measure.

In cells, many reactions seem to run only one way. That's because the cell keeps supplying starting material and removing products, so the reaction never reaches equilibrium. The one-way direction comes from concentrations (ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, where Q is the current ratio), not from the enzyme.

x1A_129.trap: Thinking an enzyme can push a reaction further toward products. A catalyst can never move an equilibrium; at equilibrium it changes nothing.

fig.cap: Cartoon of shape complementarity. The active site fits the transition state best; a stable analog of that shape makes the same contacts and binds more tightly than the substrate.
fig.alt: Three panels with the same V-shaped enzyme pocket: a flat substrate bar touching only the pocket edges, an orange V-shaped transition state filling the pocket with four contact dots, and a green V-shaped stable analog filling the pocket with the same contacts. Tags mark tighter binding as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. Active sites are shaped to fit the transition state best, not the substrate. So a molecule that looks like the transition state fits better. You'd expect weaker binding from a molecule that looks like neither the substrate nor the transition state.

Not quite. If the enzyme held the transition state no more tightly than the substrate, it would lower both energies equally, the hill would stay the same height, and nothing would speed up. Holding the transition state more tightly is exactly how enzymes work.

Not quite. A transition-state mimic looks like what forms inside the active site during the reaction, so it binds the active site and blocks the substrate (competitive inhibition). Allosteric sites are separate regulatory spots, and the molecules that bind there usually look nothing like the substrate.

Correct. An enzyme lowers the activation energy because its active site holds the transition state far more tightly than the substrate. A stable molecule shaped like the transition state can make all those good contacts without reacting, so it binds much more tightly than the substrate. That's why transition-state analogs make strong competitive inhibitors. Several real drugs, including the flu drug oseltamivir (Tamiflu) and many HIV protease inhibitors, were designed this way.

p: Enzymes speed reactions by holding the transition state more tightly than the substrate. If an enzyme held the substrate too tightly, the substrate would sink into a deep energy pit, and the climb out of that pit would be even higher. So active sites are shaped and charged to fit the transition state instead.

A transition state lasts only about as long as a single bond vibration, around 10⁻¹³ s, so you can't bottle it. Chemists instead build stable look-alikes. These transition-state analogs bind the active site very tightly and block it, acting as competitive inhibitors.

On the MCAT, connect three ideas: enzymes lower Ea, they do it by holding the transition state tightly, and transition-state analogs are therefore strong competitive inhibitors. Competitive inhibitors raise the apparent Kₘ but leave Vₘₐₓ unchanged.

x1A_130.trap: Assuming the enzyme fits the substrate best. It fits the transition state best, so a stable mimic binds more tightly than the substrate.

fig.cap: Lock and key (top): a rigid site already matches. Induced fit (bottom): binding reshapes the site, which closes around the substrate.
fig.alt: Two rows of cartoons. Top: a rectangular pocket in a blue enzyme accepts an orange substrate with no change in shape. Bottom: a wide green pocket narrows and its rim closes around the substrate after binding. Tags mark induced fit as correct and the lock and key, concerted and fluid mosaic models as incorrect.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. The lock-and-key model pictures a rigid active site already shaped to match the substrate exactly, like a key fitting a lock. It explains why enzymes are picky, but it predicts no shape change when the substrate binds. So structures showing the site reshaping go against it.

Not quite. The concerted model describes proteins made of several subunits, like hemoglobin, where all the subunits flip between a low-grip and a high-grip shape together. It's about how binding sites affect each other (cooperativity), not about one active site reshaping around its substrate.

Correct. The induced-fit model says the active site is flexible, and binding the right substrate makes the enzyme change shape. That brings the chemically active parts into position and wraps the site around the substrate. Hexokinase is the textbook example: its two halves close around glucose like a clam shell. The closed form also keeps water out, which helps the reaction.
Not quite. The fluid mosaic model describes cell membranes: a fluid double layer of lipids with proteins floating in it. It's a membrane model and says nothing about how substrates bind enzymes.

concept.t: Lock and key versus induced fit
p: Two classic models describe how substrates bind enzymes. Lock and key: the active site is rigid and already shaped to fit the substrate. Induced fit: the active site is flexible, and the right substrate makes the enzyme change shape for the best fit, lining up the chemically active parts. Modern structures support induced fit for most enzymes.

Induced fit also helps explain why enzymes are picky. A molecule that binds but doesn't trigger the right shape change won't get converted. Hexokinase is the classic example: its cleft closes around glucose, which keeps water out so the phosphate from ATP goes onto glucose instead of just being split off by water.
Don't mix these up with the concerted and sequential models. Those explain how the subunits of a multi-part protein affect each other (cooperativity), not how a substrate fits one active site.

x1A_131.trap: Picking lock and key whenever specificity is mentioned. A shape change on binding means induced fit.

fig.cap: The six enzyme classes by reaction type. Ligases (green) join two molecules using ATP; the three distractor classes are shown in red.
fig.alt: Table of six enzyme classes with their reaction types and examples. Ligases are highlighted green with the description join two molecules using ATP; hydrolases, lyases and isomerases are highlighted red.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest table; enzyme classes per the IUBMB Enzyme Commission scheme.

ox: Not quite. Lyases break or form bonds without water, without moving electrons and without ATP, often by making or adding across a double bond. Aldolase is an example. Some lyases can join molecules, but they don't use ATP to do it. The similar-sounding names are the trap.

Correct. Ligases join two molecules into one by forming a new bond, and they pay for it by breaking down ATP or a similar molecule. DNA ligase seals nicks in DNA, and the enzymes that attach amino acids to tRNAs are ligases too. Many ligases are called 'synthetases,' a hint that ATP or a similar molecule is used.

Not quite. Hydrolases do the opposite kind of job: they split one molecule into two by adding water across a bond. Protein-cutting enzymes (proteases), fat-cutting enzymes (lipases) and phosphatases are hydrolases. They don't join molecules or use ATP.

Not quite. Isomerases rearrange the atoms inside one molecule to make an isomer, a molecule with the same formula but a different structure. One molecule goes in and one comes out, so they can't join two molecules.

p: Enzymes are grouped by the reaction they run. 1. Oxidoreductases move electrons (dehydrogenases, oxidases). 2. Transferases move a chemical group from one molecule to another (kinases move phosphates). 3. Hydrolases split bonds by adding water. 4. Lyases break or form bonds without water or electron transfer, often making or adding across a double bond. 5. Isomerases rearrange one molecule. 6. Ligases join two molecules using energy from ATP.

Watch the names. 'Synthetase' usually means ligase (uses ATP or similar). 'Synthase' usually means no ATP is needed. A kinase uses ATP too, but it's a transferase, because ATP is handing over its phosphate rather than paying for a joining.

On the MCAT, ask these in order. Is water added? Hydrolase. Do electrons move? Oxidoreductase. Does a group hop from one molecule to another? Transferase. Are two molecules joined using ATP? Ligase. Is one molecule rearranged? Isomerase. Anything else that splits or adds without water is a lyase.

x1A_132.trap: Confusing ligases with kinases or lyases. Joining two molecules with ATP's energy = ligase; using ATP as a phosphate donor = kinase (transferase).

fig.cap: Hexokinase moves the γ-phosphate of ATP onto glucose's 6-OH, giving glucose-6-phosphate (phosphate shaded) and ADP: a group transfer.
fig.alt: Glucose plus ATP converted by hexokinase to glucose-6-phosphate plus ADP, with the phosphate group of the product highlighted. A green box explains that a group moves from one molecule to another, defining a transferase. Tags mark transferase as correct and ligase, hydrolase and oxidoreductase as incorrect.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

fig.cap: The six enzyme classes, with transferases highlighted as correct and the three distractor classes in red.
fig.alt: Table of six enzyme classes; transferases highlighted green with examples kinases and transaminases; oxidoreductases, hydrolases and ligases highlighted red.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest table; enzyme classes per the IUBMB Enzyme Commission scheme.

ox: Correct. Hexokinase takes the last phosphate group from ATP and attaches it to glucose, making glucose-6-phosphate and ADP. Moving a chemical group from a donor molecule to an acceptor molecule is exactly what a transferase does. All kinases are transferases, even though they use ATP.

Not quite. Ligases join two molecules into one and break down ATP to pay for the new bond, like DNA ligase. Hexokinase doesn't glue glucose and ATP together. It moves one phosphate from ATP to glucose. Using ATP alone doesn't make an enzyme a ligase.

Not quite. Hydrolases split bonds by adding water. If water attacked ATP here, you'd just get ADP and loose phosphate. In fact, hexokinase closes around glucose to keep water out, so the phosphate goes to glucose instead. No bond is split by water.

Not quite. Oxidoreductases move electrons, often using carriers like NAD⁺ or FAD. In the hexokinase reaction, no electron carrier is involved and glucose isn't oxidized or reduced. Only a phosphate group moves.

p: A transferase moves a chemical group, such as a phosphate, amino, methyl or acyl group, from one molecule to another. Kinases are the most common example: they move ATP's last phosphate onto something else, like glucose (hexokinase), fructose-6-phosphate (phosphofructokinase-1) or a protein (protein kinases).

The reverse job, removing a phosphate with water, belongs to phosphatases, which are hydrolases. Phosphorylases are different again: they split a bond using phosphate instead of water, as glycogen phosphorylase does, and they're transferases.

The MCAT trap is the word ATP. Ask what happens to the atoms. If a group moves from ATP to another molecule, it's a transferase. If ATP's energy is used to join two separate molecules into one, it's a ligase.

x1A_133.trap: Calling a kinase a ligase because it uses ATP. Kinases move a phosphate group; they don't join two molecules.

fig.cap: Aldolase cleaves the C3–C4 bond (shaded) of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into DHAP and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate with no water, redox or ATP: a lyase reaction.
fig.alt: Open-chain fructose-1,6-bisphosphate with carbons 3 and 4 highlighted, converted by aldolase into dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. A green box states no water added, no electrons transferred, no ATP used. Tags mark lyase as correct.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

fig.cap: The six enzyme classes, with lyases highlighted as correct and the three distractor classes in red.
fig.alt: Table of six enzyme classes; lyases highlighted green with examples aldolase and decarboxylases; oxidoreductases, hydrolases and ligases highlighted red.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest table; enzyme classes per the IUBMB Enzyme Commission scheme.

ox: Not quite. Hydrolases split a bond by adding water across it: an H goes to one piece and an OH to the other. Aldolase adds no water. The starting molecule is C₆H₁₄O₁₂P₂, each product is C₃H₇O₆P, and two of those add up to exactly the original formula. Nothing extra came in.

Not quite. Oxidoreductases move electrons from one molecule to another, usually with NAD⁺ or FAD. Aldolase uses no electron carrier, and the two products together are at the same oxidation level as the starting sugar. It's a reverse aldol split, not a redox step.

Correct. Lyases break or form bonds without water and without a redox step. Aldolase breaks the bond between carbons 3 and 4 of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, giving two three-carbon sugars. Like many lyases, it can run in reverse: when the body makes glucose (gluconeogenesis), the same enzyme joins the two sugars back together, with no ATP.

Not quite. Ligases join two molecules and break down ATP to do it. Aldolase splits one molecule into two, and even when it runs backward to join them it uses no ATP. So it isn't a ligase. Pyruvate carboxylase, which attaches CO₂ to pyruvate while using ATP, is a real ligase.

p: A lyase breaks a bond without water and without moving electrons, or forms one by adding a group across a double bond. Typical lyase jobs include splitting a sugar (aldolase), removing CO₂ (decarboxylases) and adding or removing water across a double bond (fumarase, enolase). Note that adding water across a C=C double bond isn't hydrolysis, because no bond gets split by the water.

In glycolysis, aldolase turns fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into dihydroxyacetone phosphate plus glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. The fastest check is to balance atoms: the two products together have the same formula as the starting molecule. So no water was added (not a hydrolase), and no hydrogens went to a carrier (not an oxidoreductase).
MCAT strategy: compare formulas. Water added → hydrolase. Hydrogens handed to NAD⁺ or FAD → oxidoreductase. Same atoms, one molecule becoming two (or two becoming one) without ATP → lyase.

x1A_134.trap: Assuming any splitting is hydrolysis. Check whether water is actually added; if not, it's likely a lyase.

fig.cap: LDH: NADH gives a hydride to pyruvate's ketone carbon (shaded), reducing it to L-lactate (shaded C–OH) and oxidizing NADH to NAD⁺.
fig.alt: Pyruvate plus NADH and H⁺ converted by lactate dehydrogenase into L-lactate plus NAD⁺, with the ketone of pyruvate and the alcohol carbon of lactate highlighted. A green box explains the hydride transfer and that lactate has two more hydrogens than pyruvate. Tags mark oxidoreductase as correct.
fig.credit: This diagram was originally developed for the 520 Quest app.

fig.cap: The six enzyme classes, with oxidoreductases highlighted as correct and the three distractor classes in red.
fig.alt: Table of six enzyme classes; oxidoreductases highlighted green with examples dehydrogenases and oxidases; transferases, lyases and isomerases highlighted red.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest table; enzyme classes per the IUBMB Enzyme Commission scheme.

ox: Correct. Lactate dehydrogenase moves a hydride ion (H⁻, carrying two electrons) from NADH onto the C=O carbon of pyruvate, and an H⁺ from the water around it goes to the oxygen. Pyruvate is reduced to lactate, and NADH is oxidized to NAD⁺. Any enzyme that moves electrons between molecules is an oxidoreductase, and every dehydrogenase belongs to this class.

Not quite. A transferase moves a chemical group, like a phosphate, amino or methyl group, from one molecule to another. NADH does hand over a hydride, but that's a transfer of electrons, which is what defines an oxidoreductase. No group of the transferase kind is passed along.

Not quite. Isomerases switch a molecule between isomers, molecules with the same formula but a different arrangement. Pyruvate (C₃H₃O₃⁻) and lactate (C₃H₅O₃⁻) differ by two hydrogens, so they aren't isomers. That gain of hydrogen is itself a sign of reduction.

Not quite. Lyases break bonds without water or electron transfer, often making a double bond. Here, no carbon–carbon bond breaks. Pyruvate's C=O just gets hydrogen added to become C–OH, using electrons from NADH.

p: Oxidoreductases run redox reactions, where electrons move from one molecule to another, often as a hydride ion (H⁻) or as hydrogen atoms. They use electron carriers: NAD⁺/NADH and NADP⁺/NADPH (made from niacin) and FAD/FADH₂ (made from riboflavin). The family includes dehydrogenases, oxidases (which use O₂) and reductases.

Lactate dehydrogenase matters when there isn't enough oxygen. Glycolysis needs NAD⁺ to keep going, and turning pyruvate into lactate turns NADH back into NAD⁺. In hard-working muscle this makes lactate, which the liver can turn back into glucose (the Cori cycle).
Quick redox check: a carbon that gains H or loses O is reduced; one that loses H or gains O is oxidized. If a question mentions NAD⁺, NADH, FAD or 'dehydrogenase,' think oxidoreductase.

x1A_135.trap: Calling a hydride handoff a group transfer. Moving electrons is oxidoreduction; every dehydrogenase is an oxidoreductase.

fig.cap: Cofactors sorted by chemistry and by binding. Metal ions such as Mg²⁺ and Zn²⁺ are inorganic cofactors; coenzymes are the organic ones.
fig.alt: Diagram: apoenzyme plus cofactor gives holoenzyme. Cofactors are sorted by chemistry into inorganic metal ions (highlighted) and organic coenzymes, and by binding into cosubstrates and prosthetic groups. A glossary defines substrate, zymogen and coenzyme. Tags mark cofactors as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. Coenzymes are the organic (carbon-based) kind of cofactor, small molecules often made from vitamins, like NAD⁺, FAD and coenzyme A. Mg²⁺ and Zn²⁺ are inorganic metal ions, so they're cofactors but not coenzymes. People often use the two words as if they mean the same thing; the MCAT doesn't.

Not quite. Substrates are the molecules an enzyme turns into products, and they get used up. Metal ions like Zn²⁺ in carbonic anhydrase or Mg²⁺ stuck to ATP in kinases come out of each cycle unchanged. They're helpers, not substrates.

Not quite. Zymogens are inactive starting versions of enzymes, like pepsinogen and trypsinogen, that switch on when part of the chain is cut off. They're whole proteins, not small ions that enzymes need to work.

Correct. A cofactor is any non-protein part an enzyme needs to work. Cofactors are either inorganic, like the metal ions Mg²⁺, Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺ and Cu²⁺, or organic, which are called coenzymes. Mg²⁺ usually sits on ATP and helps hold its phosphates in place. Zn²⁺ helps carbonic anhydrase pull apart water.

p: Many enzymes need a non-protein helper to work, called a cofactor. Cofactors split into two groups. Inorganic: metal ions like Mg²⁺, Zn²⁺, iron, copper and Mn²⁺. Organic: coenzymes, most of which are made from water-soluble B vitamins (NAD⁺ from niacin, FAD from riboflavin, TPP from thiamine, PLP from B₆, CoA from pantothenate).

Metal ions help by holding the substrate in the right spot, steadying negative charges, making water better at attacking, and carrying electrons. Coenzymes usually carry something from one place to another: electrons (NADH), carbon chains (CoA) or CO₂ (biotin).

Words to keep separate: apoenzyme = the protein without its cofactor (inactive); add the cofactor and you get the holoenzyme (active). A prosthetic group is a cofactor bound very tightly. A zymogen is an inactive enzyme that gets switched on by cutting.

x1A_136.trap: Treating 'cofactor' and 'coenzyme' as the same. All coenzymes are cofactors, but metal ions are cofactors that are NOT coenzymes.

fig.cap: Water-soluble vitamins and their coenzymes. Niacin (B₃) is the source of NAD⁺ and NADP⁺; the three distractor vitamins are shown in red.
fig.alt: Table listing vitamins B1 thiamine to TPP, B2 riboflavin to FAD and FMN, B3 niacin to NAD⁺ and NADP⁺ (highlighted green), B5 pantothenate to coenzyme A, B6 pyridoxine to PLP, B7 biotin, B9 folate to THF, and vitamin C used directly; thiamine, riboflavin and ascorbate rows are red.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest table; vitamin-coenzyme pairs from standard biochemistry texts.

ox: Not quite. Riboflavin (vitamin B₂) is used to make FAD and FMN, the flavin coenzymes used by enzymes like succinate dehydrogenase and in the electron transport chain. FAD and NAD⁺ both carry electrons, which makes this an easy mix-up, but riboflavin doesn't make NAD⁺.

Correct. Niacin (vitamin B₃) provides the nicotinamide ring of NAD⁺ and NADP⁺. The name NAD itself means nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide. That ring is the part that grabs a hydride ion (H⁻) when NAD⁺ becomes NADH. The body can make a little niacin from the amino acid tryptophan. Severe deficiency causes pellagra: rash, diarrhea and confusion.

Not quite. Thiamine (vitamin B₁) is turned into thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), the coenzyme that helps remove CO₂ in pyruvate dehydrogenase and similar enzymes. Those enzymes work alongside NAD⁺, but thiamine isn't part of it. Thiamine deficiency causes beriberi.

Not quite. Vitamin C (ascorbate) isn't built into any of the usual coenzymes. It works directly as a reducing agent, for example keeping the iron of the collagen-modifying enzymes in its Fe²⁺ form. It isn't part of NAD⁺.

p: Most water-soluble B vitamins get turned into coenzymes. B₁ thiamine → TPP (removes CO₂). B₂ riboflavin → FAD and FMN (carry electrons). B₃ niacin → NAD⁺ and NADP⁺ (carry electrons). B₅ pantothenate → coenzyme A (carries carbon chains). B₆ pyridoxine → PLP (amino acid reactions). B₇ biotin → adds CO₂. B₉ folate → carries one-carbon pieces. B₁₂ cobalamin → a couple of special coenzymes.

That's why you only need small amounts of vitamins: coenzymes get recycled, not used up. NAD⁺ picks up electrons to become NADH when food is broken down, and it's turned back into NAD⁺ by the electron transport chain or by fermentation.

MCAT tip: the name often tells you the source. Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide → niacin. Flavin adenine dinucleotide → riboflavin. Thiamine pyrophosphate → thiamine. Pyridoxal phosphate → pyridoxine.

x1A_137.trap: Swapping NAD⁺ and FAD sources. NAD⁺ = nicotinamide = niacin (B₃); FAD comes from riboflavin (B₂).

fig.cap: Cofactors sorted by chemistry and by binding. A prosthetic group (green) is tightly or covalently bound and stays; a cosubstrate binds loosely and leaves.
fig.alt: Diagram: apoenzyme plus cofactor gives holoenzyme; cofactors sorted into metal ions and coenzymes by chemistry and into cosubstrates and prosthetic groups by binding, with the prosthetic group box highlighted. A glossary defines apoenzyme and allosteric effector. Tags mark prosthetic group as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. A cosubstrate is a coenzyme that binds loosely, gets chemically changed in the reaction, then leaves, to be restored by some other enzyme later. NAD⁺ in most dehydrogenases and coenzyme A are typical examples. The question describes the opposite: a cofactor that stays put.

Correct. A prosthetic group is a cofactor that's bound tightly, often covalently, and stays attached through every reaction cycle. If it gets changed during the reaction, it's put back the way it was before the next round. Examples: heme in cytochromes, FAD bolted onto succinate dehydrogenase, and biotin attached to a lysine in carboxylases.

Not quite. An apoenzyme is the protein part of an enzyme without its cofactor, and it doesn't work. It's the enzyme missing its helper, not the helper itself. Apoenzyme plus cofactor gives the working holoenzyme.

Not quite. Allosteric effectors bind a separate regulatory spot and turn an enzyme's activity up or down, like ATP and AMP on phosphofructokinase-1. They come and go depending on how much of them is around. The enzyme's chemistry doesn't depend on them the way it depends on a prosthetic group.

p: Cofactors can be grouped by how they bind. Prosthetic groups hold on tightly or covalently and stay with the enzyme. Any change they go through gets undone within the same cycle. Cosubstrates bind loosely like a substrate, get changed, and drift away. They're restored somewhere else, like NADH being turned back into NAD⁺ by the electron transport chain.

Prosthetic groups can be organic (heme, FAD in some enzymes, biotin) or inorganic (a tightly held metal ion, like Zn²⁺ in carbonic anhydrase). Non-enzyme proteins can have them too: the heme in hemoglobin and myoglobin is a prosthetic group.

Putting the words together: apoenzyme (protein alone, inactive) + cofactor → holoenzyme (active). Cofactors are metal ions or coenzymes (organic). By how tightly they bind, cofactors are prosthetic groups (tight) or cosubstrates (loose).

x1A_138.trap: Mixing up the two binding styles. Tight and stays = prosthetic group; loose and leaves each cycle = cosubstrate.

fig.cap: Apoenzyme (green) + cofactor → holoenzyme. The glossary defines holoenzyme, ribozyme and isozyme, the three distractors.
fig.alt: Diagram showing apoenzyme (protein only, inactive, highlighted) plus cofactor gives holoenzyme (complete and active), with cofactor categories below and a glossary of holoenzyme, ribozyme and isozyme. Tags mark apoenzyme as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. A holoenzyme is the complete, working enzyme: the protein plus every cofactor it needs. That's the opposite of what the question describes. Memory hook: holo = whole.

Not quite. A ribozyme is an RNA molecule that speeds up a reaction, like the part of the ribosome that links amino acids together. Ribozymes are defined by being made of RNA, not by missing a cofactor. Many of them actually need Mg²⁺ to work.

Not quite. Isozymes are different protein versions, often made from different genes, that run the same reaction but differ in speed, control or where in the body they're found. Hexokinase and glucokinase are an example. They're working enzymes, not ones missing a cofactor.

Correct. An apoenzyme is the protein part of an enzyme without its required cofactor (a metal ion or coenzyme), so it can't do its job. When the cofactor binds, the complete, working form is the holoenzyme: apoenzyme + cofactor → holoenzyme. For example, pulling Zn²⁺ out of carbonic anhydrase with a metal-grabbing chemical leaves the inactive apoenzyme.

concept.t: Apoenzyme, holoenzyme and other look-alike terms
p: Enzymes that need a cofactor come in two forms. The apoenzyme is the protein alone, without its cofactor, and it doesn't work. The holoenzyme is the apoenzyme plus its cofactor, and it does. The cofactor can be a metal ion or an organic coenzyme, and if it's held very tightly it's called a prosthetic group.

Other terms that get confused: a zymogen is an inactive enzyme that gets switched on by cutting (like trypsinogen). A ribozyme is an RNA enzyme. Isozymes are different proteins that run the same reaction. An allosteric enzyme is one whose activity is adjusted by molecules binding a separate spot.

Apoenzymes show up on the MCAT in experiments. Remove a cofactor (for example with a chemical that grabs metal ions) and activity drops. Add the cofactor back and activity returns. That proves the cofactor is required.

x1A_139.trap: Swapping apo and holo. Apo = protein alone (inactive); holo = whole enzyme with cofactor (active).

fig.cap: Water-soluble vitamins and their coenzymes. Thiamine (B₁) → TPP, used by pyruvate dehydrogenase; the three distractor coenzymes come from B₆, B₇ and B₉.
fig.alt: Table listing vitamins and coenzymes with the B1 thiamine to TPP row highlighted green and used by pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase; the B6 pyridoxine to PLP, B7 biotin and B9 folate to THF rows are red.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest table; vitamin-coenzyme pairs from standard biochemistry texts.

ox: Correct. Thiamine (B₁) becomes thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP). In the first enzyme of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, TPP grabs pyruvate's carbonyl carbon so CO₂ can be pulled off. Without enough thiamine, pyruvate can't be turned into acetyl-CoA well, so pyruvate and lactate pile up and energy from glucose drops. The brain and heart suffer most.

Not quite. Biotin (B₇) is the helper for carboxylases, enzymes that ADD CO₂, like pyruvate carboxylase (pyruvate → oxaloacetate). That's the opposite of what pyruvate dehydrogenase does, which is pull CO₂ off. The complex doesn't need biotin.

Not quite. Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), made from vitamin B₆, is the helper for transaminases (enzymes that move amino groups) and some other amino acid enzymes. It isn't one of the coenzymes of pyruvate dehydrogenase.

Not quite. Tetrahydrofolate (THF), made from folate (B₉), carries single carbon units used to build DNA bases and some amino acids. Low folate causes a type of anemia with large red cells and raises the risk of neural tube defects, not a block in pyruvate dehydrogenase.

p: Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) connects glycolysis to the citric acid cycle: pyruvate + CoA + NAD⁺ → acetyl-CoA + CO₂ + NADH. It's a big complex of three enzymes that uses five coenzymes: TPP (from thiamine, B₁), lipoic acid, coenzyme A (from pantothenate, B₅), FAD (from riboflavin, B₂) and NAD⁺ (from niacin, B₃). A memory aid: 'Tender Loving Care For Nancy.'

TPP does the CO₂-removing step. The same TPP chemistry is used by α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase in the citric acid cycle and by transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway. That's why low thiamine causes trouble in several pathways at once.

Thiamine deficiency is common with heavy alcohol use and poor diet. It causes beriberi and Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome. Doctors give thiamine before glucose to these patients, because a load of glucose puts extra demand on the thiamine-dependent enzymes.

x1A_140.trap: Mixing up CO₂ removal and CO₂ addition. Pulling CO₂ off α-keto acids needs TPP (B₁); adding CO₂ needs biotin (B₇).

fig.cap: Asp102 positions His57, which pulls the proton from Ser195 so its oxygen can attack the substrate's C=O. The table lists each part's job.
fig.alt: Schematic of aspartate 102 hydrogen-bonded to the imidazole ring of histidine 57, which is hydrogen-bonded to the hydroxyl of serine 195, with curved arrows showing histidine taking serine's proton and serine's oxygen attacking the substrate carbonyl. A table lists the roles of histidine, serine, aspartate, oxyanion hole and S1 pocket, with histidine highlighted as the general base.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; mechanism as in standard biochemistry texts (chymotrypsin numbering).

ox: Not quite. The covalent bond to the substrate is made by serine. Its side-chain oxygen attacks the substrate's carbonyl carbon and stays attached to that half of the substrate for a while (the acyl-enzyme). Histidine makes this possible by activating serine, but histidine itself never bonds to the substrate.

Not quite. Which proteins get cut is decided by a separate pocket next to the active site, called the S1 pocket, which holds the side chain of the amino acid just before the bond being cut. Its shape differs between trypsin, chymotrypsin and elastase, but all three have the same histidine. So histidine can't be what picks the substrate.

Correct. Histidine acts as a general base: one of the nitrogens in its ring pulls the H⁺ off serine's -OH as serine attacks. That turns serine's weak -OH into a strongly attacking oxygen. Aspartate holds histidine in the right orientation and steadies its new positive charge. Later in the cycle, histidine hands that H⁺ back to the piece of substrate that leaves, acting as an acid.

Not quite. Serine proteases break peptide bonds by adding water (hydrolysis). Breaking a disulfide bond is a reduction, which needs a reducing agent or a different kind of enzyme. The triad has no cysteine and does no redox chemistry.

p: Serine proteases, like chymotrypsin, trypsin and the clotting enzyme thrombin, use three amino acids in their active site: serine, histidine and aspartate. They're far apart in the chain but end up side by side once the protein folds. Aspartate positions histidine. Histidine pulls the H⁺ off serine. The activated serine oxygen attacks the substrate's carbonyl carbon and forms a short-lived covalent bond. The negative charge that builds up on the substrate's oxygen is steadied by a pocket called the oxyanion hole.

Next, one half of the cut protein leaves, taking an H⁺ from histidine. The other half stays stuck to serine. Then a water molecule, activated by histidine the same way, cuts it free and resets serine for the next round.

This one mechanism shows several catalytic tricks the MCAT names: acid–base help (histidine), forming a temporary covalent bond (serine), steadying the transition state (oxyanion hole), and picking the substrate with a binding pocket (S1). Nerve agents like sarin permanently block the reactive serine.

x1A_141.trap: Thinking histidine bonds to the substrate. Serine makes the covalent bond; histidine is the general base that activates it.
mem: Serine = attacker; histidine = H⁺ handler; aspartate = holds histidine in place
Histidine's pKₐ ≈ 6, close to body pH, so it can take or give an H⁺
Order: Ser-His-Asp
x1A_141.sc: If a question says 'general base taking a proton' in a serine protease, the answer is histidine.
x1A_141.mn: Ser-His-Asp: 'SHeD the proton.' Serine attacks, Histidine moves the proton, Aspartate holds it steady.
x1A_141.plain: Histidine is the team's proton handler. It takes serine's H⁺ so serine is free to attack the substrate.

fig.cap: Zn²⁺ (held by three histidines) binds water, lowers its pKₐ to about 7 so it loses H⁺, and the resulting Zn–OH⁻ attacks CO₂ to give HCO₃⁻, which is then released.
fig.alt: Three panels of a zinc ion coordinated by three histidines: with bound water, with bound hydroxide (highlighted), and with bound bicarbonate. A box explains that zinc is a Lewis acid that turns water into a hydroxide nucleophile. Tags mark the zinc-hydroxide nucleophile as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; mechanism as in standard biochemistry texts.

ox: Not quite. Carbonic anhydrase adds water to CO₂: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺. The carbon's oxidation state stays at +4 the whole time. Turning CO₂ into formate (HCOO⁻) would be a reduction, needing an electron donor, and that's done by completely different enzymes.

Not quite. A catalyst has to come out of each cycle ready to go again. After the zinc-bound hydroxide attacks CO₂, a fresh water molecule pushes the bicarbonate off the zinc and it leaves. If the enzyme stayed permanently bonded to its product, it would be stuck after one use. That's how an irreversible inhibitor behaves, not a catalyst.

Not quite. No catalyst changes the equilibrium constant. Keq depends only on ΔG° for the reaction, and the enzyme doesn't change that. Carbonic anhydrase speeds both directions equally, which is why it can make bicarbonate in your tissues and turn it back into CO₂ in your lungs.

Correct. Zn²⁺, held in place by three histidines, is a Lewis acid. It pulls electron density away from the water bound to it, which lowers that water's pKₐ from about 14 to 16 for free water down to about 7. So at body pH, much of it is zinc-bound hydroxide (OH⁻), a far stronger attacker than water. It attacks the carbon of CO₂ to make HCO₃⁻. This is called metal ion catalysis, and it makes carbonic anhydrase one of the fastest enzymes known.

concept.t: Metal ion catalysis in carbonic anhydrase
p: Metal ions help enzymes in several ways. They can act as Lewis acids that pull on electrons and make water a better attacker. They can steady negative charges. They can hold substrates in place. And in redox enzymes, they can carry electrons. Zinc is a classic example of the Lewis acid role, and it never gains or loses electrons in the cell.

In carbonic anhydrase, Zn²⁺ drops the pKₐ of its bound water to about 7, so there's a zinc-bound hydroxide ready to go at normal pH. The hydroxide attacks CO₂ to form bicarbonate, water pushes the bicarbonate off, and a histidine carries the leftover H⁺ away. The enzyme can process up to about 10⁶ CO₂ molecules per second.

Body connection: in red blood cells, carbonic anhydrase turns CO₂ into HCO₃⁻ so it can travel in the plasma, and then reverses the reaction in the lungs so CO₂ can be breathed out. Drugs that block it, like acetazolamide, are used for glaucoma and altitude sickness.

x1A_142.trap: Thinking the metal changes the product or the equilibrium. The zinc only makes water a better attacker.

fig.cap: In solution, reactants A and B rarely meet in the right orientation. In the active site, they are held side by side with their reactive groups (red) aligned, so the entropy cost is paid by binding.
fig.alt: Left panel: scattered A and B molecules with red reactive bars pointing in random directions. Right panel: an enzyme pocket holding A and B together with their reactive bars touching. A box explains ΔG‡ = ΔH‡ − TΔS‡ and the entropy cost. Tags mark lower entropy cost as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Not quite. How much energy a reaction releases overall (ΔG) depends only on the energies of the starting molecules and products, and an enzyme changes neither. Holding the substrates together lowers the energy hill for the reaction, not ΔG.

Not quite. Enzymes don't supply heat. They work at the cell's own temperature. Any heat given off when substrates bind just spreads into the water around them. The speed-up comes from a different path over the hill, not from added heat.

Correct. Two free molecules have to find each other in solution and line up their reacting parts exactly right. That means giving up a lot of freedom to move and spin, which is a big loss of entropy and makes the hill high. When an enzyme binds both substrates side by side in the right pose, the energy from binding pays that cost in advance, so the hill that's left is much lower. It's like packing the reactants into a tiny space at a huge concentration.

Not quite. A catalyst comes out of the reaction unchanged. If the substrates stayed permanently stuck to the enzyme, it could only work once. That describes an irreversible inhibitor. Here, the products are released and the enzyme grabs the next pair.

p: The energy hill for a reaction (ΔG‡) has two parts: an enthalpy part (ΔH‡, about bonds) and an entropy part (TΔS‡, about freedom of movement): ΔG‡ = ΔH‡ − TΔS‡. When two molecules react, a big part of the hill is entropy: two separately tumbling molecules have to come together and freeze into one exact arrangement. Enzymes hold both substrates next to each other, lined up correctly, and use binding energy to pay that cost.

This proximity and orientation effect can speed reactions enormously. It works alongside the other tricks enzymes use: lending or taking H⁺, forming a temporary covalent bond, using metal ions, and holding the transition state tightly.

Like every enzyme trick, it doesn't change ΔG or the equilibrium constant. If the MCAT describes an enzyme 'holding two substrates together in the right orientation,' the trick is proximity and orientation, an entropy effect.

x1A_143.trap: Thinking proximity makes the reaction more favorable. It lowers the energy hill by cutting the entropy cost; ΔG doesn't change.

fig.cap: Three serine proteases with the same triad but different S1 pockets. Chymotrypsin's deep hydrophobic pocket fits an aromatic side chain such as Phe.
fig.alt: Three panels: chymotrypsin with a deep pocket holding a phenylalanine ring (highlighted), trypsin with a deep pocket holding a lysine with Asp189 at the bottom, and elastase with a shallow pocket holding alanine. Tags mark the hydrophobic S1 pocket as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; pocket features from standard biochemistry texts.

ref.t: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 23.7 Chemical Digestion and Absorption: A Closer Look

ox: Not quite. Trypsin, chymotrypsin and elastase all use the same catalytic team (serine, histidine, aspartate) and the same attacker, serine. Because the cutting machinery is identical, their different preferences must come from somewhere else: the binding pocket beside the active site.

Correct. The side chain of the amino acid just before the bond being cut slides into the enzyme's S1 pocket. In chymotrypsin, that pocket is deep and lined with nonpolar groups, so large, greasy, ring-shaped side chains like phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan fit best. Trypsin's pocket has a negative aspartate at the bottom and picks positive lysine and arginine. Elastase's pocket is partly blocked, so it only takes small side chains like alanine and glycine.

Not quite. Phenylalanine's side chain is a benzene ring attached to a CH₂, which is nonpolar and carries no charge at any pH. Positively charged side chains (lysine and arginine) are what trypsin picks, using the attraction to its negative pocket. Chymotrypsin likes phenylalanine precisely because it's big and greasy.

Not quite. Chymotrypsin doesn't look for disulfide bonds in its target. Where it cuts depends on which side chain fits its S1 pocket, the one right before the bond. Chymotrypsin's own disulfides help hold its shape, but they don't decide where it cuts.

concept.t: How proteases pick where to cut
p: Proteases cut specific peptide bonds. In the serine protease family, the cutting machinery is the same in every member, but each one has a different S1 pocket that holds the side chain just before the cut. Chymotrypsin: deep and greasy, likes big ring-shaped side chains (Phe, Tyr, Trp). Trypsin: deep with a negative aspartate at the bottom, likes Lys and Arg. Elastase: shallow, likes small side chains (Ala, Gly, Val).

This is a clean example of a general rule: binding interactions (greasy contacts, charge attractions, fit) decide which substrate is picked, and the catalytic amino acids decide how fast it's cut. Change a few amino acids in the pocket and you can change what the enzyme prefers, without touching its catalytic team.
On the MCAT, this shows up when proteins are chopped into pieces for analysis. Trypsin cuts right after Lys and Arg. Chymotrypsin cuts right after Phe, Tyr and Trp.

x1A_144.trap: Crediting the catalytic triad for specificity. The triad is shared; the S1 pocket's shape and charge decide where each enzyme cuts.

fig.cap: Model pH–activity curves for a pepsin-like stomach enzyme (peak near 2) and a trypsin-like intestinal enzyme (peak near 8), with the four answer pH values marked.
fig.alt: Graph of relative activity against pH from 0 to 12. A green curve peaks at pH 2 and a blue curve peaks at pH 8. Dotted lines mark pH 2 (stomach, correct), 7.4 (blood), 8 (small intestine) and 11 (no such compartment).
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from a two-pKₐ ionization model (illustrative pKₐ 1.0 and 3.0 for the stomach enzyme, 6.5 and 9.5 for the intestinal enzyme).

ref.t: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 23.7 Chemical Digestion and Absorption: A Closer Look

ox: Correct. The inside of the stomach is very acidic, about pH 1.5 to 3.5, because cells in the stomach lining release HCl. Enzymes that work there, like pepsin, are built to stay folded and active at low pH. Pepsin is even switched on by the acid itself (it starts out as inactive pepsinogen), and it works best near pH 2.

Not quite. pH 7.4 is the pH of blood and the fluid around cells, where enzymes like clotting factors work. A stomach enzyme would barely work at 7.4. In fact, pepsin is permanently ruined near neutral pH, which is one way its action stops once food moves into the small intestine.

Not quite. About pH 8 is where pancreatic enzymes like trypsin and pancreatic lipase work best. They act in the small intestine after bicarbonate from the pancreas neutralizes stomach acid. That'd be the right answer for an intestinal enzyme, not a stomach one.
