x1A_197.trap: Calling the plateau something else. It's saturation of the active sites, not denaturing, equilibrium or substrate inhibition.

fig.cap: Apparent kcat, Kₘ and kcat/Kₘ relative to control when α or α′ = 2. kcat/Kₘ falls for competitive and pure noncompetitive inhibitors but is unchanged for an uncompetitive one.
fig.alt: Grouped bar chart for no inhibitor, competitive, uncompetitive and pure noncompetitive inhibition showing apparent kcat, Kₘ and kcat over Kₘ; kcat over Kₘ is 1, 0.5, 1 and 0.5, with the last highlighted green.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the general inhibition model with α = 1 + [I]/Ki and α′ = 1 + [I]/Ki′ set to 2.

ox: Not quite. No reversible inhibitor makes an enzyme more efficient. Every type either leaves kcat/Kₘ the same or lowers it, never raises it. An increase would point to an activator, not an inhibitor.

Not quite. kcat/Kₘ stays the same in uncompetitive inhibition: an inhibitor that binds only the enzyme–substrate complex lowers apparent kcat and apparent Kₘ by the same factor, so the ratio doesn't change. A pure noncompetitive inhibitor lowers kcat but leaves Kₘ alone, so the ratio can't stay the same.

Not quite. Reversible inhibition is partial and depends on how much inhibitor there is. At any normal inhibitor level, some enzyme stays free and working. kcat/Kₘ gets divided by (1 + [I]/Ki), which only gets close to zero when [I] is enormous.

Correct. A pure noncompetitive inhibitor binds free enzyme and the enzyme–substrate complex equally, so it divides the apparent kcat (and Vₘₐₓ) by (1 + [I]/Ki) while Kₘ stays the same. kcat/Kₘ then drops by that same factor; at [I] = Ki, it's cut in half. It's as if there were fewer working enzymes.

p: kcat/Kₘ controls the rate when substrate is scarce: v = (kcat/Kₘ) × [E]T × [S]. How each inhibitor changes it follows from what it does to kcat and Kₘ separately.

Competitive (binds free E): kcat the same, Kₘ goes up, so kcat/Kₘ goes down. Uncompetitive (binds only ES): kcat and Kₘ both drop by the same factor, so kcat/Kₘ stays the same. That's why uncompetitive inhibitors barely matter when substrate is scarce. Pure noncompetitive (binds E and ES equally): kcat drops, Kₘ the same, so kcat/Kₘ goes down. Mixed: kcat/Kₘ goes down.
A neat pattern: kcat/Kₘ (the low-substrate rate) is only hurt by inhibitors that bind free enzyme. kcat (the high-substrate rate) is only hurt by inhibitors that bind the enzyme–substrate complex.

x1A_198.trap: Mixing up noncompetitive and uncompetitive. Uncompetitive leaves kcat/Kₘ unchanged; pure noncompetitive lowers it, because Kₘ stays put while kcat drops.

fig.cap: Purification table from the question: protein fell 100-fold and activity 2-fold, so specific activity rose 50-fold, from 2 to 100 units/mg.
fig.alt: Table with rows start (500 mg, 1000 units, 2 units per mg) and final (5 mg, 500 units, 100 units per mg); a change row shows divide by 100, divide by 2 and times 50; pills mark times 50 correct and times 100, divide by 2 and unchanged wrong.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram using the values in the question.

ox: Not quite. Halving is the change in total activity (1000 → 500 units). That's the yield: 50% of the enzyme was recovered. Specific activity divides activity by total protein, and since protein dropped far more than activity, specific activity goes up.

Not quite. 100-fold is how much the total protein dropped (500 → 5 mg). If no enzyme had been lost, specific activity would rise 100-fold. But half the activity was lost, so the real rise is 100 ÷ 2 = 50-fold.

Correct. Specific activity = total activity ÷ total protein. Before: 1000 units ÷ 500 mg = 2 units/mg. After: 500 units ÷ 5 mg = 100 units/mg. 100 ÷ 2 = 50, so the enzyme is 50 times purer. It rose because the purification steps mostly removed other proteins, making the enzyme a much larger share of what's left, even though half of it was lost.

Not quite. Specific activity stays the same only if activity and protein drop by the same factor, meaning the steps removed enzyme and other proteins equally and didn't purify anything. Here protein dropped 100-fold and activity only 2-fold, so the enzyme got much purer.

p: Total activity (units) measures how much enzyme is there, by what it does. Total protein (mg) measures everything in the sample. Specific activity = total activity ÷ total protein (units per mg), and it measures purity: it goes up as other proteins are removed.

A purification table tracks two things. Yield = activity now ÷ starting activity (here 500 ÷ 1000 = 50%). Fold purification = specific activity now ÷ starting specific activity (here 100 ÷ 2 = 50-fold). Good steps raise specific activity a lot while losing little activity. Once the enzyme is completely pure, specific activity stops rising.
Common mistakes: mixing up yield with purification, and using only the protein change. Always work out both specific activities, then divide one by the other.

fm.f: specific activity = total activity ÷ total protein, where total activity is in units and total protein is in mg
fm.v: Before: total activity = 1000 units, total protein = 500 mg. After: total activity = 500 units, total protein = 5 mg. Specific activity before and after = ?
fm.s: Before: 1000 ÷ 500 = 2 units/mg. After: 500 ÷ 5 = 100 units/mg. Fold change = 100 ÷ 2 = 50
fm.why: Specific activity tracks how much of the protein in the sample is the enzyme you want.
fm.nc: Yield is a separate number: 500 ÷ 1000 = 0.5, or 50%.

steps: Write the formula: specific activity = total activity ÷ total protein.
Write down the values: before, 1000 units and 500 mg; after, 500 units and 5 mg.
Before: 1000 units ÷ 500 mg = 2 units/mg.
After: 500 units ÷ 5 mg = 100 units/mg.
Compare: 100 ÷ 2 = 50, so specific activity rose 50-fold.
For comparison, the yield is 500 ÷ 1000 = 0.5, or 50%: half the enzyme was lost, but the sample is 50 times purer.
x1A_199.trap: Using only the protein change, or confusing yield with purity. Work out both specific activities (activity ÷ protein), then compare.

fig.cap: Mild mercurial treatment separates ATCase (c₆r₆) into two catalytic trimers and three regulatory dimers. The free catalytic trimers still work but give a hyperbolic curve and ignore allosteric effectors.
fig.alt: Left: native enzyme with two catalytic trimers and three regulatory dimers. Arrow labeled mild mercurial. Right: separated catalytic trimers labeled still catalytic and regulatory dimers labeled bind CTP and ATP, no catalysis. Below: a small graph with a sigmoidal native curve and a hyperbolic curve for free catalytic trimers, and pills marking subunits separated as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; small curves computed from the Hill equation (n = 2 and n = 1). Facts after the classic Gerhart and Schachman ATCase experiments as described in Lehninger and Berg biochemistry texts.

ox: Not quite. If the active site were destroyed, the enzyme couldn't make product anymore. The question says it still works and now gives a normal, simple curve, so the chemistry part is fine. What's been lost is the regulation and the S shape, not the catalysis.

Correct. ATCase is built from catalytic subunits and regulatory subunits. Mercury compounds react with cysteine -SH groups in the regulatory chains and make the complex fall apart, without cutting peptide bonds. The free catalytic subunits still make product, but without the regulatory subunits and the contacts between subunits that drive the T ⇌ R switch, they lose cooperativity (S-shaped → simple bend) and stop responding to the inhibitor CTP.

Not quite. Breaking the amino acid sequence means cutting peptide bonds, which needs a protease or harsh acid or base, not a mild mercury treatment. Cutting the chains would probably wreck the enzyme's activity too. The results fit subunits coming apart, not chains being cut.

Not quite. If the inhibitor were permanently stuck in the active site, the enzyme would be blocked and stop working. Instead it keeps working and just ignores the inhibitor. That points to losing the inhibitor's binding site, which is on the regulatory subunits.

p: Allosteric enzymes are usually made of several subunits, and molecules binding at spots other than the active site can change their activity. In some of them, the chemistry and the regulation happen on different subunits.

Aspartate transcarbamoylase (ATCase), the first committed step in making the pyrimidine building blocks of DNA and RNA, is the classic example. It has six catalytic and six regulatory chains. CTP, the end product of the pathway, slows it by binding the regulatory subunits (feedback inhibition), and ATP speeds it up. Mercury treatment pulls the subunits apart: the catalytic ones still work but follow a simple curve and ignore regulators, while the regulatory ones still bind regulators but can't do any chemistry.

This experiment shows that cooperativity and allosteric control come from how the subunits interact with each other (quaternary structure), not from the active site itself. Protein kinase A is another enzyme with separate regulatory subunits.

x1A_200.trap: Assuming catalysis was damaged. Losing cooperativity and regulation while the enzyme still works means the catalytic and regulatory subunits came apart.

ox: Wrong. +1 counts only the amino group. The side-chain and the α carboxyl are both negative at pH 7.4, so they outweigh it. Trap: forgetting the side chain.
Wrong. 0 is what you get if you leave the side-chain carboxyl neutral. Its pKₐ is about 3.9, far below 7.4, so it has lost its H and is negative.
Correct. α-NH₃⁺ is +1, α-COO⁻ is −1, and the side-chain COO⁻ is −1. Total: +1 −1 −1 = −1.
Wrong. −2 would need the amino group to be neutral. Its pKₐ is about 9.6, well above 7.4, so it still holds its H and stays +1.

p: A pKₐ is the pH at which a group is half protonated (holds an H) and half deprotonated (has lost it). If the pH is BELOW the pKₐ, the group mostly keeps its H. If the pH is ABOVE the pKₐ, it mostly loses its H.
Acids (COOH) are neutral with H and −1 without. Amines (NH₃⁺) are +1 with H and neutral without. Add up every group to get the net charge.

mem: α-COOH pKₐ about 2, α-NH₃⁺ pKₐ about 9-10
Aspartate and glutamate side chains are acidic (pKₐ about 4) and negative at pH 7.4
pH below pKₐ means protonated; pH above pKₐ means deprotonated

fm.f: Net charge = sum of group charges, where each group's charge depends on whether pH is above or below its pKₐ
fm.why: Charges of separate groups simply add together.
fm.nc: Only compare pH to each pKₐ and add three small integers.

q1.sc: Acidic side chain (Asp, Glu) at body pH means one extra negative charge on top of the neutral zwitterion backbone.
q1.trap: Forgetting the side chain. The backbone alone is neutral (+1 and −1), so the side chain sets the net charge.
q1.plain: Think of each group as a kid holding a balloon. In a weak 'acid crowd' (low pH) they hold on. In a strong 'base crowd' (high pH) they let go.

ox: Correct. The inhibitor competes with substrate for the active site. Extra substrate can outcompete it, so Vₘₐₓ stays the same (100). More substrate is needed to reach half Vₘₐₓ, so apparent Kₘ rises (2.0 to 5.0).
Wrong. Same Kₘ and lower Vₘₐₓ is the pattern of noncompetitive inhibition, where the inhibitor removes working enzyme. Trap: mixing up the two types.
Wrong. Both falling is uncompetitive inhibition (Vₘₐₓ 50, Kₘ 1.0). The inhibitor binds only the enzyme-substrate complex. This is not competition for the active site.
Wrong. A lower Kₘ means higher apparent affinity. An inhibitor that fights the substrate makes binding look weaker, not stronger.

p: Kₘ is the substrate concentration that gives half of Vₘₐₓ. A higher Kₘ means the enzyme looks like it grabs substrate less well. Vₘₐₓ is the top speed when every enzyme is busy.

A competitive inhibitor looks like the substrate and sits in the active site. If you flood the system with substrate, the substrate wins, so top speed is unchanged. But you need more substrate to get halfway, so Kₘ goes up.

mem: Competitive: Vₘₐₓ same, Kₘ up
Noncompetitive: Vₘₐₓ down, Kₘ same
Uncompetitive: Vₘₐₓ down, Kₘ down
Competitive inhibition can be overcome by adding more substrate
q2.trap: Mixing up which constant moves. Competitive keeps Vₘₐₓ because substrate can win the fight.
q2.plain: Two kids want the same swing. If a huge crowd of kids lines up for it, eventually the swing is always full (same top speed), but each kid has to push harder to get a turn (higher Kₘ).

ox: Wrong. Competitive lines share the same y-intercept (1/Vₘₐₓ) and cross on the y-axis, with different slopes. They are not parallel.
Wrong. Noncompetitive lines share the same x-intercept (−1/Kₘ) and cross on the x-axis. They have different slopes, so they are not parallel.
Correct. Uncompetitive: Vₘₐₓ falls 100 to 50 and Kₘ falls 2.0 to 1.0, both by the same factor. Slope = Kₘ/Vₘₐₓ = 2/100 = 1/50 and 1/50 again. The slope is unchanged, so the lines are parallel.
Wrong. Mixed inhibition changes both Kₘ and Vₘₐₓ by different amounts, so the lines cross somewhere off both axes. They are not parallel.

p: A Lineweaver-Burk plot graphs 1/rate (y) against 1/[substrate] (x). It gives a straight line. The y-intercept is 1/Vₘₐₓ, the x-intercept is −1/Kₘ, and the slope is Kₘ/Vₘₐₓ.

Inhibitors change these numbers. If Kₘ and Vₘₐₓ both drop by the same factor, the slope Kₘ/Vₘₐₓ does not change. Lines with the same slope are parallel. That is the signature of uncompetitive inhibition.

mem: Parallel lines: uncompetitive
Lines cross on the y-axis: competitive
Lines cross on the x-axis: noncompetitive
x-intercept = −1/Kₘ, y-intercept = 1/Vₘₐₓ, slope = Kₘ/Vₘₐₓ

fm.f: Slope = Kₘ / Vₘₐₓ, where Kₘ = substrate level at half Vₘₐₓ, Vₘₐₓ = top speed
fm.v: No inhibitor: Kₘ = 2.0, Vₘₐₓ = 100. Uncompetitive: Kₘ = 1.0, Vₘₐₓ = 50
fm.why: Equal slopes mean parallel lines on the plot.
fm.nc: Both ratios reduce to 1/50 by simple division.

q3.trap: Remembering only the crossing points and forgetting that parallel is the odd one out.
q3.plain: Two ramps with the same steepness but starting at different heights never meet. Parallel lines means the same slope.

ox: Correct. Proline's side chain loops back and bonds to its own backbone nitrogen, forming a rigid ring. That fixes the backbone angle so it cannot fit a helix. Its nitrogen also has no H, so it cannot donate the H-bond that holds helix turns together.
Wrong. Disulfide bonds come from cysteine, and they link distant parts of the protein. They are not what disrupts helices. Trap: mixing up proline and cysteine.
Wrong. Proline's side chain is nonpolar and uncharged. A full positive charge describes lysine or arginine.
Wrong. Proline is not limited to β-sheets. It breaks β-sheets too and is common in turns and loops.

p: An α-helix is a spiral held together by hydrogen bonds. Each backbone N-H donates its H to a backbone C=O four residues away. The backbone must also twist at specific angles.
Proline is special. Its side chain bonds to its own nitrogen, making a ring. The ring locks the angle, and the nitrogen has no H to donate. So proline kinks the helix and is often found at turns.

mem: Proline: rigid ring, no backbone N-H, helix breaker and turn former
Glycine is also a helix breaker (too flexible)
Cysteine forms disulfides
q4.trap: Picking a charged or disulfide answer. The reason is shape plus a missing H-bond donor.
q4.plain: A helix is like a spring held in shape by tiny hooks. Proline is a stiff metal bar with no hook, so the spring bends.

ox: Wrong. Methionine has sulfur, but it is a thioether (S bonded to two carbons) with no H to lose. It cannot link to another residue by oxidation. Trap: sulfur does not equal disulfide.
Correct. Cysteine has a thiol (-SH). When two thiols are oxidized, they lose their H atoms and form an S-S disulfide bond. This covalent bridge stabilizes tertiary and quaternary structure.
Wrong. Serine has a hydroxyl (-OH). Oxygen does not form this kind of covalent cross-link. It is a site for phosphorylation instead.
Wrong. Tyrosine has an aromatic ring with an -OH (phenol). It can be phosphorylated but does not form disulfides.

p: A thiol is an -SH group. Oxidation removes H atoms. When two cysteine thiols are oxidized, their sulfur atoms join to make an S-S bond called a disulfide bridge.

This is a covalent bond, much stronger than hydrogen bonds or ionic interactions. It holds parts of a protein together, which is common in secreted proteins like antibodies and insulin. Reduction breaks the bridge.

mem: Only cysteine makes disulfide bonds
Oxidation forms S-S; reduction breaks it
Two cysteines joined are called cystine
q5.trap: Choosing methionine because it also has sulfur. Only cysteine has a free -SH.
q5.plain: Two Velcro strips that get permanently glued together is a disulfide bridge. Glue is stronger than Velcro.

ox: Correct. Vₘₐₓ = kcat x [E]total. Double the enzyme and you double the number of active sites, so Vₘₐₓ doubles (100 to 200). Kₘ is a property of how the enzyme binds the substrate, so it stays the same.
Wrong. Kₘ depends on the enzyme-substrate pair, not on the amount of enzyme. Trap: thinking more enzyme means better affinity.
Wrong. Vₘₐₓ does double, but Kₘ does not. Kₘ is intrinsic.
Wrong. More enzyme means more catalytic sites working at once. Maximum rate rises.

p: Vₘₐₓ is the top speed when every enzyme is busy. More enzyme molecules means more workers, so a higher top speed. Kₘ is how much substrate it takes to reach half of Vₘₐₓ. It tells you how tightly one enzyme grabs the substrate.
Adding more of the same enzyme does not change how well each one grabs substrate. So Vₘₐₓ changes with enzyme amount; Kₘ does not.

mem: Vₘₐₓ = kcat x [E]total
Kₘ is intrinsic to the enzyme and substrate
Changing enzyme amount changes Vₘₐₓ only

fm.f: Vₘₐₓ = kcat x [E]total, where kcat = turnover number (reactions per enzyme per second), [E]total = total enzyme concentration, Vₘₐₓ = top speed
fm.v: Original Vₘₐₓ = kcat x [E] = 100 (example). New enzyme = 2 x [E]
fm.why: Each enzyme works at the same rate, so twice as many gives twice the top speed.
fm.nc: Just multiply by 2.

q6.sc: Ask: does the change affect the enzyme's shape or its amount? Amount changes Vₘₐₓ only. Shape or inhibitors can change Kₘ.
q6.trap: Assuming Kₘ changes too. Kₘ never changes with enzyme amount.
q6.plain: More cashiers means more customers served per minute (higher Vₘₐₓ). Each cashier picks up a customer just as readily as before, so how well each one grabs a customer (Kₘ) stays the same.
